Jaim_ = Jaimini; Mīmāṃsāsūtra (? = uncertain.
The Śāstradīpikā. First Chapter, First Section: The Tarka-pāda.

[I bow to] the enemy of Mura, whose chest bears the Lakṣmī and Kaustubha gems, who holds the conch, sword, and Kaumodakī mace in his hands, whose eyes are copper-red like lotus petals, who wears yellow garments, and who wields the Śārṅga bow.

With joy, I bow to Mukunda—the immortal one, the Lord of the Lordless, marked with the Śrīvatsa, the supreme beyond primordial matter (Pradhāna), possessing four noble, thick, and dark-blue arms. //1//
I shall compose the *Śāstradīpikā*, which illuminates the true meaning of the treatises obscured by the darkness of fallacious reasoning, according to the view of Kumārila.
Now, therefore, begins the inquiry into Dharma.
By this sūtra, for the sake of establishing the inclination of the listeners toward the treatise about to be commenced, the knowledge of Dharma is stated as the purpose.

For when it is said that "the inquiry into Dharma ought to be undertaken" and the treatise is seen to be beginning, it is then understood that this treatise indeed has the knowledge of Dharma as its purpose.
The purpose has indeed been understood.
Now, the connection (*saṃbandha*) of the treatise, which serves as the reason for its commencement, must also be stated;
just as in other treatises a connection such as "following a question from a disciple" is described as the introductory cause, so it should be here as well.

At the commencement of a treatise, a connection such as the sequence following a disciple's question is described as an introductory context; likewise here, at the beginning of this treatise, one of the motivating connections must be stated—by means of which connection this treatise has come into being.
Otherwise, it would be an incoherent rambling.
True.

However, in this context, it is precisely this relationship between the treatise and its purpose—namely, that of the means and the end to be accomplished—that serves as the introduction to the treatise, and nothing else.
For it is indeed the status of being a means that constitutes the motive for one who desires the goal to engage with the means.
If this relationship is understood implicitly through the very statement of the purpose, there is no fault in the fact that the author of the Sūtras did not state it separately.

In this regard, the following is considered: should one remain in the teacher’s house after the study [of the Veda] for the sake of the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), or should one return home from the teacher’s house?

For if the injunction regarding the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) prescribes study solely for the sake of Dharma, as if it were for the sake of heaven and so forth; [then one must remain].

Therefore, since the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by that alone, and because of the force of the Smṛti injunction "having studied, one should bathe," one must perform the formal return home (samāvartana).
This concludes the investigation into the injunction for study.
Now, study is enjoined for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the meaning of sentences, which arises through a succession beginning with the apprehension of syllables.
Since that [knowledge] is impossible without inquiry, inquiry is effectively enjoined by the injunction of study itself; therefore, one must remain in the teacher’s house and investigate Dharma.
In this regard: "Knowledge is obtained even without an injunction; therefore, the injunction does not have that [knowledge] as its sole purpose."
"But heaven may be postulated by the force of the injunction, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others."

Since it is already established by other means of knowledge—even without an injunction—that study is a cause for the knowledge of meaning through the medium of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of recitation (*svādhyāya*), an injunction for that purpose would be redundant.
Nor can it have the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatva*) like the injunction for threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth;
for threshing is restricted as a subordinate element (*pūrva*) to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Just as the transcendental result (*apūrva*) is accomplished only by means of rice-grains produced through the act of threshing— and not by the mere nature of the rice-grains themselves,
because that would contradict other means of valid cognition—

so too here, since knowledge is observed even without formal study, a restriction regarding its essential nature is impossible; therefore, the injunction of study must be prescribed specifically for the sake of the ritual *apūrvas*.
It might be argued that ritual acts understood through the Vedas alone are what yield results;
however, this is not correct,
because study is not for the sake of the ritual acts, as it is taught independently (*anārabhyādhīta*).
Furthermore, because there is an absence of scriptural injunctions (*śruti*) and other such means of proof, [recitation] does not serve the purpose of a ritual (*akratvartha*).

Therefore, since the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) has only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), once the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by mere recitation, one should return home from the teacher’s house. To this prima facie view, it is replied: "When a visible fruit is being obtained, there is no postulation of an unseen one."
And because the injunction serves the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyama), it will not be meaningless.

For instance, if the injunction for Vedic study did not exist, the scriptures concerning the Agnihotra and other rites, finding no learned person [to perform them], would— since performance is impossible without knowledge— implicate the acquisition of knowledge and, without distinction, would authorize all four castes. However, since the injunction for Vedic study does exist, authorization for performance belongs only to the learned members of the three higher castes, and not to the fourth caste or others.
For instance, in the injunctions, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring,
a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn," the use of the accusative case indicates that the three castes, having been consecrated by the initiation ceremony, expect: "What is to be done by us?"
Furthermore, the study (*adhyayana*) being enjoined in proximity to that [initiation], while its agent has not been specified, requires an agent.

There, by means of expectancy (*apekṣā*), proximity (*saṃnidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatva*), it is understood as follows: "The knowledge of meaning—through the sequence of grasping syllables, study, and so forth—must be accomplished by those of the three castes who have been initiated.
And thus, because it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the boy who is the agent of the fruitful study, initiation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to study.
Study (*adhyayana*) also has the purpose of knowing the meaning;
however, since the knowledge of the meaning is useful for ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), it possesses a well-known result. Thus, all [stages] possess a result.
This concludes the rule regarding the qualification for study.
And thus, when learned persons among the three higher castes are available, the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites do not imply the acquisition of knowledge by the fourth caste;

rather, they authorize only those of the three higher castes who possess such knowledge. This restriction of eligibility, which will be discussed in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, is obtained through the grace of the injunction for Vedic study; therefore, the injunction [for study] is indeed fruitful.

Therefore, since study—defined as culminating in the knowledge of meaning—is enjoined by the rule of study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), and since that [study] would be unattainable without inquiry (*vicāra*), it is established that the very injunction of study implies inquiry; thus, it sublates the bath prescribed by the Smṛti which contradicts it. Consequently, it is proven that the desire to know Dharma (*dharma-jijñāsā*) must be undertaken immediately after study.

Others, however, while accepting that study is prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), deliberate whether the purpose of study is merely the accomplishment of the status of a teacher or the knowledge of the meaning;
they conclude that it is the knowledge of the meaning because it is the more proximate factor.
But what is the reason that study is prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher?

Since the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) lacks a specific qualified agent (*adhikārin*), and since its own existence is established through the impulsion of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), it is improper to postulate a fruit [for study] as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others.
But what, then, is the injunction for becoming a teacher, and how does that injunction impel the act of study?
It is said: "But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, should teach him the Veda..."
They declare that teacher to be one who possesses both intention and laughter.
Thus, [the injunction] is inferred from the Smṛti:
"One should perform the office of a teacher by initiating and teaching"—this is the injunction for the production of a teacher.
And here, teaching is the means for attaining the status of a teacher.

The *upanayana* (initiation), however, is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of that [study] because of the suffix *-ktvā*. When the expectation arises as to by what means it assists the study, the proximity of the person being initiated (*upaneyāsatti*) is accepted as the means on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, since even the person being initiated is not an auxiliary that performs no function, he is determined to be such through his own activity.
Thus, the injunction for teaching, employing initiation—which is its own constituent part—induces study by means of that [initiation].
This is untenable;

for it is thus: it is impossible for the scripture to teach that the study [of the Veda], which has the nature of a mandate (*niyoga*), has as its purpose both the attainment of the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) and the knowledge of the meaning, because two things to be accomplished cannot coexist in one place.

If it is argued that the scripture teaches only the nature of the mandate, while the fact that it serves the purpose of knowing the meaning is merely permitted (*anujñāmātra*), even so, there would still be a duality of purposes.

Furthermore, there would be a structural inconsistency (*vairūpya*) in a single occurrence of the optative suffix (*liṅ-pratyaya*) having both the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) and the sense of permission (*anujñā*). Therefore, the doubt itself is untenable.

Likewise, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is also untenable—that because it is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the purpose of knowing the meaning does not fall within the scope of the scripture (*śāstra*).

In this regard, that very thing which we intended—the restrictive nature (*niyamārthatva*) of the injunction—which you have refuted with great effort, must now be accepted even by you, who are devoid of shame, as there is no other alternative.
Furthermore, if a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is not accepted, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) alone becomes superior;
for since the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) is not something perceived through the senses, its purposefulness is established [as a result].

Moreover, if the study were for the sake of knowing the meaning, then Vedic study would be a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) of the *svādhyāya*; however, if it were for the sake of the injunction (*niyoga*), it would be a primary ritual act (*pradhānakarma*). Thus, there would also be a discrepancy in nature (*vairūpya*).
If it is argued that the purpose is the knowledge of the meaning arising from the subject matter itself and not from the treatise,
then even the status of being a teacher would not be a purpose, since that too arises from the subject matter.

Furthermore, there would be no postponement of the ritual bath (*snāna*) by means of sublation through recollection (*smṛti*), because the inquiry would not have been accepted as part of the treatise.

In the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), there must be the postulation of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Furthermore, a person to be enjoined must be postulated here because the purpose of the injunction would otherwise be unaccounted for. Moreover, initiation (*upanayana*) does not possess the status of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) with respect to teaching (*adhyāpana*).
By the force of the second hearing, that [initiation] is a refinement of the student.
This being so, because it is internal, study is an auxiliary (aṅga) to that [Veda].
As for the claim that the injunction lacks purposefulness because of the absence of a person to be enjoined— which would contradict the act of study—
that is incorrect, because such an absence is unestablished.
For even that which is not explicitly heard [in the text] may be postulated, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others;
for the meaning of an injunction is an action to be performed (*kārya*), and this term "action to be performed" is a relative term.
For a particular thing is the effect of something specific, not of everything;
therefore, there arises a dependence on a related entity as to whose effect this is.
It must necessarily be brought about by something supplied through implication, namely: "this is his task";
he for whom this is the task is said to be the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined).
Even if its own existence were somehow to arise solely from performance prompted by another, nevertheless, its status as a "task" (kāryatva) is not established thereby;
for being a task does not consist merely in being achievable through volitional effort (kṛti).
What then? That which is achievable through volitional effort (*kṛti*) and is primary with respect to that effort is called an "effect" (*kārya*).
Primacy, moreover, consists in the fact that volitional effort proceeds toward it as its objective;
therefore, since the injunction to study (*adhyayana-niyoga*) is an effect, it must necessarily have the activity of the person as its objective.
Moreover, in the absence of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), no one would engage in action for the sake of that [unseen result].
For a boy being impelled by the injunction to teach (*adhyāpana-vidhi*) might somehow perform mere recitation, but he would not aim at the *apūrva* (the unseen potency);
for that [result] cannot be his objective, as there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for it.

The *apūrvas* of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are rightly understood to be performed by the person authorized for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices with a view toward achieving those sacrifices, because they assist the *darśapūrṇamāsa-apūrva*; thus, even though there is no direct mention of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), they attain the status of being things to be accomplished (*kāryatva*).
However, the injunction regarding Vedic study (*adhyayana-niyoga*) has no other utility through which it could be made the object of such a designation.
Furthermore, since the knowledge of the meaning depends upon an injunction because it has the restriction [of that injunction] as its fruit,
therefore, for the sake of establishing its status as something to be accomplished (*kāryatva*), an enjoined person (*niyojya*) must necessarily be postulated.

Furthermore, the claim that the injunction for teaching has the status of being the motivator for study by way of initiation (*upanayana*) is also incorrect; since there is no such motivation for initiation itself,
the motivation for study through that medium is cast far aside.

For by the *ktvā* suffix, only the identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is expressed, and from that, a single performance (*ekaprayogatā*) is inferred; however, the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) must be inferred on the basis of that single performance. By the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*), however, the status of being the principal itself is directly expressed.

Therefore, just as the threefold winding of the rope around the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is for the sake of the post itself and not for the sake of the preliminary rite (*upākaraṇa*), so too initiation (*upanayana*) is for the sake of the refinement of the student (*māṇavaka*) and not for the sake of teaching.
Furthermore, the suffix *ktvā* occurs in the Smṛti,
whereas in the direct Vedic text, "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa [should be initiated]" (*vasante brāhmaṇam*), the accusative case is used.
For this reason as well, it has the sense of "maṇavaka."

If it is argued that the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the student (*māṇavaka*), and by means of him it is an auxiliary to the desire to study (*adhyāpana*) rather than an auxiliary to the act of studying (*adhyayana*),
this is not so;
because studying is the more immediate factor (*antaraṅga*), it is logical that the rite is for the sake of that very [studying].

Since both study and teaching bear fruit, when the question arises as to which of these two is the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) for the boy and which constitutes its auxiliary (*aṅga*), it is more logical that study alone serves the purpose of the boy; for teaching, by virtue of its result residing in another person, is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

Just as, setting aside the view that study has the attainment of the status of a teacher as its purpose, one relies on the fact that study aims at the knowledge of meaning because it is intrinsic—even while overriding the Smṛti injunction "having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath" (*vedam adhītya snāyāt*)—so too here.
In the same way, it should be understood that the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) also has the purpose of study.
Even from Pāṇini’s grammar, it is understood that initiation is indeed an auxiliary to study;
for, remembering that it is an auxiliary to study, the author [Pāṇini] prescribes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *nī* in the sense of "making someone one's teacher" (*ācāryakaraṇa*).

For if [the act of teaching] were a subsidiary element (*aṅga*), then because the fruit of the action would be intended for the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be established by that very fact of there being three [initiations].

Indeed, the suffix *ktvā* in the phrase "he who, having initiated a pupil... could somehow be justified—even in the absence of a relationship between principal and subsidiary—as in the case of "having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices..."; however, a further injunction of the middle voice would be utterly redundant.
Therefore, initiation must be an auxiliary element of Vedic study.
It would not [be so].
For the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [perception] inheres in the boy (*māṇavaka*).
True; yet, although it inheres in the boy, it does not have him as its object.
Furthermore, the "intendedness for the agent" (*kartr-abhiprāyatva*) of the fruit consists in its being intended by the agent, and not in its inherence (*samavāya*) within that agent;

otherwise, the *ātmanepada* ending in the injunction "one should establish the sacred fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*) would not occur, because the fruit of the establishment—such as the status of being an *āhavanīya* fire—inheres in the fire and thus lacks inherence in the agent. And this is the traditional rule (*smṛti*): "But he who, having initiated a pupil... (*upanīya tu yaḥ śiṣyam*).
Therefore, the second scriptural statement (śruti) is more powerful;
consequently, initiation (upanayana) is not a subordinate part (aṅga) of teaching, and thus there is no impulsion (prayukti) of teaching by way of that [initiation].
Regarding the refutation of the Prābhākara view:

as for the claim that "when there is a requirement for an operation on the part of the [subject] brought forward (*upanīta*), the study (*adhyayana*) enjoined in connection with that bringing forward is determined to be that very operation," this too is the result of a lack of reflection; for by speaking thus, it is effectively established that study is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of teaching (*adhyāpana*).

For when, with respect to the initiated boy (*māṇavaka*) for whom teaching is the purpose, there arises a requirement for an activity conducive to that [purpose], the injunction for study prescribes study as an activity conducive to it— namely, "the activity of study must be performed by the three castes who have been initiated and who require an activity conducive to teaching"—
even then, it clearly prescribes study for the purpose of knowing the meaning, not as being merely conducive to teaching.
For in that case, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the study's suitability for that [purpose] understood?
For perception and the other means of knowledge do not operate here.
If it is argued that it is "due to proximity" (*saṃnidhānāt*), [we reply:]...

Proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is not itself an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Rather, for a word that is conveying its meaning, proximity is merely a requirement—along with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic competency (*yogyatā*)—just as the opening of the eyes is for the eye.
If the word were to enjoin [the study] solely for the sake of teaching (*adhyāpana*), then the purpose of knowing the meaning would not be established.

Therefore, it is not possible for the study enjoined by the rule "one's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*) to be prompted by the injunction for teaching through the medium of initiation (*upanayana*), simply because of the proximity [of the two rules].

If it is argued that because teaching is impossible without study, the study for that purpose is implied, even so, since that [teaching] can be accomplished through unenjoined worldly study, there is no mandatory application of the enjoined study. Nor does one rely on the enjoined [study] merely for the sake of parsimony in the application [of effort].
Even if one subsists upon that [study], there is no loss of the application [of the injunction];
for in your view, even though study is enjoined, it is applied solely by the injunction to teach (*adhyāpana-vidhi*) and not by its own injunction.
Therefore, the injunction to teach would merely imply a worldly study for those who have been initiated (*upanīta*).
Study prescribed by rule, in the absence of being prompted by another, establishes one's entitlement [to the fruit].

Furthermore, if initiation (*upanayana*) were a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of teaching (*adhyāpana*), then the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), being intended for the purpose of knowing the meaning, would be connected with the members of the three higher castes who have been initiated for the sake of teaching.

In that case, it would follow that those members of the three castes who have been initiated for the sake of teaching—and who require an activity useful for that purpose—would study for the sake of knowing the meaning; this would be utterly incoherent.

Consequently, since the injunction for study would not be connected with those who have been initiated [for teaching], it would apply to all four castes, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that Śūdras would be entitled to perform Vedic study.

Therefore, for those who have been initiated and who stand in need of a purpose, the cultivation of the knowledge of the meaning—having study as its instrument—is enjoined; thus, initiation is indeed a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of study, and study is impelled by its own injunction.
This position has been refuted at length in the *Nyāyaratnamālā*, so we shall not pursue it further.

Therefore, the inquiry remains as previously stated: is study for the sake of an unseen result (adṛṣṭārtha), or is it for the sake of knowing the meaning through the successive stages beginning with the grasping of the syllables?
This is the conclusion regarding the injunction for Vedic study.
Alternatively, nothing further need be deliberated here,

since it is established by the logic of the ninth book (*navamika-nyāya*) that the purpose of Vedic study— through the successive stages of phonetic refinement and so forth— is the knowledge of the meaning.

For in the ninth [book], it will be stated that because the Sāmans are seen to be useful for praise by means of manifesting the syllables of the Ṛks, they serve that very purpose and not an unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose;

by that same logic, since the fact that study has the purpose of knowing the meaning is established, it is already proven that the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) must be undertaken immediately after study. With the intention of stating this specific purpose, the author of the Sūtras says what they have said:
"In order to state the subject matter called Dharma, the purpose of Mīmāṃsā [is stated]."
But surely, some meaning of the Vedic sentences is being investigated here.

To this they say: “Nor is there here an explanation of the *codanā* (Vedic injunction), for that was addressed [in the first chapter] as being too extensive. Thus it is established that after the study [of the Vedas], the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken.
And that [inquiry] is fourfold: by way of the nature of Dharma, its means of knowledge, its instruments, and its results.

But surely, since the injunction for study (adhyayana-vidhi) only necessitates an inquiry into the meaning of the Vedic sentences, what occasion is there for an inquiry into the nature of Dharma and its means of valid cognition? It is said: the occasion arises because it is an introductory topic (upoddhāta). For if Dharma were the meaning of the Vedic sentences and the Veda were the means of valid cognition, then that inquiry would indeed have to be undertaken.

Otherwise, it would be like an investigation into the teeth of a crow; therefore, the injunction to study [the Vedas] itself implies the inquiry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the mention of "dharma" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), because *adharma* is also to be investigated for the purpose of its abandonment.
Alternatively, by eliding the vowel 'a', the Sūtra may also be explained as referring to the desire to know what is non-dharma; thus, it is faultless.
Dharma is a purposeful object characterized by Vedic injunction.

First of all, by means of this Sūtra, two things are determined through both the literal expression and its implied meaning: what Dharma is, and what its characteristic is. That which is Dharma is characterized by *codanā* (injunction);
injunction alone is its characteristic—that is, its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And injunction alone is its characteristic; thus, by the literal expression, the prescription of the means of valid cognition is established, and by implication, it is established that Dharma consists only of such acts as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, which are accessible through injunction, and not such acts as the worship of a shrine (*caityavandana*), which do not have that characteristic. In this way, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is also established.

Likewise, it should be understood that when the definition "Dharma is that which is characterized by an injunction" is prescribed as its essential nature, the establishment of its object and its means of valid cognition is thereby accomplished.
Someone says: by this sūtra it is stated that the meaning of the Veda is of the nature of something to be accomplished (kārya) and not of the nature of an already established entity (siddha);
for by the term *codanā-lakṣaṇa* "that which is characterized by an injunction" the thing to be accomplished is expressed, and by the word *dharma* the meaning of the Veda is expressed.

That is incorrect. First, as for those sentences that are injunctive (*vidhi-vākya*), their authority lies solely in the injunction itself, and it is perfectly clear that they lack authority regarding the actual nature of things; thus, there is nothing further to be said on that point.
Furthermore, even sentences such as "the swiftest" (*kṣepiṣṭha*) possess authority only within the context of the injunction, as they form a single syntactical unit with it.

As for the mantras, their status as subordinate elements to the primary injunctions by virtue of the *prakaraṇa* (context) will be explained in the second chapter (*dvitīya-pāda*); therefore, there is likewise nothing to be said regarding them.

If it is argued that, having set aside the status of these as *siddhārtha* (statements of established fact), they are instead said to have the status of *kāryārtha* (statements of what is to be done)—
referring to Upaniṣadic passages such as "This Self, indeed, is indestructible"— we say no.
For if even those possess the character of being syntactically unified with an injunction (*vidhi*), then they are already accounted for by the section concerning *arthavāda* (explanatory passages).
Now, if they do not exist, how could they have the status of being objects of purposeful action?

Now, since there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with other injunctions due to the non-hearing of an injunction regarding their performance, and because it is impossible for them to have a purposeful action as their object and because they lack the capacity for linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), it is intended that they possess no authority (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding the meaning of the *sigaddhi* (the ritual act).
Is this Sūtra now intended to establish the lack of authority for sentences concerning the Self (*ātman*) and so forth?
Then it is well said: at the very commencement of the treatise, the author of the Sūtras first establishes the lack of authority of Vedic sentences!
And how is it that validity belongs only to the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished)?

If it is argued: "Because linguistic mastery (*vyutpatti*) occurs precisely with respect to that; for linguistic mastery depends upon purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), and since that activity depends upon the comprehension of the *kārya*, linguistic mastery also occurs only with respect to that."

Acquisition of linguistic competence (*vyutpatti*) is necessarily dependent upon usage; for even in present-tense statements such as "He cooks rice in a pot with firewood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ sthālyām odanaṃ pacati*), one observes that persons who are already familiar with the meaning of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyārtha*) acquire competence regarding the meaning of the nominal stem *kāṣṭha* (firewood), which is unfamiliar to them. This constitutes the primary acquisition of linguistic competence.

Now, if it is argued that initial linguistic acquisition occurs only through specific effects— for at that time, the acquisition of the meaning of one word by means of another word is impossible because every property [of the object] remains unestablished—
let it be so.

Nevertheless, since we observe the frequent subsequent use of words for accomplished entities (*siddhārtha*) in questions, answers, and so forth—such as "Who is this king? or "The Pāñcāla"—and because the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished) is subject to deviation, it is well understood that what is denoted must be the non-deviating entity-in-itself (*arthamātra*).
For just as, when one first observes the use of the word "cow" (*go*) with respect to a certain individual, one understands that very individual to be the denotatum; so too here.
Even though there is a subsequent usage of other words, because that contradicts the previous usage, it is determined that the meaning is indeed the non-deviating universal (*sāmānya*);

likewise, although the dependence on an action (*kārya*) was understood, since this is sublated by the observation of subsequent usage for established facts (*siddha-artha*), it is logical that the meaning alone—which is non-deviating—is what is expressed.

Furthermore, at the time of the first acquisition of linguistic competence (*vyutpatti*), the fact that only a few words have an action as their meaning is understood, not all words; there is no fixed rule of priority and sequence.

Therefore, when all words are subsequently derived [by etymology], some may become established as having fixed meanings (*siddhārtha*). However, if all words were restricted to denoting only what is to be accomplished (*kāryārthatva*), then in ordinary worldly sentences that primarily concern established facts (*siddhārtha*), every word would be merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*); consequently, no word at all would be capable of expressing a related meaning (*anvitābhidhāyin*).
In that case, how could the cognition of a related meaning be established?
The speaker’s cognition must be inferred;
however, since the sentence uttered does not itself convey the related meaning (*anvita*), how can there be an inference of the cognition of that related meaning?
If it is argued that the cognition of the related [meaning] is inferred by means of words that cause the recollection of the nature of the objects [denoted],
then, because this is unestablished even in the case of a word expressive of an action (*kārya*), there would be no expression of the related [meaning].
Furthermore, the deviation from the action can be understood right from the very first instance.

For when a bystander observes the facial expression of someone who has been told, "A son has been born to you," he infers that the word has communicated a cause for joy; thus, he postulates the capacity of the word to convey a fact that serves as a cause for joy.

And although at that time the specific nature of the object is not known—since there are many possible causes for joy—nevertheless, the fact that it conveys an established fact (*siddhārthatā*) is nonetheless understood.
Even by that much, deviation regarding the effect is established.
Furthermore, since such verbal usage occurs only when a son is born many times, and not in other causes of joy, the specific object consisting of the birth of a son is indeed easily known.
Furthermore, even linguistic acquisition dependent upon activity does not necessarily concern only the object of an action to be performed;

for instance, when someone utters the sentence "There are five fruits on the riverbank" for the sake of diverting an elderly person or a sick person who is utterly incapable of acting, another person who happens to be there and is in need hears that sentence in its actual sense.
Having gone to the riverbank, he gathers fruits;
observing all this, another person who seeks to acquire linguistic proficiency learns the capacity of words to convey the actual existence of things.
Therefore, it is not the case that words have exclusively a purposive (injunctive) meaning.
This is a refutation of the meaning of the second sūtra as interpreted by the Prābhākara school.
Furthermore, what is the verbal formulation (*vacanavyakti*) of this sūtra?

If, first of all, it is formulated such that "whatever is a ritual action (*kārya*), that alone is the subject matter of the Veda (*vedārtha*)," whereby the status of being the Vedic subject matter is enjoined with reference to ritual action;

If that were the case, because there would be a restriction of the accent by the relationship between the subject (uddeśya) and the predicate (upādeya), even every worldly activity such as bringing a cow would become a matter of Vedic meaning.
Furthermore, since the predicate—which is the Vedic meaning—is not pervaded by the subject—such as smoke—the validity of the Veda would be discarded even with respect to what is not its effect.

Now, if it were the case that "the meaning of the Veda consists solely of that which is of the nature of an action to be performed," then the formulation would have to be: "That which is Dharma is characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇa*).
In that case, the word *artha*, signifying prosperity (*abhyudaya*), would be a qualifier of what?

If [the term "object"] refers to that which is to be undertaken—an entity characterized by an injunction—then it would follow that the entire meaning of the Veda is both an action (*kāryatva*) and an object (*arthatva*); consequently, even the injunctions for the Śyena sacrifice and others would possess the status of being objects.

Now, if the qualification "the specific meaning of the Veda" is intended as the subject, then the following sense results: that which constitutes the meaning of the Veda, being of the nature of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), is of the nature of what is to be done (*kārya*);
consequently, injunctions such as the Śyena sacrifice—which, having prohibited fruits, are not of the nature of prosperity—would lack the status of being what is to be done.
If it is argued that this should not be so,
[we reply] that since even those [acts] are understood to have the nature of being effects (*kāryatā*),
the effect-nature of the Śyena sacrifice can indeed be precluded, but not that of the *niyoga*.
Because that [Vedic sentence] has the nature of having action as its sole essence;

and if it were not an action, then since the Śyena-sentence would lack the status of having action as its meaning, it would have to be declared to have a merely established fact (siddha-artha) as its meaning,
which is not possible because of its connection with an injunctive suffix (vidhi-pratyaya).

Furthermore, since the goal has already been accomplished, the sentences concerning the Śyena sacrifice and so forth would lack the capacity for linguistic derivation and thus would necessarily be non-authoritative.

Now, if one were to take the word *dharma* from the preceding sūtra as referring to the subject matter of the Veda (*vedārtha*), and thus form two separate statements— "The subject matter of the Veda is characterized by injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo vedārthaḥ*) and "Dharma is the [Vedic] subject matter" (*artho dharmaḥ*)—
this would be nothing more than a mere display of one's own ingenuity.

Because one would have to resort to [the faults of] prolixity and syntactical split without any purpose, and because it is improper to provide a definition for a property that has not been previously proposed as the subject of inquiry.
Now, in order to establish that the very object of the Veda which has been promised is something to be accomplished (*kārya*), its status as *dharma* is stated.

[The opponent asks: Is it the case that only that which is to be accomplished constitutes the nature of *dharma* as the object of the Veda, and that alone is what is to be investigated, and nothing else?

If so, then by destroying the words of the Sūtra, the investigation would be promised for that *dharma* alone which is to be investigated; thus, the statement promising the object of the Veda would be rendered meaningless.

Now, if one were to disregard the word "artha" and claim that whatever is the meaning of the Veda is of the nature of something to be done (*kārya*), then the word "artha" would be redundant; it would merely be a synonym for "thing-in-general" (*vastumātra*) and a tautological restatement.
Furthermore, its purpose as an exclusion of what is useless (*anartha*) has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya;
therefore, this [word] is indeed a qualification.

Furthermore, if [the injunction] were merely a qualifier, then because the meaning of the Veda consisting of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) would be designated as something to be accomplished (*kārya*), that which consists of non-prosperity—the meaning of the Upanishads (*vāda*)—would not be something to be accomplished; consequently, the authority of the entire Veda would be undermined, and thus the *niyoga* (mandatory injunction) could not exist.
Therefore, one must not deny that such passages as "This Self, indeed, is indestructible" are intended to establish the nature of the Self; let this matter rest for now.
Therefore, this sūtra is intended solely for the purpose of establishing the nature and the means of valid cognition regarding dharmas.
Therefore, taking *dharma* as the subject here, it is considered: is there no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this [dharma] at all;
or is it only perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of knowledge] that are the means of valid cognition; or is it only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)?
Alternatively, there is the option of disjunction (*vikalpa*) or the option of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

In that regard, one position is that *dharma* lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), because verbal testimony (*śabda*)— as it conveys what has already been established by other means of knowledge— is not itself a means of valid cognition, and because perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of knowledge] lack the capacity [to apprehend it].
One position is that [the object] is accessible solely through perception and other such means;
another is that it is accessible through the perception of yogins, whereas for those of limited vision, it is accessible only through scriptural injunction (*codanā*).

By the presumption (*arthāpatti*) based on the diversity of the world, it is established in a general sense that some unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) exists; this *dharma* is then understood through Vedic injunction (*codanā*) in its specific forms such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice. Therefore, there is another position [of the opponent] that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) [of these two means].
The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the injunction alone is the authority and that it is indeed the authority.
Thus, in this context, a double restriction is asserted: "The injunction alone is the authority" and "it is indeed the authority."
This is a summary of the subject matter to be established in the first chapter.

However, in the *Nimitta-sūtra*, by considering only the first and second sūtras, there might arise the suspicion that this is a treatise of instruction (*upadeśa-śāstra*), similar to statements such as "the Veda is the root of Dharma. Therefore, in order to make it known that this is indeed a treatise of investigation (*parīkṣā-śāstra*), the formal proposition of investigation (*parīkṣā-pratijñā*) is stated.

Although the status of this work as a treatise on critical examination (*parīkṣāśāstra*) is understood from its subsequent operations alone, nevertheless, that which is about to be stated is mentioned here for the sake of focusing the minds of the listeners. //***//

In the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*, however, because perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists in the apprehension of what is presently existing, it lacks the capacity for authority regarding *dharma*; since the other means of knowledge are also devoid of authority because they are preceded by that [perception], and because the restrictive, alternative, or cumulative application of other means of knowledge has been refuted, the meaning "codana alone" is established.

In the *Autpattika-sūtra*, however, it is established that intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) exists, while invalidity arises from either the cognition of the object being otherwise than it is or from the cognition of defects in its cause; thus, since an indubitable cognition arises from the injunctions regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites, their intrinsic validity is attained. Furthermore, there is no direct cognition of the object being otherwise that could serve as a sublater (*apavādaka*).
Nor is there knowledge of defects in the cause [of the Veda], because verbal defects reside in persons;

and since the relationship between words and their meanings is non-artificial, there is no entry of persons into the Vedic injunctions by way of that [relationship]. Thus it stands, being fully established.
Let it not be that there is human intervention by way of the relationship between words and their referents;

however, since no such relationship is observed in the world between a sentence and its meaning, the cognition of the meaning of sentences such as "the agnihotra sacrifice" must be either baseless and thus a delusion,
or merely conventional.

Therefore, having raised the objection that the Veda lacks authority regarding the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), it is established by the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that its authority with respect to the sentence-meaning is indeed possible, provided that the words do not depend upon the apprehension of the relation between word-meanings or upon convention (*samaya*).

Furthermore, since the Vedas consist of sentences and are designated by names such as *Kāṭhaka* and so forth, one might suspect they are of human origin and thus tainted by defects through that medium.

However, because their author—though he would have to be remembered if he existed—is not remembered, and is thus ruled out by the non-perception of a perceptible object (*yogyānupalabdhi*), it is impossible to infer such an author.

Moreover, since the designations are based on the act of recitation (*pravacana*), the Vedas are not of human origin; thus, the authority of the *codanās*, which are parts thereof, is established. Such is the argument.
The first pāda in its entirety is an elaboration (parikara) of the meaning promised in the *Codanāsūtra* by means of establishing that very point.
This summary of the contents of the pāda has been presented according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra;
however, we shall subsequently present the opinion of the Vṛttikāra.
The fact that Dharma is accessible through means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth.
Let us return to the subject at hand: it was asserted that injunction alone is the authority [for Dharma], and that it is indeed authoritative.
Now, one might object: since the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge is possible independently of anything else, they themselves should possess authority regarding Dharma.
"But since verbal testimony always has as its object that which is already cognized by another means of knowledge, its validity cannot possibly be independent of such [other] means.
To this it is replied:
"First of all, perception, because it has a conjoined object and thus apprehends only what is presently existing, is not capable [of apprehending] dharma, which is yet to come."
Although there are substances such as the *godohana* vessel,
actions such as sacrifice,
and qualities such as being low-voiced, and so forth—

It will be stated in the *Śreyaskara-bhāṣya* that [the Veda] is called by the word "dharma" because it is the means of accomplishing the fruit (*phala-sādhana*), and not because of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) and so forth;

nevertheless, since those [means] constitute dharma only insofar as they are the means of accomplishing the fruit, and since the fruit occurs in another birth and so on, it is impossible for dharma to be an object of perception in its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Furthermore, because inference and other means of knowledge are preceded by perception, they too cannot be valid authorities regarding it.
The notion that yogic perception, born from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), will be capable even regarding future phenomena is mere wishful thinking.
For cultivation produces a memory in the form of a certainty only with respect to objects already experienced;
and it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in this case, precisely because it is a memory.
It is absolutely not perception because it is not produced by the sense faculties (*anindriyajātva*).

If you argue that being produced by the sense faculties is not the definition of perception, but rather being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*), then all the more so is *dharma* imperceptible, since it is impossible to apprehend it non-conceptually in its form as the means to the fruit (*phalasādhana*).
Therefore, perception is signless;
and because it is preceded by that, inference and the other means of knowledge are also [signless].
The Kāśyapīyas, moreover, say that the dharma of the sages proceeds from intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*);
however, because that [intuitive knowledge] arises from fallacious signs and the like, it is not even a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), much less regarding the dharma.
But since verbal testimony (*śabda*) generates cognition, its validity is appropriate provided there is no sublation.
Is it not the case that validity cannot be established merely from the production of a cognition, since even sentences that do not correspond to reality produce cognitions without distinction?
True;
however, in those cases, invalidity is rightly established by means of defects in the cause and by sublating cognitions.
Since that [validity] is known from its very existence, its status as a means of valid cognition is established as unrefuted.
Now begins the investigation into the nature of validity.
How, then, is the validity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) attained intrinsically?

To that end, this is considered with reference to all cognitions: are both validity and invalidity understood intrinsically, or is either of them—being undefined by its own nature—understood through the cognition of the excellence or defect of its causes?

Alternatively, is it that invalidity is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*), while validity— having been initially attained intrinsically— is subsequently sublated by invalidity which is itself apprehended through the cognition of a discrepancy in the object or the cognition of defects in its causes?

Regarding this, some maintain that since the capacity of all causes for their respective effects is inherent (*svābhāvikatva*), both [validity and invalidity] are apprehended from the very nature of the cognition itself.
That is incorrect; for knowledge cannot simultaneously cognize both the suchness and the non-suchness of its own object, due to contradiction.

Now, if it is argued that one particular cognition makes its own validity known intrinsically (*svataḥ*), while another makes its invalidity known [intrinsically], even so, this is not tenable. For if cognition itself, independent of any other cause, is the means for the apprehension [of its own status], it is impossible to distinguish which [status] occurs in which specific cognition.

Therefore, others maintain that both [the object and the cognition] are undetermined by their own intrinsic nature, and are understood through the knowledge of the qualities and defects of their causes.
This too is unsatisfactory;

for in this way, prior to the ascertainment of qualities and defects, a cognition that does not make the object known through even one of its aspects would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Therefore, it is only logical that invalidity is intrinsic, whereas validity arises from factors such as corroborating cognition.
This is the demonstration of the reasoning:

for it is not logical that the determination of the reality of an object follows merely from the arising of a cognition, because of the possibility of error and the lack of certainty; rather, at that moment, non-validity itself would result, which is subsequently set aside by the cognition of the excellence of the causes or by the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), through which validity is understood.
Furthermore, being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) is a quality in the case of verbal testimony;
however, this is absent in the Veda because its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) is accepted.
This is because such passages as "The Vasus performed a sacrificial session" and "Listen, O pressing-stones," are like the ravings of a madman.

When it is argued that the Vedas possess no authority at all because they were composed by those who are not more reliable [than others], the following is stated: The status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) never attains its own nature if it depends upon something else.

For who indeed would adopt a position that destroys its very root? If every cognition were itself incapable of determining the reality of its object and required another cognition for that purpose, then even the cognitions of the excellence of the causes, of corroboration, and of successful practical efficacy (*arthakriyājñāna*)— [...would likewise require further cognitions ad infinitum.]

If [the senses] were to depend on another for the ascertainment of the qualities and so forth that constitute their own objects, and that other [cognition] likewise depended on yet another, then no object whatsoever would be determined even in a thousand lifetimes; thus, the very status of being a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) would perish.
Now, if it is argued that "the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) is intrinsically valid" (*svataḥpramāṇa*), what is the distinction?
If it is argued that there is no deviation [from the rule], we say no;
for even in the state of dreaming, one observes a cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) despite the absence of the actual fetching of water.

Now, if it is argued that the very cognition of pleasure is itself the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and that this is indeed non-erroneous— since there is never a cognition of pleasure when pleasure is absent—
this is true; however,
by means of that [subsequent cognition], it is not possible to determine the validity of the preceding cognition.

Since pleasure is observed even in the state of dreaming through the cognition of union with a beloved—though that cognition is not a valid means of knowledge—it must necessarily be accepted that intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is set aside by two factors: the cognition that the object is otherwise than it appears (*arthānyathātva-jñāna*) and the cognition of defects in the cause (*kāraṇa-doṣa-jñāna*).

And thus, because defects arise from contact with a trustworthy person (*āpta-puruṣa*), their absence in the impersonal Veda results in its validity being unassailable; furthermore, since there is no direct cognition that the object is otherwise than it appears, its validity remains unsublated.

Human statements, however, because they originate from human intellect, are employed through error or a desire to deceive; thus, being corrupted by a fundamental defect, they are non-conformable with reality—this constitutes the difference.
Some say: "Even in the world, there is no non-conformity of words with reality, for such [non-conformity] does not exist;
indeed, there is no verbal means of valid cognition (*śābdapramāṇa*) in the world, since human utterances merely lead to an inference of the speaker's intention."
Therefore, this deviation belongs only to inference and not to verbal testimony;
nor does verbal testimony itself function as a sign when it is not a sign, due to the failure to grasp the distinction between them.
However, if this deviation were instead admitted to belong to verbal testimony alone, [then the following would apply].
Validity would be inherent;
for a word does not incur a defect through a defect in the person, since the person's function consists merely in the manifestation of the word as it actually exists.
This is without substance.
If verbal testimony does not exist in the world, how could it exist in the Veda?

For it has been stated in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* that there is no evidence for the denotative power (*vācakatva*) of a word toward its meaning when that power is exhausted by the inference of [the speaker's] intention.
And as for the argument that if deviation (*vyabhicāra*) were admitted, there would be intrinsic invalidity (*svābhāvikam aprāmāṇyam*) because human defects do not enter into the word—
this might be so if the person who utters a sentence were the one to manifest it;
but that is not the case.
By that very [person], the phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*) are made eternal;
however, sentences (*vākya*) are indeed created by persons, precisely because they are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
If they were manifested exactly as they exist, they would be non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), just like Vedic sentences.
Furthermore, there would be no inference of the speaker's intention either;
just as Vedic sentences manifested by reciters do not indicate the intentions of those reciters, so too human statements would not indicate them.
For if it is argued that the validity of a word in the world is impossible due to the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), [then this consequence follows].
In that case, the same applies even to the inference of the speaker’s intention;
for we observe the composition of a sentence in one way even by someone who does not intend it otherwise.

Furthermore, because a word brings about cognition through its own inherent capacity—just like the eye and other sense organs—it does not lose its power to signify even when there is deviation [from the actual state of things].
Since only a non-deviant indicator (liṅga) possesses the capacity to convey [the object], it is logically established that a deviant one is not a valid indicator.
Alternatively, if it is argued that inference is employed to dispel the suspicion of deviation based on the speaker’s reliability,
then in that case, let verbal testimony itself be the means of valid cognition regarding the object, since the obstructing suspicion has been removed.
For one who wishes to infer a particular state of mind must necessarily first perceive the word-meanings and reflect upon their mutual compatibility and syntactic connection.
When these [words] are being reflected upon, they cause the meaning of the sentence to be understood immediately; thus, they do not depend upon inference.

Furthermore, it is your established doctrine that a sentence, acting as a subsequent restatement (*anuvāda*) after a specific cognition has been inferred, brings about the understanding of the sentence-meaning; consequently, one must admit that when a person is indeed perceived as untrustworthy, a cognition that is non-conformable to reality (*ayathārtha*) arises from their sentence. And since invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is dependent upon defects, and since you do not admit the transference of the speaker’s defects into the word, [invalidity] would be inherent in the word itself.
Let us set aside for now the objection that the Veda would be forced into a state of invalidity by its being rendered defective;

therefore, since invalidity occurs only in the case of the words of untrustworthy persons because it is dependent upon defects in the speaker, and since such defects are absent in the Veda, its validity must indeed be affirmed.
Consequently, the meaning is that Dharma, which brings about the highest good, is characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (codanā).

In common worldly usage, that alone which takes the form of a means to the highest good—such as sacrifice, oblation, and so forth—is called *dharma*; it is not the *apūrva* (unseen potency) or the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because these lack worldly renown.
An Investigation into the Characteristics of Phenomena.
[Objection: Is it not the case that only the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is the means to the highest good (*śreyas*)? [Reply: No, because it is merely an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
Therefore, sacrifice and the like alone are *dharma* by virtue of being the means to the highest good.
And because that [specific] form is absent, there is no occurrence of *dharma*-status for what is performed by a Śūdra.
The word "purpose" (*artha*) qualifies [the definition] so that *dharma*-status might not belong to anything merely characterized by an injunction (*codanā*).

Furthermore, by the word *codanā*, both an injunction that impels one to action and a prohibition that restrains one from action are expressed. Consequently, even acts such as killing—which are characterized as "non-beneficial" (*anartha*) by prohibitive statements such as "one should not kill"—would [erroneously] possess the nature of *dharma*. To exclude this, the inclusion of the term "beneficial" (*artha*) is intended to state that only that which is characterized as beneficial by impelling injunctions possesses the nature of *dharma*.

And in the Bhāṣya, the mention of the Śyena sacrifice and others is for the purpose of indicating the injury and so forth accomplished by them; for it will be explained later that "that [sacrifice] is indeed injury, and that is prohibited."
However, some, avoiding the [indirect] indication (lakṣaṇā), consider that the very nature of the hawk-sacrifice and so forth is what is excluded by the word "artha";

for them, it is understood that the hawk-sacrifices and so on are themselves to be performed, since they establish that these are objects of prohibition by negating their status as things to be enjoined.
But how is their status as "that which is to be enjoined" (vidheya) refuted?
To this they say: For that for which an injunction implies performance because it cannot otherwise be established in its own right is called "that which is to be enjoined.

And in the case of optional rites (kāmya-karma), since engagement is already established by the force of desire itself, the injunction—being accomplished through that very [desire]—does not imply performance on its own, as there is no lack of establishment otherwise.
But surely, instigation (*pravartana*) is nothing other than the communication of "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*),

and since the status of sacrifice as "what ought to be done" has been communicated in the Veda even without [an explicit injunctive suffix], how can it lack the character of being an injunction (*avidheyatva*)?
True.
But it is not the performability of the sacrifice that is denoted by the optative suffix;
rather, it is the performability of its own meaning [the sacrifice] that is denoted by the optative suffix.
The sacrifice is its object and its instrument;

thus, this meaning of the *niyoga* (the mandate), which consists in the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*), is called "that which impels performance" because, by the principle of inexplicability otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), it makes known the state of being something to be done for its own object.

However, since the performance of the *Śyena* and other such rites is already established through passion (*rāga*) alone, the *niyoga* does not necessitate their performance; therefore, they do not possess the status of being things to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

And since, in the absence of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), they would be objects of prohibition and thus constitute what is harmful (*anartha*), the word "beneficial" (*artha*) is included for the purpose of excluding them.

In this regard, the following must be stated: in what respect does their exclusion occur? If it is argued that it is in the sense of being a *dharma*, we say no; for their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) has not been specified.

For this Sūtra is intended to establish that the meaning of the Veda consists of what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), and not to define the essential nature of ritual acts (*karman*). Since it is necessary to prevent the misconception that rites such as the Śyena sacrifice are themselves *dharma*, the word "artha" (meaning/purpose) serves to exclude them.
If, at best, there were an exclusion of "being an effect" (kāryatva), that too has been shown previously to be untenable.
Or, let us grant that the Sūtra is intended to define dharma by accepting a split in the sentence;
even so, it is your view that, by means of the term *codanālakṣaṇa*, the apūrva—which consists of an effect—is indicated, and its status as dharma is then predicated of it.
In that case, what relevance would there be for sacrifices such as the Śyena, for the sake of whose exclusion the word "artha" (purposeful) would be required?
For even sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma do not possess the nature of *dharma*, since it is accepted that only the *apūrva* (unseen potency) possesses the nature of *dharma*.

Now, if by the word *artha* (purpose) the status of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the Śyena sacrifice and others as being *dharma* is excluded, then the Bhāṣya’s statement that "the *apūrva* accomplished by that [sacrifice] is indicated by the term 'Śyena' and so on, which is the name of the ritual action" would involve an indistinctive indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, if the *apūrva* itself were the counter-example, then the Bhāṣya passage "for that is violence, and it is prohibited" would be inconsistent.

Is the Śyena sacrifice itself, or its fruit, the act of violence? Certainly not the *apūrva* (unseen potency), for that can in no way be the locus of the term "violence. And if this [latter] alternative is accepted, how could it be objected that this [violence], being an evil, is taught as something to be performed? This is the challenge.
Furthermore, the response that "the hawk-sacrifice and others are not understood as things to be performed" would concern the *apūrva* (the unseen potency);
yet its status as something to be performed cannot be denied, because its very nature is that of an effect (*kārya*).

And thus, if one accepts this Bhāṣya as being for the purpose of negating the necessity of performing the sacrifice, and then strives to resolve that [objection] by saying, "The injunction (niyoga) has the necessity [of the act] as its object, but it does not state the necessity of that [act] itself," then that is pointless;
for even in the case of optional rites (kāmya), it is the injunction alone that is the motivator, not the fruit.
Since that [result] arises as dependent upon an injunction, it has no requirement for a sacrifice;
however, since the injunction itself achieves its fulfillment through dependence on the sacrifice, it is logical that it enjoins the performance of the sacrifice.

Even in the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*), it is the injunction (*vidhi*) alone that is the motivator. For if the injunction were not the motivator in optional rites, even the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would not be subject to injunction; this is because the performance of that procedure is already established by the very fact of the result, since the fruit is accomplished through the principal rite together with its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
For [the author] will say: "But when [an act] is joined with that [prohibition], there is the hearing of a fruit; therefore, there is a desire to perform everything [including prohibited acts].

Consequently, since even the killing in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice would fall within the scope of prohibition due to the absence of an injunction [for it], the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice joined with that [killing] would also result in being an evil (anartha). Thus, the [Bhāṣya's] statement—"What is the purpose [of the Veda] which is for the sake of the highest good (niḥśreyasa), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth?"—would be untenable.

Now, it might be argued that the prohibition "one must not kill" is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha) because it is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*); therefore, by this [prohibition], only those acts of killing intended for the person should be prohibited.
For if it were a prohibition intended for the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then that [prohibition] itself would become a part of the sacrifice.

However, if there were no distinction, there would be a defect of inconsistency (*vairūpya*) in a single prohibitory injunction, as it would result in being both for the sake of the sacrifice and for the sake of the person.
Therefore, it is indeed only those acts of violence that serve human purposes which are prohibited here, not those that serve the purpose of the sacrifice.
This is a delusion of the ignorant.
For even in the absence of a qualification, there is no structural inconsistency (*vairūpya*) in a prohibition.

If, indeed, the prohibition were made by specifically designating the two forms—being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—then there might be such inconsistency, because the prohibition would then have as its domain both the sacrifice and the person as presented by the objects of the prohibition.
For when a prohibition is made with reference to violence in general, what inconsistency is there in this?

For example, although the prohibition applies without distinction to both types of violence— the violence involved in producing meat for the sake of food and that which is a direct human purpose for the sake of avenging an enemy— there is no difference between them [regarding the prohibition].
There is a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) here as well;

otherwise, there would be a lack of uniformity because the prohibition would then have both the status of being a subordinate part of a ritual (*bhojanāṅgatā*) and the status of being for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārthatā*).
Therefore, whatever violence is occasioned by any means whatsoever, all of that is prohibited in a general sense.
Furthermore, the prohibition pertains to human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) because it is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*).

Therefore, even the killing of the Agniṣomīya animal would fall within the scope of the prohibition in the absence of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). However, if there is a mandatory injunction, since that injunction has a specific object, the general prohibition—due to its conflict with that injunction—applies to other instances of killing.
Regarding violence, there is the Sāṃkhya position and its refutation:

[The opponent objects,] "Even though [the injunction to sacrifice] is something to be performed, since the injunction serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*) while the prohibition serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), there is no contradiction because their spheres of application differ; thus, there is no sublation [of one by the other].
For it is not contradictory that the ritual must involve violence, while for the person it must be avoided."
True;
there is no contradiction when considering the injunction regarding the subsidiary parts alone.

However, the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma, enjoining the principal rite along with its subsidiaries for the sake of the person, precludes the prohibition of non-violence—which serves the purpose of the person—from applying to the violence involved in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
For the Jyotiṣṭoma cannot be performed by one who avoids the violence involved in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice;
therefore, since there is a contradiction, the general rule is set aside.
But if the injunction were not an instigator [to action], then even the killing of the Agniṣomīya animal would be prohibited.
And for what purpose is the status of the Śyena sacrifice as something to be enjoined rejected?
If it is argued that it is for the sake of establishing a prohibition, then what is that prohibition? It is: "One should not harm any living beings."
This prohibition does not apply to the Śyena sacrifice, because its object is violence;
rather, it is the fruit of the Śyena that is violence, not the Śyena itself.
And so it has been said:
"For this is the means by which one who wishes to harm [them] may do so"—such indeed is their instruction.
Someone says: "Since the *śyena* sacrifice is something to be performed, its result—namely, violence (*hiṃsā*)—must also necessarily be performed; therefore, it cannot be prohibited.
Consequently, in order to negate the necessity of the result, the necessity of the *śyena* itself is negated by implication.
This is incoherent.

For just as, even though the *apūrva* of the Śyena sacrifice has the status of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*), the status of being something to be performed does not necessarily follow for the fruit accomplished by it; so too, even though the sacrifice itself has the status of being something to be performed, there is no contingency of the status of being something to be performed for the fruit obtained through passion (*rāga*).
Therefore, the refutation of the Śyena’s status as something to be performed is useless.
Therefore, this very [example] serves as the counter-example here.
Furthermore, this other proponent must be asked: what is meant by the word "artha"?
If it means the means to attain the highest good (*śreyas*), then eternal things (*nitya*) would not possess the nature of dharma.
Now, if that which does not have a prohibited result is expressed by the word "artha" (purpose),
then it would follow that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) residing in the domain of the negative particle (*nañ*) is itself *dharma*,
because it is characterized by a Vedic injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*) and lacks a prohibited result.
If you say, "Let it be so," we reply: no, because it contradicts common worldly understanding.

For one who is intent on violence but turns away from it due to the force of a prohibition is not called "virtuous" (dhārmika); rather, he is merely said to have "desisted from unrighteousness" (adharmāt nivṛtta).
Regarding this, they say: "The definition of that which is established in the world must be stated by the investigators; it is not a mere technical convention like [the term] *vṛddhi* and so forth.
Let this suffice for now. Thus ends the Sūtra on the Injunction (*codanāsūtra*).
The Section on the Examination of the Means of Valid Cognition of Dharma //3//
The investigation of its indicative mark [is now undertaken]. Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.3.

By this sūtra, the examination of the cause known as *codanā*, which is to be discussed in this pāda, is mentioned by way of reference for the sake of easy comprehension—just as in the cases of "Now, therefore, the definition of the subsidiary (*śeṣa*)," and "Now, the definition of the specific (*viśeṣa*). //3//

In order to establish that [the Vedic] injunction alone is the means [of knowing dharma], it is stated that perception and the other [means of knowledge] are not the causes [for its cognition]: this is the section concerning the fact that dharma is not accessible through perception and so forth. //4//

When there is contact of a person's sense organs with existing objects, the resulting birth of cognition is perception; it is not a means [for knowing Dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is already present. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.4)

To begin with, perception—because it arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object and thus involves the apprehension of what is presently existing—cannot be the means for knowing *dharma*, which is yet to come.
The Naiyāyikas criticize this by arguing that "arising from contact with what exists" is not a valid definition, as it applies equally to illusory appearances;
however, that criticism is invalid because [the opponent] has not actually stated a formal definition [of perception].
This is not the definition of perception, but merely a statement that it lacks [other] causes;
the reason for this is its status as the apprehension of what is present, and the proof of that is its being produced from contact with what exists.
For it is not possible for that which arises from the contact with an existing [object] to be the apprehension of something non-existent.
If it is argued that being produced from the contact of a sense-faculty (*indriya*) with its object is not a valid reason because it does not apply to cognitions such as pleasure, we say no;
for even those [cognitions] are produced from contact with a sense-faculty designated as the "mind" (*manas*).
And regarding the existence of the mind, the very cognition of pleasure and so forth is the proof.

Since knowledge that possesses immediate manifestation is observed to be invariably concomitant with dependence on a sense organ in the case of cognitions of form and so forth, immediate knowledge regarding objects such as pleasure leads one to infer a sense organ.
In that regard, since the eyes and other organs are impossible [as the source], something other than them must exist.
Regarding this, someone says: "Because pleasure and the like are specific qualities residing in eternal substances, they must be produced by conjunction with another substance;
for we observe that the color and other qualities residing in earth-atoms are produced by conjunction with fire.
And that which is the other substance is the mind. This is not tenable.

For the body is the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*). Furthermore, its status as the locus of experience is due to nothing other than the arising of pleasure and so forth in dependence upon conjunction with it, and because it is the substratum for what is eaten, drunk, and so on; thus, pleasure and so forth do not arise outside of the body.

Therefore, since [the required properties] are established through conjunction with the body alone, there is no inference of another substance. Furthermore, it is observed that only the qualities of earth require conjunction with another substance, not the qualities of substances in general.
Moreover, conjunction with fire alone is seen to be the cause of [certain effects], not conjunction with a substance in general; therefore, the mind is not established in this manner.
The very direct cognition of pleasure and so forth is the inferential mark of the mind.
The definition of a faculty (*indriya*).
What, then, is this definition of a faculty that is common to the eye and so forth, as well as to the mind?
It is said: that which, when conjoined [with consciousness], produces a cognition with a clear manifestation, is called a faculty.
And that is of two kinds: external and internal;
the external is fivefold, consisting of the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear.
The internal sense-faculty, however, is the mind alone.
Among these, the first four are accepted as having earth, water, fire, and air as their respective material bases (prakṛti), just like the visual faculty and others;
the auditory faculty, moreover, is accepted by them as being of the nature of space (ākāśa).
We, however, on the basis of the scriptural teaching that "the ear is the quarters of space," maintain that the auditory organ is simply a portion of space delimited by the ear-canal.
As for the mind (*manas*), it is either composed of one of the elements such as earth and so forth, or it is something distinct from them; in any case, the mind certainly exists.
Furthermore, it functions independently only with respect to the self and its qualities, and not with respect to external objects such as form and the like; therefore, it is called "internal."
Even in the cognitions of form and so forth, that [mind] functions with the assistance of the eye and other [faculties];
likewise, in inference and so forth, it functions with the assistance of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth;
for cognition does not arise regarding forms and other objects even when they are in contact, if the mind is directed elsewhere.
In memory as well, [cognition] proceeds either dependent on mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) or independently.

[Objection: But surely, since inference and the other means of knowledge are produced by the mind, and since they also operate with respect to the past and the future, their being produced by the sense organs would be inconclusive (anaikāntika) because they do not apprehend what is currently present.
