[Reply: This would not be the case;
for it is not "being produced by the sense organs" that is the reason, but rather "being produced from the contact of the sense organs."
Furthermore, in the case of inference, there is no contact with the mind regarding rain that has passed or is yet to come when it is being inferred; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule].
Now, as for perception:
first of all, perception is not the means [for knowing dharma], and because inference and the other [means of knowledge] are preceded by it, they too are not the means.
For it is not possible for anyone to grasp a relationship with that [dharma] if the dharma itself has not been apprehended.
Furthermore, because its object is similarity (*sādṛśya*), analogy (*upamāna*) is utterly irrelevant.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) as well is incapable, since nothing is observed that would be inexplicable without the dharma.
[Objection: But surely the diversity of the world is untenable.
[Reply: No; for it is tenable as being inherent (*svābhāvikatvena*).

Even if some unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) were to be postulated because of that untenability, nevertheless, since there would be no distinction between what is dharma and what is adharma, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) alone must necessarily be sought.
And that [negation] is accepted either through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
[Objection: But surely the apprehension of the relation [between word and object] is the cause of conceptual construction; how then can it be preceded by perception? [Reply:

There is no fault, for even determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*)—arising while the operation of the sense organ has not ceased—is indeed perception, because it possesses the character of immediate manifestation (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*).
The Buddhist view on direct perception is as follows:
it is a manifold [cognition] consisting of conceptual construction and a non-conceptual appearance.
For "non-conceptual" refers to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, an appearance whose object is that [particular characteristic] is called a "non-conceptual appearance."
Conceptual construction, however, because it does not manifest as something capable of being associated with verbal expression, does not touch upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For verbal expression does not touch upon the particular characteristic;
if it did touch upon it, then even by mere verbal expression, there would be a direct manifestation without the operation of the sense faculties.
And that [self] does not exist;
as it has been said: "For one who is burned by contact with fire perceives the burning as something entirely different [from the fire]."
Otherwise, the meaning of "burning" would not be manifested by the word "burning.

As for this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—such as "this is a cow"—which appears clearly to one with eyes wide open, its clarity is produced by its association with a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) that appears clearly at the same time;
for in the absence of that [non-conceptual cognition], there is a lack of clarity in the mere verbal expression, in inference, and in the appearance of the form of a conceptual construction.
Therefore, perception is indeed non-conceptual;
for it is in that alone that there is the manifestation of the clear particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
[This concludes] the refutation of the Buddhist position.
Not so;

for even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of one whose eyes are open is perceived as having a direct manifestation (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*), such as "this is white," and this is not produced by association with something else, as there is no evidence for that.

Furthermore, it is entirely logical that while the generic form (*sāmānyākāra*) is capable of being associated with verbal expression, it appears indistinct through words, inferential signs (*liṅga*), and the like, yet appears distinct through the sense organs.
For this distinction between the remote and the non-remote is not produced by the object;
for if it were so, the universal would always be remote,
and yet that is not the case.

For even in the case of a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*), a distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible is observed. To illustrate: one who sees from a distance a white particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) but has not yet determined whether it belongs to the class of cow or horse, perceives "horseness" as imperceptible (*parokṣa*) even while inferring it within that very same particular upon hearing a specific sound of neighing.
For indeed, one says, "Even this horse does not appear thus to my eye," while one who is nearby says, "Now I see its horse-nature with my eye, which I did not see before. However,

since its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) was already perfectly clear even previously, this distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest for those situated far and near pertains solely to the aspect of the universal (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, this distinction is based on its cause.

For even with respect to a single object, why is it not reasonable that consciousness produced by the sense organs generates immediacy (*āparokṣya*), whereas that produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth does not?
This specific result residing in the object, produced by cognition and called "immediacy," is experienced by everyone;

it is through the presence or absence of this [result] that the linguistic usage of those with eyes wide open proceeds, such as "I see" or "I do not see" based on the two reasons [of sense-perception and inference].
Therefore, since even conceptual cognition possesses a vivid manifestation, its status as perception is established.
[This concludes] the determination that cognition is necessarily conceptual and the refutation thereof.
However, some maintain that all cognition is exclusively conceptual and that there is no such thing as non-conceptual cognition.

But that contradicts experience; for we indeed perceive, immediately following the contact of the sense organ, a non-conceptualizing awareness (*ālocana-jñāna*) whose object is a mere indistinct thing, in which the distinction between the universal and the particular has not yet been differentiated.
In the absence of that [non-conceptual awareness], conceptualization itself would not arise.
For as a conceptualization, one must first recollect a previously experienced specific genus and a specific name, and then conceptualize the object standing before one by means of those.
Nor does the recollection of an object arise for one who has not previously perceived it as something entirely accidental;
therefore, non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) exists,
because according to the Advaita doctrine, the non-conceptual has "pure Being" (*sanmātra*) as its sole object.

Some maintain that this [perception] has only pure existence (*sanmātra*) as its object, because difference is cognizable only through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and as long as difference is not grasped, particulars cannot be grasped.
Furthermore, difference consists in the absence of another; it cannot be grasped by perception, much less by non-conceptual [perception].

Therefore, since there is no contradiction with perception regarding prohibitions such as "there is not even the slightest diversity here," the non-dual Brahman is established by scriptural passages such as "one only, without a second. Refutation of the Advaita Position: This is an act of extreme temerity. Do you have the same cognition regarding blue and yellow, bitter and sweet, cold and hot, or pleasure and pain?
If this is so, no further answer need be given here.

Nor should it be said that there is no grasping of specific qualities by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) regarding the nature of an existing thing, because it is impossible for a distinct conceptual cognition to arise from a non-conceptual one (*nirvikalpaka*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that difference must necessarily be apprehended only through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and not through non-conceptual [perception], for that is impossible.
We do not say that there is an apprehension of "difference" as such, but rather of "distinct things.
Even of those, we do not say they are apprehended as being distinct, but rather in their own nature—that is, we say that blue or yellow, which is distinct from something else, is what is apprehended.
For blue or yellow is not the difference;
rather, the difference is a property (*dharma*) of those two.
Thus, even when that [property] is not apprehended, the apprehension of the substrata (*dharmī*) is not logically untenable.

Furthermore, if only pure existence (*sanmātra*) were apprehended by perception, and not "blue" or "yellow," then how could difference be apprehended even by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) in the form "this is different from that"?
For it is impossible for that which is existence itself to be different from existence.
Therefore, since qualities such as blue and substances such as earth are apprehended by perception, the denial of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-apalāpa*) is directly contradicted by perception.
If, however, one were to say that while we do not deny the manifold world of earth and so forth, we do deny its property— namely, difference— that too would be impossible,
because it is impossible to deny the mutual absence between blue and yellow, which is established by both direct perception and non-apprehension.
For even the non-existence of perception is stronger than other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) precisely like perception itself;
otherwise, one might infer that a hare has horns because it is a four-footed animal.
Therefore, the denial of difference is not possible.
If it is argued that, because mutual dependence makes the apprehension of mutual non-existence impossible, it is therefore caused solely by ignorance (*avidyā*), even that is untenable:
for mutual non-existence could only be apprehended if the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the locus were first apprehended as distinct;

however, in the case of blue and yellow, which are first apprehended in their own forms without regard for their mutual non-existence, the apprehension of mutual non-existence occurs only subsequently.
What is this state of mutual dependence?

If, however, duality is denied—such that earth and the other elements do not exist, nor their mutual distinctions—that too contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because number is an object of direct perception.
If it is argued: "Even though there is a contradiction with direct perception, the scripture (*āgama*) proceeds by overriding it and, through its sublation, makes non-duality known," we say: no.
Because [scriptural cognition] cannot arise [simultaneously].

For perception, arising rapidly and independently, indeed obstructs the very operation of scriptural cognition— which is contrary to it— since the latter’s operation is delayed by its dependence on the proximity of words and their referents, as well as upon suitability and the investigation of logical principles.

Furthermore, it is simply impossible for the Śruti to make known the unreality of the phenomenal world (prapañca). For if it were so known, the Śruti itself—being included within that phenomenal world—would have to be understood as unreal.
And how could the unreality of the Śruti be understood by the Śruti itself?
For if it were perceived as non-existent, it could not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
However, once its status as a valid means of knowledge is established, it is impossible to claim that the Veda, being perceived as existent, is false;
for it is not possible to comprehend the existence and non-existence of one and the same entity simultaneously and as a unified whole.
For one [aspect] must necessarily be sublated for the other to appear in cognition;
and if it is argued that there is therefore scriptural authority [for both], the negation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is not possible.
But surely, if Brahman is self-luminous, what need has it of another means of knowledge?
Let Brahman be self-luminous; what does that have to do with the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), for that certainly requires a means of knowledge?
And how is there the appearance of a proliferation that does not exist?
If you say "by means of ignorance," then whose is this ignorance?
If it is argued that [the self] belongs to living beings, no; for they do not exist. Or, if they did exist, it would entail the consequence of duality.
But in Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness, ignorance has no place at all.
If it is argued that Brahman, though consisting of knowledge, is perceived through delusion as if variegated by ignorance,
then whose is this delusion?
If it is argued that this is not well-stated for anyone,
and that it refers to living beings (*jīva*), we say no, because such beings do not exist.
It has been stated that if one is a Brahmin, delusion cannot possibly occur for him;
furthermore, if ignorance were present even within the nature of knowledge, by what could it be eradicated?

If it is argued that [the Self is known] through meditative absorption (dhyāna) and so forth, we say no; for even those do not exist [in the ultimate sense], and if they did exist, it would entail the consequence of duality (dvaita).
However, because ignorance coexists with Brahman, it is not contradictory [to its existence], and thus it cannot be destroyed by that [Brahman];
consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of no liberation.

Therefore, for those who are deluded by the Upaniṣadic doctrines—which, for the sake of praising Brahman, employ figurative expressions regarding the unreality of the phenomenal world (prapañca) due to its non-permanence—and by the Itihāsas and Purāṇas that follow them...

The prattle of those who do not understand the intended meaning of statements and who lack application to the methods of logic—namely, the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda)—is to be disregarded. Thus, it is established that non-conceptual perception has particulars as its object. This concludes the refutation of the Buddhist position regarding the object of non-conceptual cognition.
Others, however, maintain that non-conceptual [cognition] has as its object only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). This too contradicts experience.

For an object with a vague form is perceived all at once, which is subsequently conceptualized in five ways by the conceptualizing [cognition] through genus, substance, quality, action, and name—as "this is a cow," and so forth.
This one is to be punished;
this one is capable;
this one goes.
"This is seen.
In that regard, non-conceptual [cognition] grasps the object in its multiplicity of aspects in a confused manner,
whereas conceptual [cognition], having distinguished each individual aspect such as genus and so forth, makes them its object.
But surely there is also a sixth conceptualization, namely "this is that very same thing"; so how can it be said that conceptualization is fivefold?
This is not a conceptualization of genus (*jāti-vikalpa*), for this is a recognition of an individual (*vyakti-pratyabhijñā*);
nor is it a conceptualization of name (*saṃjñā-vikalpa*).
This is because [recognition] occurs even among those who lack linguistic awareness.

For even animals, having first perceived their mother and perceiving her again a moment later, recognize her as "this is that very same one" in a manner entirely devoid of the interpenetration of words; therefore, this sixth type of conceptual construction is untenable, as it would result in an over-extension of the categories.
It is said: this very thing is what we call "conceptual construction of a name" (*nāmakalpanā*).
For instance, when one thinks, "This is *Ḍittha*," the object is conceptualized in its nature as *Ḍittha*, just as it is in its nature as a "cow";
it is not conceptualized as being related to that [name], because—as in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*)—there is no inclusion of a possessive suffix (*matvartha*).

In this regard, the word "Ḍittha" does not constitute the essence of the object in the same way that a genus (jāti) does, because [the name] is absolutely distinct [from the object], such that the object could be colored by it.

This should be understood as follows: by means of the word "Ḍittha," the previously apprehended individual named Ḍittha—who is the denotatum of that word—is presented, and the object standing before one is then conceptualized through the identity of that [name], as "this is Ḍittha.
What is being said is this:
"That which is our Ḍittha is this very person standing before us, and not another"—
this is precisely the recognition of the individual (vyakti-pratyabhijñā),
which constitutes the fifth conceptualization.
And since that [conceptualization] among those who know words is invariably clothed in names, it is conventionally designated as "conceptualization by means of a name.
By this, they say:

"This is Ditttha"—because there is a conceptualization of an object that lacks the form of a word (*aśabdākāra*) by means of the form of a word (*śabdākāra*), conceptual cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Thus, that too is refuted;

for in this case, the object is not cognized through the form of the word, but rather the function of the word consists merely in the recollection of an object previously apprehended, and by means of that recollected object, there arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the object standing before one through identity with it.

And it has been said: "When a certain kind of object (*piṇḍa*) is first perceived prior to the word, the word serves as the cause for the recollection of that very same kind; in that case, the word is [considered] true to reality.

Therefore, even in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a name, there is no superimposition of something other than its own nature (*atadrūpāropa*), just as there is none in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth.
Furthermore, what is it that is conceptualized by means of [categories] such as birth?
It is a substance (dravya).
But what indeed is this so-called "substance"?
Earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth.
The prima facie argument from the perspective of the Buddhist school regarding the non-existence of substance:
Indeed, we do not perceive any such thing as "substance" distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities],
nor is there any means of perceiving it.
Because the five [faculties], beginning with the eye, are exhausted in relation to [their respective objects] such as visible form,
earth is a collection of odor, visible form, taste, and tangibility;
water is a collection of taste, visible form, and tangibility.
The Saugatas maintain that fire is a collection of color-form and touch,
and wind is a collection of sound and touch;
thus, the divisions of earth and so forth are merely distinctions within the collections of color-form and the rest, and there is no such thing as a substance.
That is incorrect: that which persists through forms and other qualities—which arise and pass away—and for which a continuous recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) arises, is a substance (*dravya*).
Furthermore, it is apprehended through both sight and touch.

And this recognition is as follows: just as the substance of clay persists through the states of the jujube fruit being green and then red, or as the substance of clay persists through the states of a jar, a lump of clay, and shards.

For in that case, despite the difference in the state of the lump and the difference in color between dark and red, there is a recognition of the substance: "This very clay, having abandoned the state of a lump, has come into the state of a jar; having cast off its dark appearance, it became baked and has assumed a reddish hue;
subsequently, having abandoned the state of a jar, it has become a potsherd."
The same should be understood regarding the states of the threads and the cloth and so forth.
According to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), the production of the whole (*avayavin*) occurs within its parts.
But is it not the case that, in the instances of threads and cloth and so forth, the intended position is simply the production of a distinct substance?
Otherwise, there would be a denial of the whole (avayavin). We do not deny the whole;
however, we do not accept the production of a distinct substance (dravyāntara), because there is no means of cognizing it.

For it is the threads themselves that, through a particular conjunction, attain the state of being a single substance and become a composite whole; and such [composites], bearing the universal "cloth" and grossness, are apprehended by the cognition of a single gross cloth—this is the common worldly understanding.
Therefore, there is never any coming or going of a substance.
Only the states of the jar, cloth, cow, horse, white, red, and so forth, undergo coming and going.
And it has been said: "That which persists through things characterized by appearance and disappearance..."
And that substratum (dharmin) is that in which cognition would occur even prior to the apprehension of its attributes.
Likewise, it has been stated by us that for every substance exactly as we have described it, only the quality (guṇa) differs, not its essential nature (svarūpa).
Thus, substance (dravya) is established.
And that [perception] is divided into five types by means of genus (*jāti*) and so forth through conceptual construction (*savikalpa*).

Therefore, even conceptual perception is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and since inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by it, it is established that they too are not the cause [of Dharma]; such is the meaning of the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*.
The section concerning the authority of the Vedas with respect to Dharma. //5//
But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate;
the knowledge thereof is instruction, which is non-deviant regarding an object not perceived [by other means]; that is a means of valid cognition, according to Bādarāyaṇa, because it is independent.
It has been stated that perception and the other means of knowledge are not the basis [for knowing Dharma];
for that very reason,
the word of a person who takes those as his source is also not a basis.

If that is so, then since it is observed that verbal testimony (śabda) possesses authority only by depending on other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) in all cases, and since it would lack authority in their absence, it follows that Dharma must be cognizable through non-existence (abhāva) alone; in order to dispel this doubt, the authority of the Vedic injunction (codanā) is stated.
This is true.
In the world, it is observed that the validity of those [cognitions] rooted in other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) exists, while the invalidity of those not so rooted exists;
yet even in this case, validity is dependent [on something else], whereas [in our view] it is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

However, the invalidity of the speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*) does not arise from a lack of a root cause, but rather from the defectiveness of its root; because the word itself is defective, there is an exception to its inherent validity.
Because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

For although the Veda, being non-human, lacks the quality of being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*), its validity remains unrefuted because it does not depend upon that [person] and because there is an absence of defects caused by contact with an unreliable person.

Indeed, in this case, the intrusion of a person occurs in three ways: either through the relation between words and word-meanings, or through the relation between sentences and sentence-meanings, or because the text itself is of human origin, like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works.
But this is not the case; for here, by the word "autpattika," the eternality of the relationship between words and their meanings is expressed,
and it will be explained later that the meaning of a sentence is rooted in the meanings of its constituent words, and that the Veda is not of human origin.
This is the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since there is no direct sublation (*bādhaka*), it is expressed by the term "non-deviation" (*avyatireka*).

Furthermore, because its object has not been previously apprehended, it does not possess the character of invalidity as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); this is what is stated by the phrase "when the object is unapprehended."

By employing these three qualifications, the author of the Sūtra indicates the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as: "Valid cognition is a cognition that is free from defects in its cause and free from sublation, and which apprehends what has not already been apprehended. This is the definition of valid cognition according to the view of Prabhākara. [Objection: But in this way, subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika*) would lack validity, because they would have as their object that which was already apprehended by the preceding one. Therefore, the definition of valid cognition must be: "Valid cognition is experience (*anubhūti*)."
Furthermore, experience (*anubhūti*) is a cognition distinct from memory (*smṛti*).
Memory is defined as knowledge produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

The inclusion of the word "solely" (*mātra*) is intended to ensure that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which arises from both mental impressions and the sense organs, does not incur the status of being non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇya*) due to the unwanted consequence of it being classified as memory.
Thus, it has been stated that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is knowledge produced by causes other than mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
However, this definition is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) with respect to dream-cognition;
for you yourselves accept that even a cognition arising solely from mental impressions possesses validity regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*) and its object (*kartr*).
Now, if it is argued that memory possesses the nature of memory only with respect to the object to be remembered— because it is produced from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of that object—
but that with respect to its own nature and its agent it is indeed a direct experience (*anubhūti*), and therefore its validity is established; [we reply:]
If that is the case, then the mention of the word "only" (*mātra*) is redundant;

for even recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is a form of memory (*smṛti*) precisely because it depends upon a previously experienced portion, and its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in that respect is indeed accepted.
However, in the portion where it possesses authority, it is simply direct experience (*anubhūti*).

Furthermore, since even those restatements (*anuvāda*) such as "one who knows thus [should perform] the full moon sacrifice" do not arise from mere mental refinement (*saṃskāra*), they would possess authority.
If you say, "Let them have it," we reply: no, because that would contradict common worldly experience.
Likewise, even a worldly statement, while functioning as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) regarding an object inferred from the speaker’s knowledge, would become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Yet this is not desired by you,
because you accept that the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*) is for the purpose of excluding restatements from being considered scripture (*śāstra*).

Now, that which is independent is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that is, a means of valid cognition is that which does not depend on another means of valid cognition regarding its own object.
Since restatements (*anuvāda*) depend upon a preceding statement (*purovāda*), they lack validity.

If this is so, then even a worldly sentence, when operating toward an object already inferred, would be a means of valid cognition; for while it serves merely to dispel doubt regarding inference, it does not depend upon that [inference] in the actual communication of the object.
Likewise, inference would lack validity, for it depends upon the apprehension of an invariable concomitance (niyama);
and according to your own view, it does not apprehend even slightly more than the object already apprehended.
Even the cognition of a yellow conch would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is an experience;
however, for one who asserts that this is indeed accepted [as valid], there is a contradiction with common worldly consensus.
Therefore, it must be stated that a valid means of knowledge is a cognition that apprehends an object as it truly is and does not apprehend what has already been apprehended.

Even in the case of continuous streams of cognitions, validity is appropriate because each subsequent cognition apprehends a connection with a later time that was not apprehended by the preceding one.
Regarding the examination of the perception of time:
if it is argued that "the distinction of time does not exist, because it is not perceived due to its extreme subtlety," oh,
how subtle-sighted is the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāmpriya)!

For one who has ceased after remaining for a long time with a stream of consciousness directed toward the same object remembers that object by virtue of its connection to the immediately preceding moments.

Thus, when asked, "Was a jar present here? a person of the sixth [cognitive stage] replies, "It was perceived by me at this moment," or likewise, "It was perceived by me from morning until this point in time."
But if the difference in time were not apprehended, how could one speak in this way?
Therefore, there is a reflection upon the difference in time;
and because of that addition, the validity of the subsequent [cognitions] is established.
Now, if being in accordance with reality (*yathārthatā*) is also a defining characteristic of validity (*prāmāṇya*), then the cognition of hot water would be valid.
This is indeed accepted [by us].
Surely there would be a contradiction with worldly consensus.
This would be so if worldly people, while knowing it to be non-correspondent with reality, were nonetheless to consider it authoritative.
Those who consider this [cognition] to be indeed in accordance with reality (yathārthatā) regard it as valid and non-erroneous;
however, those who know it to be not in accordance with reality do not regard it as valid,
nor do they regard it as non-erroneous.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction for us either, because they consider the cognition of a yellow conch to be invalid due to the conceit of it being a memory and the failure to recognize it as an experience, that is incorrect.
For ordinary people do not consider even the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell to be a memory, much less the cognition of a yellow conch;
therefore, it is well said: "when the object is unperceived."

However, the author of the Vṛtti explained this differently; thus, by means of the words "the author of the Vṛtti, on the other hand, explained this otherwise," etc., the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) explains the three sūtras beginning with "tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ" by reinterpreting them according to the opinion of Upavarṣa.

In that regard, by means of the sūtra concerning the "cause" (nimitta), it is stated that self-validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) is the reason for the examination of the previously asserted authority of the Vedic injunction (codanā).

The validity of the means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥprāmāṇyam*). For the means of knowledge, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, are well-known, and since the scripture (*śāstra*) is included among them,
it too is indeed well-known.
Furthermore, the validity of a well-established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) need not be examined by another [means],
because it possesses the capacity to present its own object intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
And if it were to be examined, [it would lead to an infinite regress].
Consequently, that by which [the means of knowledge] is examined would itself require examination by another, leading to an infinite regress.
Therefore, because it is well-established, even *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
But surely, it cannot be determined that the object is as it appears simply because a cognition has arisen, since even well-known perception is seen to arise as non-correspondent with its object—
for example, the perception "this is silver" in a mother-of-pearl shell is non-correspondent, not because there is no cognition of silver in the shell,
but because it is a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
The definition of perception;
the section on perception.
Furthermore, what is the definition of perception that is not confused with its fallacious appearances?

He demonstrates this: "When there is contact with that, the arising of cognition in a person's sense-faculties is true perception (*sat-pratyakṣa*). When the consciousness has the appearance of what [it perceives], then, through the contact of the sense-faculties with that, whatever consciousness arises is true perception.
By the transposition of *tat* and *sat*, the non-confusion of appearances is established.
Furthermore, the indeclinable *tat* here ends in the third case, meaning "by that" (*tena*).
But surely, even if there were no transposition [of the senses], there would be no confusion; one need only say that "perception is cognition produced by the contact of the sense organs.
For the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not produced by the contact of the sense organs;
what then is it?
The mother-of-pearl fragment, in contact with the sense organ, is perceived through its common form such as luminosity;
however, its uncommon nature as mother-of-pearl is not perceived due to the weakness of the sense organ.
Immediately thereafter, silver is remembered through the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Consequently, due to a defect, the manifestation of the mother-of-pearl is apprehended as having the nature of silver that has been remembered;
therefore, the cognition of silver is not produced by sensory contact, and thus there is no over-extension [of the definition].
If it is argued that the qualification "born from contact with that" must be stated in order to exclude [cognitions] that are indirectly born from sense-object contact,
we say no;
for here, the definition is not merely being produced by some kind of contact whatsoever.
Rather, it must be the state of being produced directly from that [perception].

If, however, one were to rely on the phrase "in whatever way" (*yathākathaṃcit*), then even with the qualification included, the definition would suffer from over-extension (*ativyāpti*): the inference regarding heat that occurs when one perceives fire nearby through direct perception would also have to be considered direct perception.
Because it is produced through the mediation of the contact between the sense organ and its object, and because its object is [only] that which is conjoined [with the sense organ],
there is indeed a contact of the sense organ with heat characterized as "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that the definition consists in being produced by direct contact.
Therefore, even in the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there is no deviation [from truth]; thus, the reversal of the terms "existent" (sat) and "non-existent" (asat) is purposeless.
It is true that being produced by direct sensory contact (*sākṣāt-saṃprayoga-ja*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
And it is true that even in the case of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*); therefore, the reversal of the terms *tat* and *sat* is useless.
True—it is true that being produced from direct sensory contact (*sākṣāt-saṃprayoga-jatva*) is the defining characteristic.

And it is true that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; however, there would be over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) in the case of cognitions such as a yellow conch or two moons, because these too are produced from direct sensory contact.

Moreover, the apprehension of identity between the remembered form of silver and the proximate piece of mother-of-pearl occurs while the operation of the sense organ has not ceased; therefore, because it possesses immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), it is produced by direct contact (*sākṣāt-saṃprayoga*).
Thus, it is well said that [the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*)] is intended to exclude mere appearance (*ābhāsa*).
As for the *Bhāṣya*, its citation of the cognition of mother-of-pearl as silver is for the purpose of illustrating such an appearance; thus, there is no fault. //***//
If they arise from association with that [cognition], how can they be distinguished?
It is said: the reality of the object is determined by the very nature of the cognition itself;
however, its contrary nature must be understood either from the knowledge of a defect in the cause or from the knowledge of the object's own contrary nature.
Therefore, that cognition for which no defect in its cause or no subverting cognition is perceived even when sought with effort is valid; the other is invalid.
This applies to the cognition of the meaning of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
Thus, because both [objections] are absent, the authority of the *ṭa* [suffix] is established.
This concludes the *Autpattika-sūtra*.

Now, the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādī) objects by challenging the falsity [of cognition] on the grounds of the two previously mentioned reasons, starting with the words "Is it not the case that everything is without an objective basis?
For instance, the established rule— that falsity occurs where there is knowledge of a defect in the cause or a subverting cognition, whereas elsewhere there is truth— is untenable.
Because all cognitions are false.
An objection is raised by means of the doctrine of the emptiness of external objects:
for indeed, every cognition terminates within its own constituent part; due to the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it falsely determines itself alone as being external.
But how is it known that [cognition] terminates within its own constituent part?
Because [the object] is known through inference, and because there is an incapacity for activity toward external objects;
we shall explain how there is this incapacity later on.

Now inference is stated: Cognitions of pillars and the like are false, because they determine their own internal parts as being external, since they are cognitions, just like dream-cognitions and the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

For dream-cognitions and the like lack an external object as it is apprehended; moreover, it is possible for things existing in other places or times to appear as if present in a nearby place and time, and it is impossible for things such as the cutting off of one's own head to ever occur at any place or time [in reality].
Since [dream-cognitions] necessarily apprehend their own self as if it were external due to its appearance in a dream, this must be admitted.
Therefore, by analogy with that, since waking cognitions also terminate within their own parts, they are false—this being the position reached.
It is stated as follows:
First of all, cognitions such as those of dreams do not have their own parts as their objects;
we shall explain later that even these apprehend external objects themselves, though they exist in one way and are grasped in another.
Or, let it be that there is self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) in that case;
nevertheless, for this reason alone, cognitions of blue and so forth cannot be [reduced to] such [self-apprehension].

For in those cases—where one perceives "this is blue," "this is yellow," "this is a pillar," or "this is a jar"—the external blue and so forth, which serve as the locus for the appearance of "this" and are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), cannot be denied by means of inference (*anumāna*).
For if there were grasping at a self, it would be "I am blue."
Thus, by establishing the external object through perception itself, [perception] obstructs the arising of inference which is intent upon denying it.
In cases such as dreams, however, because the existence of the external object is refuted by another subverting cognition, self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) might be plausible;
but here, there is no such other subverting cognition apart from the inference you have stated.
And it has already been stated that inference is not capable of subverting [the matter];
furthermore, a thousand refutations of this inference have been elaborated in the Vārtika, so we shall desist.
The dispute between the Yogācāra and the Sautrāntika.

Thus, when inference has been refuted by contradiction with perception, and it is established that perception lacks the capacity for external operation, that same proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) once again establishes himself upon perception by means of the aforementioned objection beginning with "it is empty" (śūnyatvam). In this regard, the following is considered: as for this object appearing in the form of blue and so forth—such as "this is blue," "this is yellow"—does it appear as consciousness itself, or as an external object?
To that end, this is investigated: is cognition perceptible or inferable?

If it were perceptible, since a formless [cognition] could not be grasped through perception, and because only a single form is apprehended, the apprehended form would reside in the cognition itself; thus, the object, being unapprehended, would simply be non-existent.
If, however, [the object] were the object of inference, then because inference is impossible without an external object, the external object would be established.
In that case—how could it be that cognition itself appears in such a form by its own nature?
For that which is not perceived directly, there is no comprehension through any other means of valid cognition.
And because blue and other such objects are objects of cognition, it is certain that they possess the form of consciousness.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is a different entity to possess the characteristic of being the apprehended object.
For one who maintains that consciousness is directly perceived, knowledge itself would not be established, because other means of valid cognition would be possible.
If it is argued that it is through inference, no; for there is an absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
The object itself cannot be the inferential mark (*liṅga*),
because it is admitted that the object exists even in states such as deep sleep, despite its absence [in consciousness].
If it is argued that the practical usage of the object is the mark— since that necessitates the postulation of an occasional cause— then [we reply]:
In that case, prior to linguistic convention, there would be no appearance of cognition [as an object].
However, even without such convention, it is witnessed by experience that one who sees a jar connects it with the cognition, thinking, "I know the jar."
If it is argued that dharma, which arises from knowledge, is the inferential mark (*liṅga*), we say no;
for there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for its existence.
Furthermore, since dharma is impossible in the case of past and future objects, the establishment of knowledge through inference of the past and so forth would not occur.
Therefore, consciousness must necessarily be accepted as being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And in this way, the claim that "this aspect belongs to that [consciousness]" would be devoid of any means of valid cognition (*niṣpramāṇaka*).
Furthermore, blue and other objects must be aspects of cognition because they are cognizable;
for it is not possible for a non-spiritual blue object to be cognized in the same way that yellow is.
And if blue were a distinct entity, then what would its characteristic of being cognizable (*vedyatva*) consist of?
If it were characterized by the nature of being an object (*arthatva*), then everything would be cognizable by everyone, because there would be no cause for a fixed determination.
Now, as for the establishing [argument]: if it is argued that "only that object which is the cause of a cognition is the cognized object, and no other," we say no;
for it would follow that the eyes and so forth would also be cognized objects.
If it is argued that being an object consists in similarity and causality, and that the blue object is similar to the cognition of blue whereas the eye is not,
even so, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) would be an object because of its causality and its similarity [to the cognition] by virtue of being a consciousness.

Now, similarity by way of the object’s form (*viṣayākāra*) through its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) is the definition of being an object (*viṣaya*). For while "cognitiveness" (*jñānatva*) is common to all cognitions, the form of blue and so forth is unique to only some; therefore, similarity by way of that form constitutes objecthood.

Even so, in the case of a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika*), the preceding [moment] would become the object of the succeeding one, because both possess the nature of blue and because the former is the cause of the latter.
It might be thought: "Similarity is not what constitutes objecthood; rather, that which is the cause capable of imparting a specific form such as blue to the cognition is the object.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), however, does not impart the forms of blue and so forth.
If that were the case, after a cognition of blue, there would always be a consciousness of blue."

In that regard, within a single continuum, this arising of diverse forms is produced by the specific proximity of various objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth; thus, the object itself possesses the status of being the apprehended.
Furthermore, there is a doubt from the Yogācāra perspective:
"But at the time when the effect exists, the cause—the object—has already passed away due to its momentariness; how, then, can it be an object of perception?
This alone constitutes the objectivity of an object: that it is a cause capable of imparting its form to the cognition."
As they have said: "If it is asked how that which belongs to a different time can be grasped, they understand its state of being graspable [in this way]."
"It is logical that it is precisely the cause [of cognition] which is capable of imparting its form to the knowledge.
If this is so, then to what does this form belong which manifests as present?
If it belongs to knowledge itself, then what is the proof for the existence of an object that does not manifest, and for its being the cause of knowledge?
It is precisely the variety of cognitions [that accounts for this],
for it has been stated that such variety does not arise from the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) alone.
If that is so, then how can it be said that the object to be inferred is apprehended by perception?
For this indeed is the nature of an object being graspable by perception: that it functions as a cause by directly imparting its form [to the cognition].
However, that which is a cause imparting its form to the cognition through a mediated succession is inferable (*anumeya*).

For example, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire is inferable when it generates the cognition of fire by way of the specific characteristic of smoke, the perception thereof, and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) thereof.

Therefore, there are only two means of valid cognition, namely perception and inference, because the cognition and its object are distinct. In the absence of identity (*tādātmya*), the determination of an object from a cognition is based solely on causal production (*tadutpatti*). In that regard, when there is direct production, it is perception; when it is through an indirect succession, however, it is inference. Thus, there are only these two types.
These very [factors] constitute validity, which is simply the correspondence with the object, because the determination of a specific object depends upon that [correspondence].
For a cognition does not become the apprehension of blue merely by being a cognition, since that would apply equally to yellow and other objects;
rather, the establishment of the apprehension of blue is achieved through its blueness.

As they have said: "It is not logical that the cognition of an object occurs by the mere existence of consciousness itself, because since consciousness is indistinct in all cases, it would follow that there is no distinction [between cognitions].
Rather, entering into similarity with the object, it can render the object similar to itself.
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that when consciousness possesses an aspect (sākāra), the existence of the object and its characteristic as a grasped entity (grāhyalakṣaṇa) are established.

To this we reply: This might be the characteristic of the apprehended object if there were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the object] being the cause of, or the provider of the form of, the cognition;
but such a thing does not exist, because the arising of various forms is possible from the specific immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) alone.

For instance: since you yourself must necessarily admit that the diversity of cognitions in the dream state is produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), even though the presence of an external object is absent;
and if this is so, let it be the same for waking cognitions as well—what is the use of postulating the apprehension of an object?
Therefore, being a cause is not the defining characteristic of the apprehended (*grāhya*).
Now, if it is argued that the object is that wherein the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of apprehension and so forth is based upon cognition,
then in that case, the atoms contained within the blue [object], as well as its taste and other qualities, would also attain the status of being objects,
because they too are being apprehended.
Now, if it is argued that only the substance (dravya) is apprehended and not the qualities (guṇa) such as taste and so forth,
then in that case, even visible form (rūpa) would not have the status of being an object.
Furthermore, everything is for the sake of pleasure.
Therefore, regarding pleasure that has been experienced, there is no linguistic convention (vyavahāra) concerning pleasure as its object, nor could such a convention possibly exist;
since there is a linguistic convention bound to pleasure itself, how can [the past pleasure] be its object?
Now, it may be objected that usage is not limited to the material cause alone, since the employment of words is also a form of usage; therefore,
because blueness is the object of the employment of words based on the cognition of blue, it possesses the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*),
and the same applies to pleasure and so forth.
Even so, since appropriation (*upādāna*) is also a conventional designation (*vyavahāra*), the atoms that constitute its object would still remain in the same state of being objects (*viṣayatva*).
Furthermore, it is not possible to determine the object of a cognition by virtue of the employment of a word, because that would be erroneous.
For the criterion is the employment of a word connected with an actual object, not the mere employment of a word;

indeed, the relationship between a word and its meaning is precisely that of the signifier and the signified. Therefore, whatever word generates a cognition having a certain object as its domain, that object is the denotation (*vācya*) of that word.

Therefore, the determination of the object of a word must be preceded by the determination of the object of cognition; for if that [determination of the word-object] were dependent upon it [the determination of the cognition-object], an inescapable circularity would result.
If it is argued that "being the recipient of an excellence produced by cognition" is what constitutes being an object of apprehension, we reply:
that [excellence] is not perceived,
nor is it possible for past and future things, as has already been stated.
Now, if it is held that the object is that which produces a cognition through the conjunction of the sense organ, or that which is produced by a pervading mark (*vyāptaliṅga*),
then touch would have to be the object of the visual cognition of blue;
for touch, like color itself, possesses a relationship with the eye characterized as inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).

Likewise, in the case of the inference of taste from its mark, which is smell, visible form (*rūpa*) would also be an object [of that inference], because it is pervaded by that [taste] just as much as taste is.
Therefore, it is established that the very nature of being cognition (*jñānātmakatva*) is the defining characteristic of an object such as blue; thus, identity (*tādātmya*) is proven. //***//

The rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) also establishes non-difference by negating difference—which is pervaded by the lack of such a rule—through the perception of what is incompatible with its pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*);
for distinct things, such as a jar and a cloth, are not invariably apprehended simultaneously.
Nor should it be said that this [rule] is unestablished, because at the time of the apprehension of the object, there is also the apprehension of the cognition.
Because at a later time, the recollection of the object is observed simultaneously with the knowledge itself— as in the thought, "the jar was known"—
and because recollection of what has not been experienced is impossible, it follows that [the cognition of the object] occurs at the very moment of the arising of the knowledge.
Manifestation must be admitted;
and since there is no perception of that which is formless, it is established that blue and other such objects have the nature of cognition.
Furthermore, in the cognition of dreams and the like, [the phrase] "the son of a barren woman goes" necessarily [occurs].

In cases such as "a herd of hundreds of elephants on the tip of a finger," since an external object is absolutely impossible, one must admit that the forms [of cognition] consist of nothing but knowledge itself.
Let it be the same elsewhere as well;
therefore, it follows that no external object exists. This being the position reached:
The Refutation of the Yogācāra Doctrine:
It is now stated: by what is the fact that the cognition of blue and so forth grasps its own portion apprehended?
Not by itself, nor by another cognition, for that too terminates in itself.
Of the non-self, such as ignorance, stability, diversity, and externality.
How can there be cognizability by consciousness, whether [an object] exists or does not exist?

For the Vijñānavādin asserts that all consciousness indeed grasps only itself and nothing else, and it is grasped by itself alone and not by another, because even that other [consciousness] terminates in its own self.
As it has been said: "There is no other object to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of that [intellect] itself."

To one who asserts that "because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] manifests by itself," it is replied: By what cognition is the self-determining nature of the cognition of blue and the fact that blue is the cause of that cognition apprehended?

It cannot be by the cognition itself—for in the case of the thought "this is blue," neither the self-referential nature of the form of blue nor its identity with consciousness manifests, because there is only the manifestation of blue.

That [cognition] must be understood through inference alone, based on such logical marks as its being an object of experience (*saṃvedyatva*), its possessing the characteristic of being graspable (*grāhyalakṣaṇayoga*), and the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*). However, if that inference itself grasps only its own constituent part (*ātmāṃśagrāhi*), it is not capable of grasping the fact that another cognition terminates within itself.

Now, if inference does not grasp its own constituent part (*svātmāṃśa*), then what offense have cognitions of blue and so forth committed, such that— even though they manifest as revealing external blue and so forth that serve as the locus for the notion "this"— they are nevertheless confined to themselves alone?

For it is not possible to say at that time that neither the cognition of a distinct self nor the characteristic of being an object of apprehension, nor the rule of simultaneous perception, is possible;
because all of these are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) within this very inference of yours.

Indeed, one must admit that [cognition], transcending the self, grasps the determination of its own subjective portion (*svātmāṃśa*), which constitutes the essence of the blue and so forth, from the cognition of the blue and so forth.

If that [cognition] as well were to terminate in itself, then it would not be established that the cognition of blue, by virtue of that [other cognition], grasps its own constituent part. And it has been said: "If cognitions such as 'Caitra' and so forth are without an objective basis..."
Being the very nature of reality, it would not be apprehended by a cognition arising from a means of proof.

Therefore, because of the diversity of objects, since it is not refuted by a counter-correlate, by what means can the existence of its attainment of an objective support (*sālambana*) based on its form (*rūpa*) be determined? //3//
Furthermore, regarding the question "What is ignorance?", the absence of knowledge must be understood as its object;
however, it is impossible for the absence of knowledge to have the nature of knowledge,
because they are utterly contradictory.
Likewise, in the cognition "this is that," the state of persisting through prior and subsequent times is manifested;
yet, for a momentary cognition, such persistence cannot possibly be its own nature.
Similarly, in a variegated cognition, there is the appearance of multiple forms.
Furthermore, it is not possible for a single cognition to possess multiple forms.
Now, it may be argued that even for an object, both permanence and the state of having multiple forms are impossible; or, whether they are possible or not,
the identity [of the object] with cognition is certainly impossible.
And if that [external object] is impossible, then either the form of the object would consist in its stability and its variegation,
or it would be of an absolutely non-existent nature; in either case, since those two— which are not of the nature of cognition— are apprehended by cognition, our desired conclusion is established.
Likewise, by one who negates that the external does not exist, it must necessarily be superimposed upon the cognition;
and the external is distinct from cognition.
Moreover, it is impossible for that [external object] to possess the form of cognition.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing such [conclusions] as these, one must necessarily admit— by force of logic— that cognitions do not grasp a self, even for the purpose of your own inference. Thus, since external objects exist as established by the power of consciousness itself, it is impossible to deny them on the grounds of their being "knowable" (vedyatva) and so forth.
For at that time, it is precisely the external object that is accepted as being cognizable on the basis of perception;

conversely, the cognizability of the self itself is not possible, because the cognitions of blue and so forth manifest as "this is blue" or "this is yellow," thus appearing as non-self and lacking any manifestation of a self.

In that case, let the notion of "I" have cognition as its object. To this we shall reply in the discussion on the doctrine of the self (*ātmavāda*) that even that has the agent as its object, not cognition.
Likewise, the characteristic of being an object of apprehension must also be admitted to belong to something external.

Otherwise, the object of apprehension for that inference— which aims to prove that cognitions of blue and so forth terminate in their own parts— would not be the status of being the objective aspect within those cognitions of blue and so forth, nor would such properties as stability belong to those cognitions.
The establishment that [the object] is inferable from cognition:
since its definition [as the locus of the action of cognition] suffers from the aforementioned defects, one must instead rely on its being the recipient of the fruit produced by cognition.
For the activity of cognition, like cooking and other such actions, possesses an object and produces a fruit in the object which serves as its locus.

And that fruit [of knowledge] produced by sensory cognition is called immediate (*aparokṣa*), whereas that produced by the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is called mediate (*pārōkṣya*).
For there exists a distinction between objects and non-objects, and even among objects, the distinction between the mediate and the immediate is universally recognized.
Furthermore, since this distinction is not possible without a result, that result is relied upon;
and since that very result, being the effect, brings about the cognition as its cause, even cognition that is not directly perceived is established.

Alternatively, that mutual relationship between the self, acting as the agent, and the object, acting as the patient— characterized by the nature of the pervader and the pervaded— which is mediated by cognition and action and is apprehended through mental perception,
brings about the construction of knowledge; for the state of being a pervader toward an object cannot arise in the self without an adventitious cause.
And that cause is designated by the word "knowledge" (jñāna) in the world.
Even those who maintain that consciousness is self-luminous must necessarily admit that this relation is accessible through mental perception;
otherwise, it would be impossible for one to employ such linguistic conventions as "the jar has been known by me," which express the relation between knowledge and the object known.
For only that which has been illuminated can be engaged with in conventional usage, and nothing else.
And here, pure consciousness alone is self-luminous, and the object as well [is manifest] by virtue of that; but by what is the relation between knowledge and its object manifested?
If it is argued that even that [object] is manifested by that very same cognition, we say no;
because at the stage of its arising, the relationship has not yet been established.
For the very nature of being a manifestor is the relationship between the cognition and the object, and nothing else.
When that cognition has arisen and the object has been manifested,
the relation being brought into existence cannot be made an object of that very same cognition,
because it is impossible for a single operation to be interrupted and then resumed.
For it is not possible for [a cognition] to first manifest the object and then subsequently manifest the relation, because of its momentariness.
Now, if you should think that the relation itself is self-luminous,
there is no evidence for this. Therefore, it is the relation of the self with the object, which is accessible through mental perception, that postulates the cognition.
This is plausible.
For there exists some relation between the object and the self that is accessible to mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) for all people; that [relation] postulates the cognition.
Or else, an excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in the object and produced by the cognition postulates the cognition.
Moreover, this excellence must necessarily be admitted even by those who maintain that a triad appears.

For one who asserts that "a triad appears," it must necessarily be accepted that there is something denoted by the term "manifestation" (prakāśana) which is common to all three—knowledge (*jñāna*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*).
Among these, "knowability" (*jñānatva*) is certainly not common; for that exists only in knowledge, not in the knower or the object of knowledge.

The state of being an object of knowledge belongs only to the object of knowledge, not to the knower or the act of knowing; likewise, the state of being a knower belongs only to the knower and the act of knowing, not to the object of knowledge.

If it is argued that being an object of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is what constitutes manifestation, we say no; for in the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*), there is an absence of linguistic usage because it has already perished [by the time such usage occurs].
If it is argued that linguistic usage consists in the employment of words, we say no.

Because of the faults already stated, there must necessarily exist a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*)— a synonym for manifestation, appearance, and so forth— which persists across all three [the knower, the known, and the knowledge], just as "cowness" (*gotva*) exists in individual cows.
And that property is cognized through the power of cognition, both in the knower and in the object of knowledge.
However, since knowledge is innate to itself— just as heat is to fire— it must be accepted that knowledge is self-luminous,
while the other two [the knower and the object] are illuminated by something else;
and it is on account of this that the object possesses its status as an object.
For the view that the defining characteristic of an object consists in its being the basis for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and so forth has already been refuted.

However, for the proponents of the "partial" view (*ekadeśin*), if they were to accept that an object is that which serves as the basis for linguistic usage, then the mother-of-pearl would have to be the object of the cognition of silver;
yet they do not accept this.

Since that very [object] is established through non-dispute (*avivāda*), once the excellence (*atiśaya*) of the object has been attained, the inference of the cognition occurs either by means of that [excellence] itself or by means of the previously mentioned relation accessible to mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).

Just as with the number "ten" and so forth belonging to days that have passed, even though the past and future do not exist and the substratum (*dharmin*) is absent, the property of manifesting [the object] arises; this is accepted on the strength of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, one should not accept that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, there is the refutation of the Vijñānavāda:
cognition cannot be established as direct perception even on the basis of its own manifestation,
for at the very moment an object is absent, there is no appearance of consciousness whatsoever.
Much less can there be direct perception [of the object].

Thus, since simultaneous apprehension itself does not exist, the rule previously stated—that "the non-difference between blue and its cognition follows from the necessity of their simultaneous apprehension"—is cast far away; this has been refuted. As for the argument that because of the subsequent recollection, the cognition must also have been experienced previously:
That too is unestablished;
for at that time it is the object itself that is remembered,
and through that specific memory, the pervasion of the self by the object is apprehended by the mind at that very moment.
On the strength of that [present cognition], one first postulates a cognition directed toward that object;

then, having determined that this cognition is a memory because it lacks causes such as the sense organs, one simultaneously postulates a prior cognition which serves as the cause of that memory. Thus, for this [cognition], there is no [further] recollection.
For this reason as well, blue and other objects do not have cognition as their essence:
because in inferences and the like, the forms of the objects are imperceptible (parokṣa),
whereas cognition is admitted to be perceptible (pratyakṣa) in all cases.
For identity between the indirect (parokṣa) and the direct (aparokṣa) is not possible.
Likewise, it is absolutely impossible for that which is considered to be of an utterly non-existent nature—such as permanence and so forth—to have the nature of a cognition whose form is existent.
Similarly, in inferences regarding past events, the state of being past appears [in the cognition].
Furthermore, it is not possible for the state of having already occurred (*bhūtatva*) to constitute the nature of a present cognition.

If it is argued that even though the object of cognition (*grāhya*) is distinct from the subject (*grāhaka*), it is only the past cognition itself that serves as the object for a subsequent [cognition], and not an external object—this is not so, because there is a lack of valid proof (*pramāṇa*).
In this regard, having analyzed the past in three ways, the refutation was stated beginning with the words, "And that past cognition... and so forth.

It should be understood that the refutation has already been stated by means of the passage beginning with "and by postulating two forms," after having likewise analyzed the subsequent [position] in three ways.
Therefore, this Vaibhāṣika view is also entirely untenable.
Consequently, blue and other such objects are indeed the forms of external things, not the forms of cognition.
How then is it so in a dream?

Even there, it is an external object situated in another place and time that, being remembered through the force of latent impressions awakened by the unseen (adṛṣṭa), is mistakenly perceived—due to the mind being impaired by sleep—as if it were present in the current place and time.
This is clearly evident from the observation that in a dream, something experienced on the immediately preceding day appears as if it were occurring in the present.
It is likewise appropriate to accept this even in the case of other dreams.
Even the severing of one's own head, though perceived elsewhere, is understood as pertaining to oneself due to the influence of a defect;
in all cases, it is merely an unreal association that appears.
But for the Mīmāṃsakas, the associated [objects] are indeed real;
this is what they call "misapprehension" (viparītakhyāti).

For one who maintains the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), it is simply the piece of mother-of-pearl that is perceived as having a nature that does not belong to itself, yet is grasped as being the self.

Likewise, even in cases such as "the son of a barren woman," the referent of the word "son" does indeed exist, yet it is understood as being associated with a barren woman due to the defect of the proximity of that term.
This is the presentation of the theory of one's own *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension).

As for what has been said by some regarding such cases— that it is an error (*bhrānti*) consisting in the denial of the appearance of that [object's] form— that should be disregarded precisely because it contradicts direct experience (*saṃvit*).

For who indeed, when their vision is pressed by the fingers, would say that the doubling of the moon does not appear? Furthermore, for one who clearly discerns with the eye that "this is one moon alone, not two," how could the delusion of duality that arises be caused by the non-apprehension of the distinction [between them]?
Likewise, for one who has understood the directions, a delusion regarding the directions cannot possibly be caused by non-apprehension.
But how, then, is duality apprehended? It is not through memory,
because the cause for that [memory] is absent.
There is no grasping, because it is impossible for the eye to grasp what has not been reached.
It is said in reply: both the location and the moon are reached by the eye.
And the conjunction of those two is understood through the influence of a defect:
having perceived the moon in two locations, one determines the duality residing in those locations to belong to the moon due to the influence of a defect.

Likewise, it should be understood that while perceiving with the eye both the yellowness inherent in the bile and the actual nature of the conch shell, one cognizes their connection due to the influence of a defect.

Furthermore, if in the cognition of real silver there appears identity [with the object], whereas in the cognition of shell-silver there does not, then one would be able to discern the difference between the two cognitions based on the difference in what is manifested even before a sublation occurs;
and upon the realization of that difference, one would not act [toward the shell-silver].
Furthermore, if one seeking silver were to understand the mother-of-pearl as something to be acquired (upādāna) as an effect,
then there would result the error of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), because a non-effect is appearing as an effect.
On the other hand, if he were not to understand it so, [the action of reaching out would not occur].
It would not proceed, because activity is dependent upon the comprehension of its result.
Now, if it is argued that activity occurs because of a similarity to the cognition of its effect, even when the fact of being its effect is not cognized,
then since there is also a similarity to the cognition of its effect [in the case of cessation], cessation would also occur, as there is no distinction between the two similarities.
Furthermore, in the absence of a cause, an object similar to that cause cannot produce its effect— just as mother-of-pearl does not produce an ornament, which is the effect of silver.
But surely, do not rice-grains (*nīvāra*) accomplish the *apūrva* which is the effect of rice?
It is not so;
it is only the constituent parts of the rice that perform the function there.

And since those [causes], even when incomplete, are understood as the means for achieving that [effect] during a state of incapacity because of the injunction to apply them according to one's ability, it is not the case that the effect arises from something dissimilar that lacks the causal capacity.
Now, if the cause of activity is simply the non-cognition that [something] is not to be done (*akārya*),

then even outsiders would engage in the meaning of the Veda, because they too do not cognize it as something not to be done. Alternatively, if they were to cognize it precisely as something not to be done, [then they would not engage].
Therefore, let it be granted for now that there is "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) because one perceives an object as something it is not.

Consequently, since even in dreams and similar states there is the appearance of an external object that exists in one way but is perceived in another, it is established that in all cases there is an external objective support (*bāhyālambanatva*). This concludes the refutation of the Yogācāra position. 59.
Now, if it is argued that the cognition of pillars and so forth is otherwise (i.e., false) because it is a cognition like a dream-cognition,
that is incorrect; for if that were the case, then since there is no distinction in being a cognition, your own inference would also be false.

Alternatively, if the inference that apprehends falsity were itself not false, then there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason (*hetu*) in that very case. Therefore, it has been well said: "That cognition alone is incorrect for which the instrument is defective or for which there is a subsequent cognition of falsity; no other [cognition] is so, such as the cognition of a shell-silver. Consequently, because it is non-deviant, perception does not require further investigation.
Thus ends the doctrine of emptiness.

The Section on Inference (*Anumānapariccheda*). Having stated the non-deviation of perception by means of its world-established definition—namely, that it is produced from the contact with an existing object—he now states the world-established definitions for the sake of establishing the non-deviation of inference and the other means of knowledge: "Inference is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses], based on the observation of one part of a known relationship. (*Śābarabhāṣya*)... [text continues] ...śā... [text continues] ...śā.

*Bhā*: For whatever [subject], of whatever kind, with whatever [correlate] of whatever kind, there exists a specific relation— whether direct or indirect— such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*),
inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*), causality (*kāryakāraṇatva*), or any other [relation] that is known to be restricted to the subjects of the example, that [relation].

Inference is that cognition which arises in one who has observed such a [logical] connection in the subjects of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), regarding a similar case where that same kind of connection is not determined by a powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through either its identity or its contrariety;

for example, the knowledge of fire in a mountain from seeing smoke, by one who has perceived in kitchens and the like the invariable concomitance of smoke— which is characterized by uninterrupted upward movement— with fire.
The Prābhākara view on inference:
[Objection] But if [inference] depends upon the ascertainment of a rule (*niyama*), how can there be activity toward that which has not been cognized as having such a nature?
For such is the rule: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire."

"Whatever possesses taste possesses color"—if this were the case, then the existence of fire would already be understood as soon as smoke is perceived; thus, it would be impossible for inference to have an unascertained object.

Fearing this very objection, some explain the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*) as being intended to dispel the misconception that [inference] is a form of memory, while they themselves accept that inference merely grasps what has already been grasped.

Nevertheless, it is not invalid; for the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not the apprehension of what has already been apprehended. Rather, its defining characteristic is direct experience (*anubhūti*).

Furthermore, although inference apprehends what has already been apprehended, it is indeed a direct experience (*anubhūti*) because it is produced by a presently existing inferential mark (*liṅga*) as its cause, and thus lacks being produced solely by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); therefore, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is logical.
Now, why is the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) not accepted?
Because of the presence of a presently arisen cause;
for [the cognition] "this is silver" occurs due to the presence of a cause other than the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
