In that case [of the silver-cognition], the loss of memory (*pramoṣa*) was admitted by resorting to its status as a memory on the strength of the cognition of silver, even though it is actually of the nature of an experience (*anubhava*).
But here, since the mark (*liṅga*)—the cause of experience—is present, it is improper to deny the nature of experience established by actual perception and instead admit the loss of memory;
this is their groundless fear.

For instance: if the existence of the pervaded and the pervader were already known [prior to inference], then one might indeed suspect that [inference] merely apprehends what has already been apprehended;
but this is not the case.
For it is only in specific instances such as the kitchen (*mahānasa*)—the subjects of the example—that the concomitance of smoke with fire is understood prior to the inference, and not everywhere.
Because of the impossibility of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How this impossibility occurs has been explained in detail in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* itself.

For one who has repeatedly perceived the coexistence of smoke with fire in the very substrata that serve as examples (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), and who, upon searching diligently even in the absence of fire, has never observed smoke anywhere, there arises the knowledge of the presence of fire in the substrata of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). As it is said: "Since the coexistence of fire and smoke is established as being limited to specific locations..."
And since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not observed, its capacity to indicate [the probandum] is postulated; thus it is said:
"By the mere observation of its presence, it indicates [the probandum] for those who associate with it.
Consequently, one who desires to infer need not ascertain that all things possessing smoke are possessed of fire.
Nor is it the case that smoke is entirely absent wherever there is no fire.
Those who seek inference need only request this much: the repeated coexistence with fire and the non-observation of deviation; nothing more than that.
As for the cognition "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," that has already been stated to be inference itself.
Refutation of the charge that [inference] grasps what has already been grasped:

But even so, since by this very inference of the universal all smoke-bearing things are understood to possess fire, the subsequent inference of fire upon seeing smoke in specific locations such as mountains would still remain subject to the same charge of grasping what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).
Not so;
because of the distinction between the general and the particular.
For by means of the general [mark], the possession of fire is understood in those things possessing smoke.
Furthermore, the specific nature of a particular place such as a mountain was not previously understood, much less its possession of fire;
yet some maintain that it was indeed already understood.
Therefore, it must be stated by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) those standing near the mountain first apprehend the very nature of the mountain itself;
it is not by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor by any other means of valid cognition.
And one who has not cognized the mountain is not capable of ascertaining its possession of fire.
For if the mountain’s possession of fire at the present time were already cognized beforehand, then one seeking fire would climb the mountain for the sake of fire even without seeing smoke.
Indeed, for one who seeks fire and already knows there is fire, seeing smoke serves no purpose whatsoever.

Furthermore, by one who asserts that the connection with fire is understood for a specific location such as a mountain characterized by smoke, it must also be admitted that the connection with smoke is likewise understood. For it is not possible to characterize a characterizable object whose relationship [to the characteristic] has not been known.

Now, if it is argued that the indication by smoke is of the location in general (*deśamātra*) and not of a specific location (*deśaviśeṣa*), then the possession of fire (*agnimattva*) would also be understood as belonging to that [location] in general and not to a specific location;
therefore, since there would be no distinction between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), the claim that "only the mark transcends space and time, but not the marked" is mere idle chatter.

Moreover, since smoke is already understood by the very statement "where there is contact between fire and fuel, there is smoke," nothing remains to be understood through the cognition of smoke; thus, enough with this prattle of fools.

Furthermore, if that which is already understood were to be understood again by means of inference, then inferential cognition would be nothing other than a memory whose specific character has been lost.
Nor can it be argued that it is not a memory because it is produced by a presently existing cause.
It is undisputed that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), when awakened, produces memory;
and the loss of memory (*pramoṣa*) in cognitions such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is already established.
Thus, by means of what is already so established...

When the knowledge of fire arises from smoke by means of the [recognized] path, who indeed would postulate that the unestablished status of the mark (*liṅga*) as the cause of the knowledge of the marked (*liṅgin*)?

Or, if such a postulation were made, then since even the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is of the nature of experience, one would have to postulate that the defect (*doṣa*) itself is the cause of that experience in order to account for it.

[Objection: But surely, because a specific fire whose relation [to smoke] has not been grasped cannot be inferred, only the universal (*sāmānya*) can be the object of inference; and since that [universal] was already known previously, how can there be the quality of "grasping what was not previously grasped" (*agṛhītagrāhitva*)?
As they have said: "If [the reason] is specific, there is a lack of concomitance; if it is general, there is the proving of what is already proven.
Thus, the elephants that are the proponents are submerged in this mire of the failure of inference.
This is not a fault.
Even though the universal has been apprehended, its connection with another place and another time remains ungrasped; therefore, its status as an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is established.

Furthermore, this must be addressed by the proponent of the partial view (*ekadeśin*): by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it understood that the perception of smoke is the cause of the knowledge of fire?
If it is argued that it is because of its immediate succession (*tadānantarya*), we say no;
for that [succession] is also possible through the mediation of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
If it is argued that having the nature of an experience is untenable, we say no;
for even in the case of memory, the conceit of being an experience arises through the loss of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that [original experience].
In reality, however, its status as an experience is unestablished, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For there is neither perception nor any other means of valid cognition for the fact that the cognition of fire is an experience;
however, there is [evidence] for its being a lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*).
Now, since even the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) is observed to be non-sublated,
the cognition of a gem in one who perceives the luster of a gem is indeed merely a loss of memory;
otherwise, it would follow that it is a case of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).
Moreover, since there is no sublation for one who has acted upon it because of obtaining the jewel,
it follows that memory itself is inference, which results in the loss of its status as a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇya*).
And how is it that inference grasps what has already been grasped?
For when fire is inferred in a place and time that have never before been perceived, by what means of valid cognition was it previously known?
Not by perception.
Because that [inference] consists in the perception of what is already present, and not by means of anything else;
furthermore, you assert merely this much: that the mutual relationship between fire and smoke is perceived by direct perception as being unconditioned by space and time.
However, by this much alone, the connection of the fire with another place or another time is not understood; therefore, inference is indeed the apprehension of what has not yet been apprehended.
What has not been apprehended here?
First of all, the generality of fire (agni-sāmānya) has indeed been apprehended,
and the mountain has also been cognized through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
However, since a mountain qualified by fire has not been apprehended by anyone, it will be the object of inference.
In that case, through the distinction between what is already established and what is not yet established, only the relation itself remains as the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Just as the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), although its scope is qualified, pertains to the qualifier, so it is here as well.
Inference has as its object only that which is qualified;

however, since the qualifier and the qualified are already established [as such], it concerns their relationship, just as in the case of the statement, "He gives the chariot yoked with a *yajus* to the *adhvaryu*. This concludes the definition of the members of inference.
However, he who intends to establish for another a matter already understood by means of inference must employ a formal proof (*sādhana*).
That is the statement by which the inferential cognition of the other arises;
and regarding that, some say it consists of two members, while others, including ourselves, say it consists of three.
That which extends up to the example, or beginning with the example, etc.

The followers of Akṣapāda, for their part, maintain that the means of proof consists of five members: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).
"Sound is impermanent" is the proposition;
"because it is produced" is the reason; "whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth" is the example.
And "sound is produced" is the application (upanaya);
therefore, "it is impermanent" is the conclusion (nigamana).

Thinking that this [five-membered formulation] is excessively prolix and its meaning already established, the followers of Sugata consider the syllogism to consist of only two members: the example and the application (*upanaya*).
For when the logical mark (*liṅga*), whose invariable concomitance has been remembered, is connected to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), the cognition of the mark arises by itself.

Therefore, having reminded one of the rule of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that "whatever is produced is impermanent"—by means of the mere application, "And sound is produced," the impermanence of sound is understood.
Thus, there is no need for further members [of the syllogism]. // *//*
In this way, however, a sentence that remains excessively expectant would have its meaning difficult to grasp; therefore, it is proper that it consist of only three members.

Thus, the author of the Vārttika employs the proof ending with the example in every case, as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar and so forth."
Alternatively, one should employ the argument beginning with the example: "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar or the like; and sound is produced; therefore, it is impermanent.
Even in this way, the proof remains neither deficient nor redundant.
And likewise, the author of the Bhāṣya employs this reasoning everywhere: "Whatever is an action possesses a fruit; since the oblation (homa) is also an action, it too must possess a fruit.

The defects of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*), such as contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) and others, as well as those such as having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), have been explained in detail in the Vārttika.
An examination of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa):
non-establishment (asiddhi), inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), and sublation (bādhakatva).

Thus, there are three types of fallacies of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), which are fivefold: "The Buddha knows dharma and non-dharma because he is omniscient" is a case of *svarūpāsiddhi* (unestablished in its own nature), for the nature of omniscience does not exist anywhere [as a perceptible entity].
"Fire is non-burning because it is cold" is a case of *saṃbandhāsiddhi* (unestablished relation), because of the coldness... [of fire].
Because of the absence of connection with fire.
[Objection: In that case, the rising of the moon would not be the cause for the swelling of the ocean, because the rising lacks a direct connection with the ocean. [Response:
There is no fault, because both are connected by virtue of occurring at the same time.

When, then, having observed the moon’s position in the middle of the sky, one infers that the rise of the ocean has occurred after fifteen *nāḍikās* have passed, how is that explained? In that case too, there is no fault because of an indirect (successive) connection; for it is not the case that a direct connection is relied upon in every instance.
For it has already been demonstrated that whatever is invariably related to something else—whether by a direct or indirect connection—is a means of inferring that thing in exactly that manner.
Therefore, a fault occurs only when the specific relationship shown by the proponent for the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished, and not otherwise.

For example, in the argument "The word 'cow' denotes that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, because it is the word 'cow'," there is a lack of establishment regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For there is no such thing as "the state of being the word 'cow' (gośabdatva)" apart from the substratum itself.
[The pervasion is unestablished] because the pervasion of "being corporeal" by "eternal ether is a partless substance" is not established, since corporeality is absent in ether.
Inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) is of two kinds: that which is erratic (savyabhicāra) and that which has a counter-probans (sapratisādhana).

The argument "Sound is eternal because it is corporeal" is inconclusive, as corporeality is found to deviate [from eternity], since incorporeality is possible even in non-eternal things such as karma and the like.

Furthermore, the pair of arguments—"Air is imperceptible because, while being a substance, it lacks color"—and "Air is perceptible because, while possessing magnitude, it possesses touch"—are both non-determinative causes of doubt (saṃśayahetu), owing to the presence of a counter-probans.
Because the relative strength or weakness of both is not being apprehended.
Someone, however, says: two reasons of equal strength with contradictory meanings cannot coexist in a single instance, because if they did, it would result in perpetual doubt regarding that object.

Since "having the nature of non-form" (arūpatva) while possessing substantiality (dravyatva) contradicts its appearing as directly perceived, the reason lacks the capacity to infer non-perceptibility; therefore, it is weak.
However, tactile inference (*spārśanānumāna*) is not contradictory and is stronger; thus, there is no equality of strength between the two.
Therefore, there is no reason (*hetu*) that possesses a counter-probans (*sapratisādhana*).

To this, it must be said: in that case, even a "deviant" (*savyabhicāra*) reason would not be a cause for doubt, precisely because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of constant doubt.

If it is argued that even though it serves as a cause for doubt, there is no occurrence of perpetual doubt because a definitive determination is possible through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then here too there is no fault, since a definitive determination is possible through another means of valid cognition.

If it is further argued that this being the case, those [cognitions] which are contradicted by another means of valid cognition are weak, while the other is stronger, and thus they are not of equal strength— then [we reply]:
And by whom was it stated that both are of equal strength?
Rather, it is merely that their relative strength or weakness is not being apprehended.
For instance, for one who has not ascertained whether a certain object is a post or a person, its verticality becomes a cause for doubt;
however, once either of these two forms has been determined, the doubt ceases.
Likewise, for one who has not ascertained the direct perception (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*) of air, [the property of] being perceived among earth and so forth—[which is] pervaded by [direct perception]—...
For one who perceives the quality of tangibility—which is pervaded by invisibility—in the air, while also observing the lack of form in space and other [substances], doubt certainly arises.
However, that doubt ceases once a definitive conclusion is reached through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); let this matter rest for now.
Therefore, like the "inconclusive" (*savyabhicāra*) reason, the "counter-balanced" (*satpratipakṣa*) reason is also a cause of doubt.

And thus the author of the Bhāṣya, by stating the counter-argument—"Whatever is an action is possessed of a fruit; the oblation (*homa*) is also an action, therefore it too must be possessed of a fruit"—and further asserting, "When an action has ceased, another substance is seen to be the fruit of substances and their conjunctions; therefore, the substance itself shall be possessed of a fruit," demonstrates that "having a counter-argument" (*sapratisthānatva*) is indeed a flaw (*dūṣaṇa*).
Therefore, that too is a cause of doubt.

However, the unique property of possessing odor (*gandhavattva*), though observed in earth, does not produce a cognition [of doubt] anywhere; thus, it is not a cause of doubt. For it is logical that a common property (*sādhāraṇa*)—being observed in both the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence—is a cause of doubt, because it produces a cognition that wavers between both sides due to its presence in both. Likewise, even two reasons (*hetu*) pervaded by contradictory meanings, when seen together in a single locus, bring their respective pervaders together within one subject (*dharmin*); since it is impossible for a single thing to possess two contradictory properties, they produce doubt.
It produces [doubt];
however, since such a state of being is not possible for that which is unique (asādhāraṇa), this is not a cause of doubt.
Likewise, there is a fallacious reason called the "sublating" (bādhaka), which is designated as the "contradictory" (viruddha) by logicians.
Some maintain that it is of six kinds,
due to the sublation of the essential nature and the specific qualities of the property, the subject, or both.

Some say there are four ways [of invalidating a thesis], because the invalidation of both [the property and the locus] is included within the invalidation of the property or the locus. Others say there is one way: in every respect, it consists in proving the opposite of the intended property.
And this alone is logical, because there is no utility for further sub-divisions.
If, however, a further sub-division must necessarily be stated, then only two types should be mentioned: namely, the sublation of the nature of the property (*dharma*) itself.

For it is impossible for a reason (*hetu*) to be subject to the fault of subverting either the locus (*dharmin*) or its specific qualification (*viśeṣa*); this has been demonstrated by the author of the *Vārttika* himself in the passage beginning: "That which is called contradictory (*viruddha*) due to the subversion of the nature of the locus," and so forth.

For instance, [the argument] "inherence is distinct from substance because it is the cause of the cognition 'here,' like conjunction"—here, being the cause of the cognition 'here' is seen in conjunction to be pervaded by both inherence-ness and distinctness;
thus, by bringing about the non-inherence-ness and distinctness of inherence, it is said to subvert the very nature of the subject (dharmin) inherence and its qualification, unity.
That is incorrect.
In this case, is the state of being a cause of cognition observed in the substrate (dharmin) that is inherence (samavāya), or not?
If it is not observed, then because it is unestablished (asiddha), it cannot serve as either a proof or a refutation for anything.
If it is observed, how could that which is observed in that very [substrate] effect its own refutation?
For it is only when there is a contradiction that one [cognition] would sublate another;
however, no contradiction whatsoever is possible between that [perception] and what is being perceived as having those very properties.
The question arises regarding the sublation of inherence-ness (*samavāyatva*). Now, it was stated that inherence-ness is being sublated.
If inherence-ness were something distinct from the substratum (the inherence itself), then even if that [inherence-ness] were sublated, the essential nature of the substratum would not be sublated.
Now, it has been stated that if [the property] itself is the subject (*dharmin*), then no sublation of it is possible.
Therefore, what is called "sublation of the essential nature of the subject" can never occur as a fault of the reason (*hetu*); rather, this is not a valid refutation.
For if, in this case, the fact that inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause of cognition were to contradict its unity, then what would be lost for one who seeks to prove its distinction from substance?
For the proof of oneness is not established by means of proving a substance distinct [from the parts], such that it could be considered a point of refutation for that [proof].
Therefore, the subverting argument is indeed twofold: because it subverts both the essential nature of the property and its specific qualification.
In that case, regarding the argument "Sound is eternal because it is produced," since being produced is pervaded by non-eternality, it subverts the very nature of eternality.

However, one who wishes to establish the point that the very form (*svarūpa*) of words is their denotation and not some external object (*arthāntara*), employs the following argument for the sake of proving it: "Even a word in a state where its relationship [to an object] has not been grasped denotes its own denotable object, because it possesses case-endings (*vibhaktimat*), just like a word whose relationship has been grasped."
The reason (hetu) for that [proposition] would establish the opposite of the specific property [of the subject];

for since it is observed that the demonstration of a thing's own nature occurs only after the apprehension of its relation [to the probandum], by that very same reason, the state of having a non-essential nature (asvarūpārthatva) would consequently follow for it as well.
Furthermore, when its own nature is being established, the communication of a sublated meaning is itself sublated as a property of that [word].

Indeed, it cannot be asserted that there is a comprehension of a different meaning prior to the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning], precisely because that would contradict experience.

In all cases, whatever reason is restricted to example-loci (dṛṣṭāntadharmin) by being determined by a particular qualification of the probandum (sādhya), that same reason— by the force of its own restriction, contradicting itself with respect to a contrary qualification because it cannot coexist with the proof due to contradiction with other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the subject-locus (dharmin) qualified by that particular— does not establish the probandum at all, since a probandum devoid of qualifications is impossible.

Just as "possessing an origin," which is pervaded by having a conscious embodied agent in the case of jars and the like, cannot establish that sprouts and so forth have a conscious agent when it is put forward for that purpose—

because it is impossible to prove a conscious embodied agent due to the contradiction with non-perception, because a bodiless agent is precluded by that very same reason (as in the case of jars), and because a conscious agent devoid of both [embodiment and bodilessness] is impossible— it does not at all establish that sprouts and the like have a conscious agent.

Therefore, a contradiction regarding the specific property of the subject (*dharmaviśeṣavirodha*) obstructs the very establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) by means of the reason; thus, it constitutes a valid refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
However, a contradiction regarding the specific nature of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣavirodha*) is not a refutation because it does not contradict the probandum.

On the contrary, since it constitutes a refutation of another established doctrine (*siddhāntāntara*), it becomes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent alone, and not for the proponent.

As for one who claims that even when there is the possibility of a contradiction with a specific property of the probandum (sādhya) observed in the example, the reason (hetu) indeed establishes the mere probandum devoid of that [contradiction], and that this [probandum] is established by implying another specific property—

for such a person, the transformation of grass and so forth, which is invariably concomitant with hot fire and yet is seen in snow, would establish a fire that is not hot, despite the possibility of heat, because of its contradiction with the direct perception of coldness.
Therefore, the fact that the reason (hetu) establishes the opposite of the specific property of the subject (dharmiviśeṣaviparyaya) is not a fault at all.
Regarding the examination of the example (dṛṣṭānta) in inference:
the illustration (udāharaṇa) is of two kinds—the illustration by similarity (sādharmyodāharaṇa) and...
And there is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*).

Having pointed out the mark (*liṅga*) through similarity (*sādharmya*), one takes it up by means of the mark: "Whatever is possessed of smoke, such as a kitchen and so forth, is seen to be possessed of fire.
When the similarity has been correctly stated, the dissimilarity need not be stated, because its purpose has already been fulfilled.

When it is necessary to state [the negative concomitance], then, with reference to the absence of the probandum (*liṅgin*), one states the absence of the probans (*liṅga*): "Where there is no fire, there is also no smoke, as in the case of water and so forth.

In cases where a positive entity is established by means of a positive entity, there alone does similarity (*sādharmya*) take the form of an affirmation and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) take the form of its negation.

However, where the absence of rain and so forth is established by means of the absence of clouds and so forth, there similarity itself takes the form of a negation, as for example: "When there is no arising of clouds in a certain place, then there is no rain there."
In the case of dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya*), however, it is of a positive form: "wherever there is rain, there is the arising of clouds.
Therefore, that which was stated by the Bhikṣu—that [the negative concomitance] consists solely of non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—is to be disregarded.
Furthermore, the fallacies of similarity (*sādharmyābhāsa*), such as the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*),
and the fallacies of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyābhāsa*), such as the deficiency of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavaikalya*), are to be understood from the *Vārttika* itself.
The restatement of the Prābhākara position regarding inference.

That [inference] is of two kinds; this statement of its twofold nature is intended to refute those who believe that inference has only the perceived particular (*dṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa*) as its object, by demonstrating that there is also an inference whose object is the unperceived particular (*adṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa*), such as action (*kriyā*). For action is never grasped as a particular by perception; rather, it is only the conjunctions and disjunctions with preceding and succeeding locations that are grasped by perception.
By means of those very adventitious [states], an adventitious cause is inferred,
and that is called "activity" (*kriyā*).
[Objection: But surely substance itself must be the cause; [Reply:
No, because it exists even prior [to the effect].
[Objection: But surely there is another substance at another moment, since all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are momentary.
Recognition, however, arises from similarity.
Thus, when each preceding [moment] initiates each succeeding [moment] in the same location, it is characterized as "standing still";
but when each preceding [moment] initiates each succeeding [moment] in an adjacent location, it is characterized as "going."

Furthermore, just as with the movement of a lamp and the resulting movement of its shadow, because successive moments— each beginning in a subsequent location— serve as the cause for the appearance of motion, there is no need for a separate action (*kriyā*). Moreover, since a moment that has not yet arisen cannot serve as a substratum for action,
and a moment that has already arisen is seized by destruction, how could it initiate action?
As they have said: "All conditioned phenomena are momentary; how can there be action for things that are unstable?
We shall refute this in the section on sound (*śabdādhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, since [action] cannot be established by that alone if stability exists, the inference of action is logical.
This is not tenable;
for an effect depends only upon its cause, and that [cause] is indeed observed here.
For immediately after a specific effort, an effect consisting of conjunction with and disjunction from a location is perceived in the body; therefore, that [effort] alone is the efficient cause.
In the same way, the conjunction of the self and the body is the non-inherent cause and the body is the inherent cause; so what is the use here of inferring an unseen cause?
Refutation of the Prābhākara through the words of another:
Now, a conjunction that serves as a non-inherent cause produces its effect either in its own substratum or in what is inherent in that substratum, and nowhere else;
just as the cloth [is produced] in the threads, which are the substrata of the conjunctions of the threads.
Or, [one might argue that] the conjunction of the shuttle with the cloth arises from the conjunction of the shuttle with the threads.
But how can the conjunction of the self possessing effort produce a conjunction in space, which is not of such a nature?
If it is argued that another cause must therefore be postulated, we say: no.
Due to the conjunction of threads, known as impulsion (*nodana*), the action arises simultaneously throughout the cloth because it pervades many threads;
for conjunctions occur only between pairs [of entities].
Furthermore, due to the conjunction of the arrow and the bowstring, known as impulsion, many actions arise simultaneously in the arrow and in all its parts, both internal and external.

In that case, there is a deviation [from the rule]: action is initiated in those parts where there is no conjunction with the bowstring, and in those substrates not inhering in their own substrate, because of the conjunction with the bowstring.
For those [parts] do not inhere in the arrow which serves as the locus of the conjunction; rather, they inhere in the arrow itself.

Furthermore, immediately following the conjunction of the self possessing effort with [the body], action arises simultaneously in the hand—which is conjoined with that self possessing effort—as well as in the limb conjoined with it, such as the finger-ring, and in the gem attached to it.
Now, in these cases, it is not from an impulse (*codanā*), nor from the conjunction of the self possessing effort [with the body] immediately thereafter;
rather, it is likewise from the conjunction of the self [with the body] in the case of the hand.
"Because of its conjunction with that [the gem], there is [color] in the limb;
because of its conjunction with that, there is [color] in the gem as well.
If this is so, then here too it can be said:

Due to the conjunction of the body with space, which is itself conjoined with a self possessing effort, there occurs a disjunction from the spatial location previously occupied by the body; and due to that [new] conjunction, there occurs a conjunction with the subsequent spatial location. Since conjunction and disjunction are thus established through conjunction alone, as observed, the postulation of *karman* (action) is not tenable.
Furthermore, this is not a property of conjunction alone;
rather, all non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa) initiate their effect either in their own substrate or in that which is conjoined with their own substrate, and nowhere else.
Consequently, if action were inferred as a non-inherent cause, it would have to be inferred in both [the air] and the bird in the sky.
For no action can exist in the sky by means of the action of a bird;
yet, from that [observation], the cognition might arise that [the sky] also moves.
Therefore, action is not inferable.
Is it then the case that the reality of action does not exist at all?
It does exist, because it is apprehended through direct perception.
[Objection: Surely there is nothing here apart from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*).

For when a snake is gliding, although there is no difference between the two—the earth and the snake—regarding their mutual conjunctions and disjunctions, the cognition "the snake moves" takes only the snake as its objective support (*ālambana*), not the earth.
Therefore, there exists for this cognition an objective support, namely a reality called "motion" (*calana*) in the snake.
Since the cognitions "the snake moves" and "the ground moves" occur through the presence or absence of those [two objects], one must admit that these two exist.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that this [cognition] cannot be inferential;
therefore, this Bhāṣya does not have such an intention.
However, the objections that [the reason] refers to a specific instance or a general instance, resulting in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*),
are refuted by this [statement],
because both are equally established as being specific instances.

Where there is the apprehension of a particular alone, there is the state of having a particular as its object; whereas where there is the apprehension of a universal, there is the state of having a universal as its object.

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*), because this involves the grasping of a connection with another place or another time that was previously ungrasped—as has been explained before. Thus concludes the discourse on inference (*anumānavāda*).
The treatise states: "From the cognition of words, with respect to an object not [otherwise] proximate, there arises that means of valid cognition called verbal testimony (*śābda*).
Since this is established in the world, it need not be examined.
And it is of two kinds: human (*pauruṣeya*) and non-human (*apauruṣeya*)."

In this regard, there is human speech composed by a reliable person (*āptavākya*) and non-human speech consisting of Vedic statements. Both are authoritative because they are free from the defect of being composed by an unreliable person, and because sound is inherently non-defective.

Furthermore, that [injunction] is of two kinds: that which enjoins an established object (*siddhārtha*) and that which enjoins a performance (*vidhāyaka*). It is also twofold: the original instruction (*upadeśaka*) and the extended application (*atideśaka*).
"This should be done in this manner" is an original instruction (*upadeśa*).
For example, in common worldly usage: "Devadatta should be fed with curds, ghee, soup, rice, and so forth."

In the Veda as well, there is an *atideśa* (extended application) such as: "One should achieve heaven by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices through the procedure of the *prayāja* offerings, the threshing, and so forth; this [other sacrifice] is to be performed in the same manner.
For example, in common worldly usage: "Yajñadatta is to be fed just like Devadatta. Likewise in the Veda: "One should perform [the *saurya* sacrifice] just as one performs the *āgneya* sacrifice."

This diverse instruction, through synonyms and so forth, as well as through direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, and through direct assertion and meaning (*śruty-artha*) and so forth, makes known the distinctions, applications, and sequences [of ritual acts]. Furthermore, by means of specific statements, names, and injunctive marks, there is an extension (*atideśa*)—the connection with the end of a procedure (otherwise known as *vidhyanta*)—of a mode established elsewhere, characterized by various constituent elements, or of the scripture that expounds it; this [extension] consists of modification (*vikāra*).
Or rather, it should be inferred that [the word] makes known the sublation (*bādha*).
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*) is for the purpose of excluding the determination of identity (*tādrūpya*) and synonymy (*paryāya*), as explained previously;
for those who hold the view that [the object is already present], however, that [term] would be entirely useless.
In the case of a determination that is contrary [to reality], there is simply no cognition arising from the word at all.

If such a cognition were to occur, then—since it is not admitted that defects of the person (puruṣadoṣa) are transmitted to the word—the word’s lack of authority would be intrinsic, and consequently, the Veda would lack authority.
At most, there could only be the rejection of a restatement whose object has already been determined as having that [contrary] form.
And that is incorrect,
because that too is a treatise;
for it is not the case that even this lacks authority.
Because it is an experience and because it is not included within perception and the other [means of valid cognition], it is indeed a scripture; let this suffice for now.

The restatement of the Āulūkya doctrine: Having stated the definition of inference (*anumāna*) as "this is the mark of that [inference] when [the relationship is such that] 'this is the cause of this,' or they are conjoined, or they inhere in the same object, or they are contradictory," the followers of Kaśyapa (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that verbal testimony (*śābda*) is explained by this very [definition], and thus there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
The Buddhists, moreover, maintain that [the cognition of the meaning of a sentence] is non-different from inference.

In this regard, as for the cognition of the meanings of individual words (*padārtha*), since its object is already known, it does not constitute a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all; so what is the point of examining whether it is different or non-different?

As for the cognition of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), since it arises even from word-meanings whose relationship has not been previously grasped, it cannot even be suspected of being an inference.
For there is no grasping of the relationship with every particular meaning of a sentence;
moreover, it is impossible to grasp a relationship with infinite [particulars].
It is well known to all people that even an entirely unprecedented particular meaning of a sentence is understood through the meanings of the words, as in the case of news from a distant land.

As for the inference of non-contradiction based on the fact that it is the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), because that occurs only after the meaning of the sentence has been understood, it does not establish its status as an inference. For immediately upon hearing the sentence, the meaning of the sentence is understood through the word-meanings themselves, without depending on the cognition of a reliable person. Even in the case of a sentence composed by a person who is entirely unknown, once the sentence-meaning has been understood, if there arises a doubt as to whether it is true or false, then [only] upon the realization of the author's reliability...

When the truthfulness of a statement is being inferred, this does not reduce it to the status of an inference—since the understanding of the sentence-meaning arises independently of the determination of the speaker's reliability.

Therefore, verbal cognition (*śābda*) is indeed a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the world; thus, the authority of the Veda, even though it is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), is established.

As for those who hold the position of the "Partialists" (*ekadeśinaḥ*) and accept that worldly speech is inferential, it has already been explained how their view fails to establish the authority of the Veda.
Thus ends the discourse on verbal testimony (*śabda*).
Now begins the section on comparison (*upamāna*).
Comparison also produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] by means of similarity.

Just as the sight of a *gavaya* [leads to] the recollection of a cow, so too the cognition of the similarity between an object currently being perceived and an object previously seen and now being remembered is *upamāna*. For example: "That cow which was seen by us in the city is similar to this *gavaya*.
But what, then, is similarity?
Similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the connection of one thing with those common properties belonging to another thing that are connected to it;

for example, the connection of the *gavaya* species with the common properties of its parts, such as its actions, which belong to the *go* (cow) species, is the similarity of the *gavaya* to the cow; and the connection of the cow with those [properties] connected to the *gavaya* is the similarity of the cow to it.

For this very reason, similarity is a distinct reality (*tattva*) altogether different from the connection with common properties; one must consider what the cause is for the distinction between the degrees of intensity and lack of intensity among those [similarities].
Furthermore, let it rest for now that there is no evidence whatsoever for its being a distinct category of reality.
Nor is this analogy included within perception,
because the cow situated in the city is not in sensory contact [with the senses].
Nor can it be inference, because [inference] arises even for one who has not grasped the [necessary] relationship.
For instance, one might infer:

"The cow is similar to the gavaya; being the counter-correlative of similarity to a gavaya, it must be seen as similar to that [gavaya], yet it was not previously seen simultaneously with anything else. However, this is not the case.
However, having perceived a cow in the city, when one sees a gavaya in the forest, one likewise infers that the cow is characterized by similarity to the gavaya; therefore, this is not inference.
Nor can its verbal nature even be suspected.
Consequently, it is a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And because it is well-known, it need not be examined.
Thus ends the discussion on analogy (upamāna).

The examination of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Presumptive testimony is the postulation of a fact because a perceived fact would otherwise be inexplicable. For example, by observing the absence of the living Devadatta from his house, one postulates his unperceived presence outside.
The postulation of a subsuming factor (upapādaka) because that which has been cognized is otherwise inexplicable (anupapanna) without it is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
But then this is nothing other than inference;
for there too, fire is inferred from smoke, which is inexplicable without fire.
It might be so, if that which is impossible were the indicator; but here, rather, that very thing which is impossible is what is to be understood.

For indeed, without the absence from the house, the existence outside is not established. Is it then the case that *arthāpatti* (presumption) is a cognition of the unestablished [from] the establishing? What is the fault in this?
Indeed, there is no fault whatsoever;
however, that [object] simply does not exist.
For a cognition of an object that is logically untenable does not arise merely from seeing its producer.
If it were so, then upon seeing "treeness," one would infer "śiṃśapā-ness," because without treeness, śiṃśapā-ness is impossible.
Therefore, that which is the indicator (gamaka) is indeed not the established (nopapādaka).
Now it is said:
it is not "impossibility" (*anupapatti*) that is meant by "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), but rather the occurrence of doubt (*saṃśaya*).

For one whose life is generally understood to be invariably connected with the house, when the absence from the house is observed, his life becomes subject to doubt; this is resolved by the postulation of his being outside.
Furthermore, because the existence of life is doubtful prior to the conceptualization of being outside, it cannot serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Indeed, that which is doubtful cannot be a logical mark.

Moreover, the mere absence from home, when devoid of the fact of being alive, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) since it exists even in the case of one who is dead; thus, it is not capable of inferring existence outside.
Therefore, since inference is impossible here, this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Just as in inference that which is certain is the indicator (gamaka),
so too in presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) that which is doubtful is accepted as the indicator, on the strength of observation.
And there is doubt here because of the discrepancy with the form previously perceived.
The resolution by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*):
this is incoherent;
for when life is itself doubtful, it is not possible to postulate external existence.
For how could one who doubts whether Devadatta is alive or dead imagine his existence outside [the body]?
Indeed, it is not possible for a doubt concerning existence and non-existence to be dispelled by the imagination of external existence.
For in all cases, the cessation of doubt occurs either through the eradication of its cause or through the ascertainment of one of the two alternatives;
and the eradication of its cause does not occur, at least initially, by means of the conceptualization of external existence.
Since life is generally associated with the home, its opposite is presented here as the cause for doubt; yet this doubt is not dispelled when external existence is postulated,
on the contrary, the very opposite is firmly established.
Nor is there any determination of either alternative here, for it is the existence or non-existence of life that is being doubted.
Furthermore, a definitive conclusion regarding either of these two does not arise from the assumption of his being outside;
for life is one thing, and connection with an external location is another.
Furthermore, the presumption (arthāpatti) based on Devadatta’s absence from the house is not capable of determining his life;
for it is not possible that "because Devadatta is not in the house, therefore he lives.
On the contrary, since his life was previously ascertained, how could it be determined by that very absence from the house, which actually renders that life doubtful?
For that which is a cause of doubt cannot itself be a cause of certainty.
Therefore, having first ascertained from another source that life is in doubt, one must subsequently postulate an external connection:
"Since Devadatta lives and yet is not in the house, he must certainly be staying outside."
However, such an assumption is not possible when life itself is still in doubt;
for if it were uncertain whether he exists at home or not, the conclusion that "therefore he is outside" would be entirely incoherent.

Therefore, having ascertained life—which is restricted to being either inside or outside—as being accompanied by absence from the house, one assumes his presence outside. Thus, this is merely inference (*anumāna*) and not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

The refutation of the logical view according to the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is stated here: First of all, the mere absence from the house is not the inferential mark (*liṅga*), because it is possible even when [the person] is dead;
nor is mere living the mark, because it exists even when [the person] is at home.
Therefore, it must be stated that the absence [of the person] from the house, as conjoined with his being alive, is the *liṅga* (probans).
Furthermore, one must first comprehend the *liṅga*, and only subsequently can there be the inference of the *liṅgin* (the probandum);
the comprehension of the *liṅgin* does not occur at the very same time as the comprehension of the *liṅga*.
And here, without the cognition of existence outside, it is impossible to comprehend the absence from the house and the state of being alive as conjoined, because of their contradiction.
For it is certain that one who is alive must necessarily be staying either in the house or outside.

Therefore, for one who attempts to apprehend the absence from the house and the state of being alive as a conjunction without including existence outside, such an apprehension results: "Devadatta is not staying in the house, yet he is staying either in the house or outside."
Thus it is said;
yet this is not possible, because it is impossible to conjoin existence and non-existence in a single location.
Therefore, the existence and non-existence of Devadatta must necessarily be conjoined by means of a difference in location.
Because the manifold existence [of things] is cognized precisely through the cognition of the connection between existence and non-existence, there remains nothing further to be known;
and it has been said: "By this cognition of the absence of the house as conjoined with its actual presence..."
"A being who has been removed from the house remains outside.

Now, even if [the non-perception] were a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), since neither mere living nor mere absence from the house individually possesses the capacity to inform [of the person's presence], it must be admitted that both combined are the informant. Furthermore, since the state of being outside is already cognized by the very cognition of the combined [factors], nothing remains to be known subsequently; thus, this fault is equal [in both cases].
It is said: let your honor rest content by understanding that this very cognition of a combined state is *arthāpatti* (presumption). What, then, is its cause?
We say it is the mutual contradiction between the two—namely, the absence from the house and the fact of being alive.

For instance, when one person says, "There are fruits on the riverbank," and another says, "There are none," a listener who does not perceive the relative strength of the two statements perceives both as mutually contradictory.
One perceives;
yet one is unable to either reject or grasp even one of the two.
Nevertheless, it is not so.
One combines existence and non-existence because they are contradictory.

Likewise here too, it is perceived by some means of valid cognition that Devadatta is situated either inside or outside the house; and by another [means], it is perceived that he is not in the house. These two [cognitions] are combined and are perceived as mutually exclusive. This is that...

The contradiction is not, like the existence of a fruit [in a non-existent tree], something that cannot be resolved; rather, the distinction is that it can be resolved by the postulation of another entity.

Therefore, when two objects established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are observed to contradict one another, and this contradiction is considered resolvable through the postulation of a different object, that is the cause of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). And for the sake of resolving that contradiction, the postulation of another object—presumptive testimony—is a distinct means of knowledge from inference.
And this sublation of what is already known by another means of valid cognition is precisely what is called the "inconsistency of the object."

The suspicion that inference is included within presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*): Let presumptive testimony be a means of valid cognition; however, inference is indeed included within presumptive testimony. For instance, it is understood that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire."
And the fact that the mountain possesses smoke has been apprehended.

If there were no fire on the mountain, then either its possession of smoke would be false, or the fact that all things possessing smoke possess fire would be false. How could both of these be non-false? It is for this reason that the presence of fire is postulated; this is *arthāpatti* (presumption).
This would indeed be the case if the fact that all things possessing smoke possess fire were known through means other than inference;
however, this is not so.
For the necessary concomitance of smoke with fire is understood only in the case of the subjects of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmin), and not everywhere.

It has been stated that inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of the presence of fire in all things possessing smoke. Nor is there any contradiction—by virtue of which there would be presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—in the fact that the restriction of fire [to smoke], which is understood only in the case of the properties of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), is absent from the state of all smoky things being fiery. Therefore, because their objects are distinct, the cognition of fire that arises when one perceives smoke on a mountain or the like, having already understood [the relation] through inference, occurs in two ways: either through the recollection of the restriction observed in the example, or it is [simply] inference.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) arises through the eye of contradiction;
therefore, presumption is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the comprehension that Devadatta, who is present in one place, is absent everywhere else is also presumption.
For it is understood from one's own body that it is impossible for a corporeal object to be simultaneously connected with multiple locations in its entirety.
Indeed, when one's own body is situated in a particular place, its absence everywhere else is understood through the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible;
therefore, it is inferred that another person, such as Devadatta, likewise lacks simultaneous connection with multiple locations.

Then, perceiving Devadatta directly in one place and determining through inference his non-connection with multiple locations simultaneously, one postulates his absence in all other places in order to account for both [perceptions].
But surely this is possible as a mere inference: "Devadatta does not exist everywhere now, because he is situated in the house, just like me.
True.
This [non-apprehension] is possible for one who is situated in the same location as Devadatta;

however, how could someone who is staying in a certain house and, after passing that house, perceives Devadatta by some means of valid cognition in a third house, cognize Devadatta’s absence in all the intervening houses and in all other locations— apart from that specific house— by means of what mark (liṅga)?

Now, suppose one perceives Devadatta in a certain place and understands his absence in a nearby location distinct from that place; then, because all other places are likewise distinct from the location occupied by Devadatta, one infers their emptiness of him.
In that case as well, the fallacy of "incompatible non-deviation" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*) is understood to apply just as before:
[the reason] "being distinct from the nearby location" [is present], just like the location occupied by Caitra.
Thus, the refutation has been stated in the Vārttika itself; therefore, this is simply presumption (arthāpatti).
By this, the postulation of the power to produce a sprout in seeds and so forth is also explained.

Furthermore, why is it that [the existence of] a potency cannot be established without [postulating] such a thing? For we observe the production of sprouts and so forth when seeds and the like are present, and we do not observe it when they are absent;
thus, the causality of seeds and the like toward sprouts and the like is understood.
Yet, even when seeds are present, because no sprout is produced if they have been smelled by a mouse, their lack of causality appears.

This contradiction between being a cause and not being a cause is resolved by the postulation of a potency (*śakti*): it is postulated that there must certainly exist a nature, even if beyond the senses, such that from its presence a sprout is sometimes produced, and from its destruction—due to the smelling of it by a mouse—the sprout is sometimes not produced;
thus, the absence of smelling is also considered a cause of the sprout.
If it is argued that since the sprout does not arise simply because the nose is absent when it exists, there is no need to postulate a causal capacity (*śakti*), we say no;
for the activity of smelling is momentary, and thus even if that [activity] is absent at a later time, the sprout does not arise.
If it is argued that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the cause and not subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), we say no.
Because there is no distinction in their being non-existent.

For between antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), there is no difference in form whatsoever apart from the distinction of preceding and subsequent time;
and it is not possible for a difference in effect to arise from a cause that lacks such distinction.

If it is argued that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) possesses a nature distinct from destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), then something must necessarily be postulated. If that is the case, one must decide whether this [distinct nature] is to be postulated in the absence itself or in the nature of the seed; since the seed is the direct cause of the sprout, it is more logical to postulate it there.
In the same way, one should infer the postulation of the capacity of sacrifices and the like to produce the unseen merit (*apūrva*) and heaven (*svarga*).
But how, when the sacrifice possessing the capacity has perished, can the capacity remain without a substratum?
It will not be without a substratum,
because its substratum is the self (ātman).
How could the power of one thing reside in another? For it is understood in that way.
There is no necessary rule that power must reside only in its own substratum; for when power is postulated on the basis of an effect, it resides precisely where it serves that effect.
That [capacity] must be postulated as residing in that very [substratum].

And since this previously mentioned capacity, being based on the sacrifice, would not suffice for the production of heaven due to the destruction of the sacrifice, it is postulated as being based on the Self.
As it has been said: "Since capacity is to be inferred from its effect, it is useful only when it resides in that [which possesses the effect]."
In that very case, it must be accepted as having either its own substratum or another substratum.

How can that which has the self as its substratum be designated as "the power of sacrifice"? For it is postulated as such precisely in order to establish that the self is the means of accomplishing the fruit; by that much alone, it possesses the status of being a power.

This is also well-known in common worldly usage: even when the act of drinking oil has long since ceased, people speak of it thus, "Today, through the efficacy of drinking oil, strength, nourishment, and so forth have arisen in me. Therefore, there is no fault.

Since the inclusion of "perceived" (*dṛṣṭa*) already entails the inclusion of mere cognition, and thus establishes the inclusion of that which is heard (*śruta*), the term "heard" (*śruta*) is employed specifically to demonstrate the distinction between presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) and presumption based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*), on the grounds that the former grasps a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, in common worldly usage, in cases such as "the door, the door," another word such as "let it be closed" is supplied to convey a complete meaning, as it forms a single syntactical unit with the word that has been heard.
is conceptualized.

Similarly, in the Veda as well, in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," whether by the words "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) or "for the sake of heaven" (*svargārtham*), whatever word— being syntactically one with the heard word (*śruti-śabda*)— brings about the expression of a complete meaning, that very word is brought to mind and joined with what is heard; thus, through this completion, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is cognized from the sentence.

Just as in injunctions such as "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," because no words expressing the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are heard and the [injunctions] are thus incomplete, one disregards the portions of the *Āgneya* injunction— brought forward by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the original impulsion (*codanā*)— which express the factors of the goal and the means; instead, that which is the third factor, namely the manner-of-performance (*itthambhāva*) consisting of the placing of the fire and so forth, is postulated as the "end of the injunction" (*vidhyanta*), and this is done by means of a word imagined through the principle of extension (*atideśa*).

However, it is merely the fact that this very *āgneya* procedure—though separated [from the modified sacrifice]—is brought to mind by the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the injunction, that is postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as forming a single syntactical unit with the modified injunction;
for this is not a case of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying an ellipsis), which would not apply to something separated.
This, however, is indeed an *atideśa* (extended application), which is possible even for something separated, since it is somehow brought to mind.

And so the author of the Bhāṣya will say: "Or rather, the *vidhyanta* (the end of the injunction) operates in the injunction according to the model; by 'vidhyanta' is meant the entire section concerning the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika-kāṇḍa*), excluding only the primary injunction."

But surely, if one accepts the extension of the ritual manual (śāstra-atideśa) in this way, there would be no contradiction with the tenth chapter and the following, yet the establishment of modification (ūha) and annulment (bādha) would remain unproven.

This would indeed be the case if the sentence "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), in its very form as heard in the scripture, were brought over to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) and its syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction of that modified sacrifice were postulated according to the circumstances.

If it were done in that manner, then in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, because the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) could not function as a designation for the sacrificial material (*havir-lakṣaṇārtha*), the threshing would be annulled.

Likewise, even in the case of wild rice (*nīvāra*) and other substitutes, the rule that "only rice is to be threshed" would apply, and thus the act of threshing would not be extended to wild rice and the like.

However, we do not say this; rather, whatever auxiliary apparatus (*parikara*) is understood to belong to this [act] through its syntactic unity with the primary rite in the archetype (*prakṛti*), that much is extended [to the ectype]. This is because, in the archetype, [the rice] possesses the status of sacrificial material (*haviṣṭva*).

The purpose is for the sake of the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and since a visible purpose for threshing—namely, the removal of the husks—is possible in those [grains], it forms a single syntactical unit with the primary injunction by means of that [visible purpose].

Consequently, the injunction regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*) is as follows: "Having made a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with rice grains that have been de-husked by threshing, one should sacrifice with it."
In this case, threshing is the direct qualifier;

for in the archetype, the oblation qualified by the act of dehusking— which itself is qualified by threshing— is the qualifier of the sacrifice, and therefore that very [act] is extended to the ectype.

Furthermore, in the sacrifice with *kṛṣṇalas*, because the word *kṛṣṇala*—which denotes the sacrificial oblation—is heard directly in the text, the word *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) is set aside due to that contradiction;
and with its removal, there is also the removal of the *vrīhi* grains.
For those [grains] cannot possibly serve as the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the *kṛṣṇalas*.

Even the term "dehusking" (*vituṣīkaraṇa*), which indicates the purpose [of the act], does not cease to apply to *kṛṣṇala* seeds because that [purpose] is impossible there; thus, the modification (*ūha*) is established.

Furthermore, in the first section of the tenth book (*Daśamādhyāya*), having raised the objection that all subsidiary injunctions (*aṅga-śāstra*) exactly as they are heard in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) should be extended (*atideśa*) by way of that form when connected with the model sacrifice, and not merely by their underlying purpose (*artha-mātra*), enough has been said on this digression.
[Objection: Let the sentence be completed simply by supplying the meaning; what is the use of postulating a word?
[Reply: Completion cannot occur through the meaning alone, for it is the word-meanings conveyed by two words that constitute a single sentence which convey the sentential meaning, and not otherwise.

For when only "bring" is said, and "the cow" is not mentioned— even though a cow is perceived through direct observation— the act of bringing is not connected with that cow. Likewise, in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *Saurya*,

because words like "Agni," whose referents are no longer present, are excluded, the insertion of words such as "Sūrya" is established for the purpose of completing the mantra-sentence, which otherwise would remain deficient in its expectancy.
The refutation of the position that [the meaning] is supplied by implication (arthādhyāhāra).

For those who maintain that words must be supplied based on the sense (*arthādhyāhāra*), however, since the word *nirvapāmi* itself would be manifested as qualified by the sense of "sun" supplied from the context, the modification (*ūha*) would not be established.

Likewise, in cases where only an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is heard in an injunctive statement—such as "Those who perform these nights certainly become firmly established"—according to your view, it is only the meaning of the injunction that must be supplied, not the injunctive word itself;
consequently, the new purposefulness (*apūrvaidamarthya*) of the archetypal assistance and the constituent elements would not be established.

For even when the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*saṃnidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) of the meanings are present, the establishment of their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) does not occur without verbal expression (*abhidhāna*). And here, there is no word that expresses the *apūrva* [transcendental result] which could be connected with the archetypal [elements], nor would there be a connection of those [elements] with the *utpattyapūrva* [the apūrva of production].

Likewise, in the case of the archetype (prakṛti) as well— in the injunction "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [are performed] for the sake of all desires"— since the injunctive word is neither recorded in the text nor supplied by ellipsis (adhyāhāra),

and since the meaning of the injunction itself— which is distinct from the qualification of one desiring heaven and from the original potencies (utpattyapūrva) of the Āgneya and other offerings— must be supplied, the subservience (aidamarthya) of the Samidh and other subsidiaries would not be established.

For the *yajati* (sacrificial) acts involving the *samidh* and other such offerings are not capable of expressing their own meaning as being connected with the *apūrva* of the qualification (*adhikāra*), in the manner of acts such as *avaghāta* (threshing), because that would contradict their status as having their own specific *apūrva* as their object.
Therefore, in such injunctions of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), it is the injunctive word itself that must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*), and not the meaning.

And how can there be an *adhyāhāra*— that is, the mental bringing to presence— of that which is intended as being absolutely non-worldly and thus impossible to be introduced into the mind by either a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or its semblance (*tadābhāsa*), whether in those sentences concerning qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*) where the word expressing an injunction is not heard, or in originative sentences (*utpatti-vākya*) such as "The *Āgneya* cake on eight potsherds [is offered] on the new moon day," and so forth?
Thus, even against one's will, the supply of a word (śabdādhyāhāra) must be accepted; let this matter rest for now.
Thus ends the discussion on presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
The determination of non-existence (*abhāva*) [through non-apprehension] (*anupalabdhi*):
non-existence, too, is the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), regarding the meaning "it does not exist" which is not in contact [with the senses].
But how can the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) be a definition of a means of valid cognition, since it is the opposite?
This word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) has in mind the five previously mentioned means of valid cognition, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), which apprehend existing things.
Since the absence of those [five] is the definition of the sixth, there is no logical inconsistency.
What is its object of cognition?
It has been stated that it is the meaning "it does not exist. For every entity is of two kinds, by way of being existent and non-existent.

Thus, when there is the capacity for means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception to arise with respect to a locus in its existent form (*sadrūpa*) for the purpose of cognizing that existent form,

yet their non-arising occurs— which is synonymous with non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) in the sense of being unfit for observation or non-observation— it is precisely by this term "absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*), mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*, which stands in place of the senses and so forth, that one cognizes: "There is no jar here on the ground."
But for one who, denying non-existence,

asserts that there is no sixth means of valid cognition because of the absence of an object of cognition— what is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the cognition that arises immediately after the non-perception of the perceptible, such as "there is no jar here on the ground"?
It is not the ground.
Because [otherwise] there would be the unwanted consequence [of such cognition] even when a jar exists.
Likewise, what is the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition that "the horse is not in the cow" and "taste is not in color"?
It is not the cow or the color.

Because its cognition does not depend upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas the cognition "it is not a horse" does depend upon a counter-correlate. Furthermore, if it were based on the form of a cow, there would be no such cognition as "this is not a horse" with respect to a lion and so forth, because the form of a cow is absent there.
Now, if it is said that the distinction from the horse which is permeated through cows and other things is its objective support (*ālambana*),
then what is this so-called "distinction"?
If it is mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) that is relied upon, then it is simply non-existence (*abhāva*).
Now, if "distinctness" (pṛthaktva) is said to be a specific quality (guṇaviśeṣa) that constitutes difference,

then, because that [quality] resides in substances, there would be no cognition of mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) regarding qualities such as color and so forth, such as "taste is not color" or "color is not taste."
Refutation of the Prabhākara View:
As for one who, out of audacity, claims that there is no such cognition as "the jar does not exist" distinct from the cognition of the ground itself,
he would likewise have to deny the cognition of the ground and so forth.
Because there is no distinction [between the two cases], what is the cause for the conventional usage "the jar is not here on this ground"?
If it is argued that the cause is the cognition whose object is the ground alone, while the jar is perceptible; then...

If that were the case, then upon perceiving the floor as it would be with a cloth, there would be no conventional usage of "the jar does not exist," because there would be no perception of the bare floor alone.
If you argue that it is the perception of the floor as distinct from the jar [that constitutes its non-existence], then:
What is this "separation from a jar"?
If it is simply the nature of the ground itself, then the same would apply even when a jar is present there.
If it is the absence of conjunction with a jar, then non-existence (abhāva) has indeed been admitted.
It might be thought: "Let that which is the cause of the cognition of non-existence for the proponent of non-existence be itself the cause of our conventional usage.
It is not possible to say this.
For me, the non-perception of the perceptible is the cause of the cognition of non-existence.
Furthermore, non-perception is the absence of perception, and this is not accepted by you,
because it would entail the admission of non-existence.
Or, if you do admit the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), what offense has been committed by the absence of the object of cognition (*prameyābhāva*)?

[Objection: "But surely, having first apprehended the ground through perception, the absence must be understood afterwards; therefore, let practical activity proceed from that very cognition of the ground which existed prior to the apprehension of the absence. [Reply: This has already been answered.
For instance: in that state where there is a cognition of the ground's own nature but an absence of cognition—namely, the non-cognition—of both the jar and its absence."

In that state, we maintain that the cognition of the bare ground is devoid of the cognition of the jar and its absence; that very cognition is what is called the "perception of the bare ground alone."
By the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "having seen the mere intrinsic nature," etc., the absence of the cognition of both the jar and its absence is expressed;
the meaning is that only the bare ground is known, neither the jar nor its absence.

Therefore, if you also accept that the cognition of the ground is conjoined with the absence of the cognition of the jar and so forth, then it has already been stated that the absence of cognition must be admitted.

Therefore, one must not be deluded in this way: even by the proponent of non-existence (*abhāvavādin*), who asserts that after perceiving the mere nature of the locus (*svarūpamātra*) there is subsequently some recollection, it is admitted that there is a cognition of that [mere locus] distinct from the cognition of the entity (*bhāva*).

Since that very [cognition of the locus] is the cause for the conventional usage "it does not exist" regarding the visible counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), one must state that the cause is simply the cognition of the ground (*bhūtalavedana*), because the word "does not exist" has no referent (*arthābhāva*).
Consequently, the refutation stands: the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows that this would apply even when a jar is present.

Now, if it is held that when an entity is located in another place, the perception of a different location is the cause [of its non-existence], then it would follow that the cowness residing in a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow) could be conventionally designated as "not existing" in a *dhāvaleyā* (a black cow); and likewise, a bamboo beam situated in one pillar, even though it is threaded through another pillar, would have to be conventionally designated as "not existing" therein.
Therefore, in this case, it is the non-existence itself that is the cause for the conventional usage "it does not exist," and not the existence elsewhere.
If it is argued that the perception of the ground when the jar is being remembered is the cause for the conventional usage "it does not exist," we say no.
This is because, even while an object is being perceived, there is the conventional usage of its non-existence in its surrounding locations;
and furthermore, when a jar is brought here and is currently being perceived, there is the conventional usage of its prior non-existence here, expressed as "this was not here before."
An Exposition of the Views of Prabhākara.

[Objection: "In your view, for a jar that is being cognized as existent, the cause of the cognition of its prior non-existence is indeed the absence of a positive means of knowledge (*bhāvapramāṇābhāva*).

And it is not the case that the jar, while being cognized, is not cognized as being connected with the prior time; therefore, since no means of knowledge directed toward its connection with the prior time has arisen, the cognition of its non-existence at that time is perfectly logical. [Reply: No.
Because it is unfit [for cognition].
For a connection with a prior time is not fit to be cognized now;
moreover, the cause of the knowledge of absence is the absence of a capable means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not merely the absence of a means of valid cognition.
In the prior time, however, there was simply no arising of valid cognition regarding the fit object;

for at that time, although the absence of the jar existed, it was not cognized because the counter-positive—the jar—was not reflected upon, and because the knowledge of absence depends upon that [reflection].
For this very reason, it is not tenable to say that "the absence of the jar is now being remembered."
Because there is a connection with the recollection of that which was immeasurable.
