Furthermore, this prior non-arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), having now been destroyed by the arising of a means of valid cognition, cannot produce a cognition of non-existence,
just as an uprooted eye cannot produce a cognition of form.
Now, even though the non-arising of a means of valid cognition has perished, it might indeed serve as the cognition of yesterday’s fire when remembered at present—

provided that the absence of a means of valid cognition, by being itself known, could make known the absence of the object of cognition, just as a logical mark (liṅga) makes known the possessor of the mark (liṅgin).
But this is not possible, because it would lead to an infinite regress.
The absence of the object of cognition must be known;
that too, being an absence, must be known by another cognition of absence,
and that by yet another— thus, even in a thousand lifetimes, the absence of a jar could not be determined.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) produces the cognition of non-existence by its mere existence, just like the eye and other [senses].
Consequently, it must be explained how there can be a cognition of the prior non-existence of a jar that is currently being cognized.
It is said: It has been correctly stated that the absence of knowledge, by its mere existence, makes known the absence of the object of knowledge;
however, there certainly exists now, even for a jar being perceived, the non-arising of a knowledge capable of having the connection with a prior time as its object.
Although it is capable of being remembered as having been connected with a prior time, it is not remembered;

and it is not the case that only the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) indicates non-existence, for even the non-arising of a memory-cognition, when there is capacity [for it to arise], indeed indicates the existence [of the object].

Therefore, even though the jar is being perceived now, if it had existed previously, it would necessarily have been cognized by one staying there; and having been cognized, it ought to be remembered now.

Yet, despite this being the case, it is not remembered. This very non-arising of memory regarding an object that ought to be remembered, existing at the present time, produces a cognition whose object is the absence [of the jar] at the previous time.
Nothing is untenable here;

furthermore, in the Bhāṣya, the term "absence of means of valid cognition" (pramāṇābhāva) is intended as an indicator for the absence of recollection (smaraṇābhāva) as well, and it is likewise in the Vārttika.
Alternatively, since the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is remembrance, its absence can also be said to be, in effect, the absence of a means of valid cognition.
The refutation of the aforementioned [view of] Prabhākara:
Now, it is not logical that the non-perception of the perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*) should cause the cognition of absence merely by its existence,
because even when that [non-perception] is present, the cognition of absence does not sometimes arise.
Because [the non-perception of the ring] sometimes arises even when it is not present.

For instance, consider one who, desiring to find a ring, has searched all around every part of a dark room with both hands; although for him the non-perception of the object in its proper locus has indeed occurred due to that exhaustive search of every spot, yet—doubting whether every spot was searched or perhaps some spot might remain—he does not ascertain the absence of the ring because he lacks certainty regarding the non-perception of the object, despite its actual presence.

However, sometimes, even when one has not searched everywhere, one determines through the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*)—based on the error that one has searched everywhere—that the ring is absent, even though such [non-perception] does not actually exist.
Therefore, it must be admitted that the non-perception of the perceptible is the cause for the cognition of absence only by virtue of being known;
and in that case, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, the non-existence of the perceptible counter-entity is simply the self-cognized cognition of that [bare] locus alone, and not a separate reality.
But surely, if non-existence is admitted, even the cognition of that bare locus can never be determined;
nor is the cognition of the ground itself the cognition of that bare locus.
Even for those whose cognitions are of a mixed nature, it would follow that they consist of that [bare ground] alone,
because even in that case, the bare ground is what appears. Therefore,
when there is no cognition of a jar or the like, the cognition of the ground is a cognition of that [ground] alone.
And thus, since the non-existence of cognition is accepted, the denial of non-existence is pointless.
How, then, is this to be determined?
It is stated as follows: the non-existence of a jar and so forth exists as an object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Furthermore, the non-arising of a valid cognition regarding that [object] indicates its existence by its mere presence, like the eye and so forth, and not by its being known;
for otherwise, there would be an infinite regress.

As for the claim that the cause [of non-apprehension] is indeed a "suitable non-perception" (*yogyānupalambha*), in that case, suitability (*yogyatva*) is a cause only by virtue of being known, not by its mere existence.

Consequently, sometimes a non-apprehension whose suitability is unknown does not determine absence; at other times, however, one determines absence by mistakenly ascertaining a suitability that is actually non-existent.
Non-perception (*upalabdhyabhāva*), on the other hand, is a cause by virtue of its mere existence, not by virtue of being known.
Therefore, there is no occurrence of an infinite regress; thus, everything is clear.
Consequently, there exists an object of cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*).
The non-existence [of a thing] is to be understood through non-apprehension.
And that [cognition] is not sensory, because its arising is observed even in the absence of sensory operation;
for instance, when someone staying in a house at the morning time on a day is asked at midday: "What was in this house this morning?"

A certain man from Mathurā—wearing white garments, very tall, and red-complexioned—has arrived; because at that very moment no recollection of him arises due to the absence of a corresponding mental impression (*yogya-smaraṇa*), he determines his non-existence at that time, even without the operation of the sense organs.
Nor should it be argued that the non-existence perceived in the morning is what is being remembered now.
Because at that time, the counter-positive, Mathura, does not ascend to the mind in any way whatsoever,
and because the cognition of the absence of an entity is impossible when its counter-positive is not present to the mind;
and thus, even in cases where the absence of an object existing in a nearby space and time is perceived right now by one whose sensory activity has not ceased—

Even in that case, since it is possible for the non-arising of a cognition of the object to be the cause— given that its causal capacity is already established— it is not possible to postulate the sense organ as the cause.
Therefore, absence is not perceptible,
nor is it inferable.
Because it is impossible to grasp the relationship of any mark with that which is unknown.

As for what is said by some in this regard— that the existence of the perceptible is pervaded by its perception, and therefore, by the cessation of the pervader (perception), the cessation of the pervaded (the perceptible) is determined— that is refuted.

For one who infers the cessation of the pervaded from the cessation of the pervader must necessarily perceive both cessations in the instances of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), and only then can the cessation of the perceptible be inferred.
Furthermore, since negation (*nivṛtti*) is of the nature of non-existence, its apprehension through perception is not possible;

if it were to be inferred by means of another negation, that too, being of the nature of negation, would have to be inferred by yet another negation, and that one likewise—thus resulting in an infinite regress.
Therefore, non-existence must necessarily be cognized through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Once that [object] has been cognized, let there subsequently be inference; thus, the status of non-existence (*abhāva*) as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established. As for verbal testimony, comparison, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), they need not even be considered here.
Therefore, the sixth means of valid cognition is established.
And there are exactly these many means of valid cognition.

As for the additional means of knowledge called *saṃbhava* (probability), which some maintain to be the cognition of a number such as "hundred" as a constituent part of a number such as "thousand," or the cognition of the measure of a *kuḍava* as a constituent part of the measure of an *āḍhaka*— that is in fact nothing but inference (*anumāna*), because its cause is invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Furthermore, traditional lore (*aitihya*) such as "At every banyan tree dwells Vaiśravaṇa" and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge at all, due to the absence of certainty.
Or even if it were valid, since it is included within scripture (āgama), it is not a separate means of knowledge.
Furthermore, some accept a means of knowledge called "intuition" (prātibha), such as [the thought] "your brother will come tomorrow," but that arises from fallacious signs (liṅga) and the like.
Precisely because it lacks decisiveness, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Therefore, that which the followers of Kāśyapa have relied upon—the fact that the nature of dharma and adharma for the sages is to be understood through intuition (*pratibhā*)—is without substance.
Furthermore, worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) is also included within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, it is not a separate means of knowledge.
Therefore, there are only six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus it is said in the *Bhagavad-Rāmāyaṇa*: "O Rāma, there are six methods in the world by which everything is perceived.
This concludes the doctrine of non-existence (*abhāvavāda*).
An objection regarding the injunctions for results such as the Citrā sacrifice, which pertain to this world.

Having established the thesis that "dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (codanā-lakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ) on the grounds that perception and the other means of knowledge possess intrinsic validity—as is observed in common worldly experience—and that the scripture (śāstra) included therein likewise possesses intrinsic validity, [the opponent] now challenges its authority by means of the sūtra: "It is not a source of knowledge, because it is the apprehension of what is already present" (animittaṃ vidyamānopalambhanatvāt). This challenge is raised by pointing out the non-correspondence and even the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding those Vedic injunctions for rites such as the Citrā sacrifice, which have results expected in this life.

As for the objection previously stated, "But surely [the Veda] does not describe things as they truly are," that refers to the domain of injunctions such as those concerning the desire for heaven, which has the afterlife as its fruit; thus, because the subject matters differ, there is no tautology.

But surely, since one might say that an injunction (*codanā*) could express even an object that is not as it is, this objection applies without distinction due to the acceptance of the injunction alone; so too here, when this [action] existed, it did not then yield a fruit; and when the fruit arises, it no longer exists—how can that which is non-existent yield a fruit? Since this objection is equally applicable to injunctions such as "one who desires heaven," there is no difference between them, and thus no distinction in their scope.
It is said: First of all, the initial objection concerns only the matter of results pertaining to the next world;
for in that case, verbal testimony (śabda) depends upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is not an independent authority.
Furthermore, there exists no other means of valid cognition regarding the subject matter of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*); therefore, the objection is that the injunction is not a valid authority.
And this [injunction] pertains exclusively to results in the next world.

For, regarding injunctions concerning the desire for cattle and the like, if the cattle and so forth were perceived immediately after the ritual act, then the authority of the injunction would be established by obtaining its required foundational means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

But if they are not perceived, then its authority can only be asserted by means of sublation by another means of knowledge; what, then, is the point of this obsession with demonstrating a formal similarity to an objection?
Therefore, that [inquiry] concerns only objects whose fruits are in the next world,
whereas this one concerns objects whose fruits are in this life;
for it is not possible to negate a fruit belonging to the next world simply because it is not perceived in the immediately following time.
For it cannot be immediate [to that],
because it has been cultivated in another birth.
[Objection: But how can that which is non-existent bestow a fruit? This [objection] is equal [to yours]. [Reply:
We say it is not so, because it is possible by means of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).

For heaven, by its very nature, is to be experienced in another body; thus, since it cannot occur immediately, at the very time of determining the meaning of the scripture, it is ascertained to occur at a later time only by including the *apūrva*.

In that case, the meaning of the scripture (*śāstrārtha*) is ascertained, and because that [result] is long-lasting due to the non-destruction of its cause, the production of heaven at a later time is possible. However, since animals and the like can be produced immediately, when sacrifices such as the *citrā* are enjoined as the means for those [results], at the time of ascertaining the meaning of the scripture—

Since there is no reason whatsoever for relying on a prior conduit (*praṇāḍī*), it is determined that the meaning of the scripture is that the action is the means to the fruit by its very nature. Consequently, the result must follow immediately; for at a later time, the essential nature of the action (*karmasvarūpa*) has perished and thus lacks causal efficacy.
And since the result is not perceived immediately thereafter, it is refuted; thus, the injunctions for the Citrā sacrifice and others lack authoritative validity.
Regarding the objections and refutations concerning injunctions such as those for painting [images] and so forth:

it is not possible to include the *apūrva* (unseen potency) within the meaning of the scripture merely because the fruit is not perceived immediately after the performance of the rite. For the performance of a rite is preceded by the ascertainment of the scriptural meaning, and not preceded by the performance itself.
Therefore, since these [rites] pertain to this world (*aihika*), there is no objection here; thus, a distinction of subject matter is appropriate.
Furthermore, the logical principle (*nyāya*) also differs according to the difference in the subject matter.

In the case of those [actions] whose fruit is the next world, the logical principle is that of "objection" (*ākṣepa*), because of the requirement for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Here, however, it is the logical principle of "contradiction with another means of valid cognition. Thus, there is no tautology due to this difference in logical principles.
Alternatively, while previously explaining the sūtras according to his own view, [the author] demonstrated the objection already formulated in the sūtra itself;
now, however, the objection is raised by means of the sūtra itself according to the view of the Vṛttikāra.
Therefore, in this context,
it is investigated whether sentences such as those concerning the painting and so forth are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not;
and for that purpose, it is examined whether they are contradicted by other means of knowledge or not.
In this regard, because the results that ought to be perceived immediately after [the performance of rituals] are not perceived, it is understood that paintings and the like do not bring them about.
Thus, since non-contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is necessarily present, their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) follows from its absence.

In some cases, however, there is invalidity due to contradiction with perception, as in the case of the statement: "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhī*), goes directly to heaven. For the term *yajñāyudhī* refers to the body because of its connection with the sacrificial implements;
likewise, the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) denotes the agent and expresses that [body] alone, not the Self.
This is because it is impossible for the Self—which is held to be omnipresent and devoid of action—to be an agent, and because it lacks any connection with the sacrificial implements.
Furthermore, this term "yajñāyudhin" (possessor of sacrificial implements) intends a connection [of the implements] with the body for the purpose of praising the piling of the vessels;

it does not intend a relationship of ownership between the self and the implements. This is because such a connection is possible even prior to the piling of the vessels. Moreover, the departure of the body to heaven contradicts direct perception.
Nor is it possible at any other time;
for since the word "goes" (yāti) is an expression in the present tense,
and because that [going] is impossible even at another time for one who has been reduced to ashes.
Furthermore, there exists no self (ātman) distinct from the body; therefore, [the Veda] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Thus, since even that which is authorless (*apauruṣeya*) lacks validity, it is not reasonable to place trust in an injunction such as "one who desires heaven [should sacrifice]," and consequently, its lack of validity is established.

Thus, when the validity [of verbal testimony] has been challenged by contradiction with perception—both through non-perception of the object and through direct perceptual contradiction—the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī), disregarding the resolution of such contradictions, demonstrates the previously stated self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) as the proof for his own position by means of refuting defects in the cause: "But the relation of a word with its meaning is innate; its cognition is instruction. (JS 1.1.5)

For previously, since the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of perception and the other means of knowledge is established in the world, and since the scripture (*śāstra*) is included therein, it was stated that the scripture is indeed a valid means of knowledge because it lacks human intervention and because verbal defects depend upon persons; thus, the scripture is faultless. This concludes the discussion on the objection regarding the variegated nature [of the world] (*citrākṣepavāda*).
The refutation of the relationship between word and meaning:

Having thus rejected the lack of authority on the grounds of the eternity of the relationship and having established intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), the opponent speaks again: "This may be so; however, there is no relationship at all between the word and its meaning; how then can it be either human-made (*pauruṣeya*) or not human-made (*apauruṣeya*)?"

For instance, there is no conjunction [between the word and its meaning], because if such were the case, then upon the utterance of words such as "razor," the primary object itself would undergo cutting.
Nor is there a causal relationship,
since both are eternal.

Now, one might argue that because the external word and its object are difficult to define—due to the dilemmas regarding phonemes, *sphoṭa*, universals (*jāti*), and so forth, as well as the dilemmas regarding individuals, forms (*ākṛti*), and their relations—the word is simply the cognition itself having the form of the letter *ga* and so on, and the object is simply the cognition produced by that which has the form of a cow and so on; thus, the relation between word and object is merely that of cause and effect.
This is not so.
Because knowledge without an object does not arise,
no other kind of relation should even be suspected.
If it is argued that the relationship consists in being the signified and the signifier, we say no;
for in the absence of a relationship, the state of being a signifier is impossible.
It is precisely this that is being examined: by what relation does a word convey its meaning?
In this regard, to claim that it conveys the meaning simply because it is a conveyor would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*);
therefore, no such relation exists.

And since there can be no cognition of one thing based on another thing in the absence of a relationship, the cognition of word-meanings— which lacks a determined specific cause and is therefore accidental like dream-cognition— is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
however, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) might somehow still be possible through other means of knowledge even if the validity of words were non-existent.
But Vedic practice, because it relies solely on verbal testimony and lacks a perceptible foundation, would not be worthy of respect.
This would indeed be so if there were no connection between word and meaning;
however, since there is a connection—namely, that which consists in being signified (pratyāyya)—this very thing will constitute the connection.

Furthermore, that communication of meaning which, unlike the senses or logical marks, does not depend on connections such as sensory contact (saṃnikarṣa) or pervasion (vyāpti), is precisely what is called "denotation" (abhidhāna).
And that very thing is the state of being the designation and the designated;
therefore, it is said that the relationship has the characteristic of the designation and the designated.
Furthermore, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the communication of meaning by a word?
It is simply the comprehension of the meaning immediately following the word.
But is this not established solely through the inference of the speaker’s intention?
We say: no.
For even by means of words devoid of intended meaning—such as those uttered involuntarily during states like deep sleep—a comprehension of meaning is observed.

Likewise, a Vedic sentence, whether composed by another person or being apauruṣeya (authorless), certainly generates a cognition of its meaning for those who are proficient in language, even when it is employed by people ignorant of its sense.
Therefore, a word is that which causes comprehension.
Why, then, does it not cause comprehension upon the first hearing?
Because of the absence of auxiliary factors; for the grasping of the word as a name is also a necessary factor for the word's causing comprehension of its meaning, just as light is for the eye.
Therefore, there is no fault, because it conveys the meaning only to that person who has previously understood from other people that "this word is the name for this object," and not to anyone else.
An objection regarding the non-eternality of the relationship between word and meaning:
"Granted, let there indeed be such a relationship;
however, by your very statement, it follows that this relationship is of human origin."
For indeed, there is no relationship between a word and its object such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or identity (*tādātmya*), but rather the capacity to convey meaning (*pratyāyakatva*).
And it has been stated that this [capacity] is dependent upon a person;

therefore, just as in the case of words such as "Devadatta," once a relationship is established in the form "this is the name for this object," the word subsequently conveys the meaning. Thus, its human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) is established.

Thus ends the objection regarding the relationship. Without having resolved the permanence of the relationship previously raised, [the author now asks] with what connection or for what purpose [he asks], "Now, in the case of 'cow' (gauḥ), what is the word? First, the nature of the word is examined as a relevant digression, since the relationship was introduced and the two relata—the word and its meaning—are also under discussion.
As for the purpose, it is the establishment of the reality of the *ūha* (modification) and other operations which depend upon those [word-components].
For if the expressive unit—whether it be a sentence or a word—is partless, then because its constituent parts would be false, the functions dependent upon them would also be false.
Furthermore, in order to establish their connection, the expressive nature (*vācakatva*) of the phonemes must necessarily be demonstrated;

otherwise, due to the absence of such a connection, their status as expressers would lack a substratum and thus could not exist, let alone their eternity. Therefore, to demonstrate that expressive nature for the sake of establishing those [qualities], one must first determine the nature of the word:
in the case of "cow" (*gauḥ*), are the phonemes themselves the word?
Now, this point— that [the word] is something distinct from those [phonemes]— is primarily investigated here.
The refutation of the phoneme-parts (*varṇāvayava*), the universal of phonemeness (*gatva*), and the universal of the word-part (*gośabdāvayavijāti*) is incidental,
intended to support the determination that the phonemes alone constitute the word.
In this regard, the Arhats maintain that it is also incorrect to designate phonemes (*varṇa*) as the constituent parts of a person (*pudgala*), because their constituent parts are not perceived.
To begin with, the constituent parts are not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because there is no apprehension of completeness or deficiency among the phonemes.
Not by inference,
because no logical mark (liṅga) has been perceived as being related to them;
nor is it [known] through general observation (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa).
For it is not necessarily the case that whatever object exists must possess parts,
because atoms are partless.
If it is argued that even those [atoms] possess parts, then...
The parts of that [whole] would likewise be so, and those beyond them as well; thus, a single whole such as a bean would possess infinite parts.
Consequently, the entire world would be pervaded by a single bean or sesame seed, because those infinite corporeal parts, not yielding space to one another, would occupy infinite locations.
Therefore, atoms and phonemes are partless;
likewise, the universal *gatva* and the universal *autva* are entirely devoid of any basis in valid cognition.

But surely, since a universal (*jāti*) is recognized across the fast, slow, and medium tempos; across the acute, grave, and circumflex accents; and across the nasalized and non-nasalized vowels, as well as the short, long, and protracted durations—how can it be asserted that such a universal does not exist?
True.
As for recognition,
that recognition is established precisely because of the identity of the individual manifestation.

However, the appearance of distinctions such as "fast" and so forth—which has as its objective support the distinct states of being fast and so on—is not capable of bringing about a distinction in the individual entity (*vyakti*).
This concludes the refutation of universals such as *gatva*.
Furthermore, the appearance of both difference and non-difference occurs in two ways.

In some cases, the difference has the property-bearer (*dharmin*) as its object, as when the universal (*jāti*) acquires its own nature through instances such as a brindled cow, thinking "this is a cow," "this is a cow," and so on.

In other cases, however, there is the appearance of the absence of difference and the appearance of non-difference from the property (*dharma*), which takes the property-bearer as its objective support—such as in the case of the very same Devadatta, where one says "he is young," "he is old," or "he is thin"; in that case, a universal is not admitted.

Thus, in this case, regarding [the phonemes] such as the fast (*druta*) and so forth, there is non-difference with respect to the substratum (*dharmī*), but there is difference with respect to the property (*dharma*). For instance, the appearance here is such that one thinks,

"This letter *a* was pronounced fast by this person" or "it was pronounced slow by this person," but not "this letter *a* is fast" or "this one is slow"— [otherwise] one would have to admit both a difference in the substratum and a universal (*jāti*).
Now, one might object: since emaciation and the like occur successively, their coexistence in a single Devadatta is logical;
however, how can phonetic properties such as nasality—which are inherent in a phoneme uttered simultaneously by multiple speakers—have a single phoneme as their locus?
For a single substratum does not simultaneously sustain contradictory properties.
True; however,
these are not properties of the phonemes (*varṇa*) in the ultimate sense, but rather properties of the sound (*dhvani*), which merely appear as such in the phoneme,
just as when a face is seen simultaneously in both a small and a large mirror, [the face appears to possess] smallness and largeness respectively.

Therefore, there is no contradiction even if the phoneme (*varṇa*) is a single individual; thus, the universal (*jāti*) such as "g-ness" (*gatva*) and so forth lacks any basis in authoritative cognition (*aprāmāṇika*).

In this way, even the composite whole (*avayavin*) consisting of the word "go" cannot be produced, because the phonemes such as *ga* and the rest do not occur simultaneously and because they are all-pervading (*sarvagata*), thus lacking the capacity to initiate a composite whole.

For in every case, the dimension of the effect is greater than the dimension of the cause, as in the case of a cloth compared to its threads; however, no increase in dimension can occur from the phonemes, which are all-pervading (*vibhu*).
Therefore, there is no composite whole (*avayavin*) here;
and in its absence, the property of being the word "cow" (*gośabdatva*), which would have that as its substratum, is cast far away.
Consequently, the phoneme (*varṇa*) alone is the word (*śabda*).
He said: "We accept this— that the doctrine of the part and the whole and so forth does not exist— but we do not accept that phonemes alone are words,
because the cognition of meaning would otherwise be impossible."
For instance: the cognition of meaning does not arise from the cognition of a single syllable alone.
And because speech proceeds sequentially, simultaneity is not possible.
It is said: Just as the rites beginning with the Āgneya, although they occur in a sequential order, [are performed together].
In the same way, our social classes (varṇas) likewise perform their duties together for a single purpose.
[The view is that] phonemes possess the capacity to convey meaning.

[Objection: But surely, even for those things that occur sequentially, their simultaneity is possible by virtue of the *apūrva* produced by their arising; however, how can this be the case for phonemes?
For those [subsidiary rites] as well, there will be [an apūrva] through the *saṃskāra*. What is the proof for its existence?
It is the very same as that which exists in the case of the *āgneya* and other [principal sacrifices].

For just as in their case, since the scripture reveals that they act in combination (*saṃhatyakāritā*) while such [combination] is impossible in terms of their own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), an *apūrva* is postulated as the medium.

Likewise, since letters are not observed to convey meaning individually, but are understood when uttered in their entirety, it is established that they act in combination; therefore, given that this is impossible in their own inherent form, the postulation of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is entirely appropriate.
And just as in that case, a single agent and a specific order are required, because no expression of meaning is observed when these are reversed.
Refutation of the Theory of Sphoṭa:

Now, if one were to postulate a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) for each individual phoneme, it would be simpler to postulate a single [impression]; therefore, it would be better to postulate "phoneness" (*śabdatva*) as a single entity.
This is not so.
As if by the non-perception of what is perceptible:
for sound is admitted to be graspable by direct perception,
yet nothing at all is manifested by direct perception.
Therefore, we understand that it does not exist.
For even you, having postulated the nature of "soundness" (śabdatva), must necessarily further postulate a refinement (saṃskāra);
for individual sounds do not manifest the sphoṭa individually.

And since literary composition (*sāhitya*) is likewise merely a means for [the manifestation of] mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) through successive occurrences, the conceptualization of that [succession] is identical [in both cases].
It might be thought:
each individual sound-manifestation (*nāda*) manifests the word-sound (*śabda*), and thus there is no pointlessness to the subsequent sounds.
For the preceding sounds manifest the word-sound indistinctly, while each subsequent one manifests it more and more clearly; thus, the later sounds are not purposeless.
If this is so, then only those later sounds which are capable of clear manifestation should exist, and the earlier ones would be superfluous.
Now, it is not that any single sound (*nāda*) by itself brings about its clear manifestation; rather, all of them are individually manifestors.
However, it does not appear clearly all at once; having been manifested unclearly at first, it becomes clear when heard again and again.
This is just as a mango tree standing at a distance first appears in a form common to elephants, haystacks, and the like.
When observed again, it appears as the nature of a tree; when observed yet again, it becomes manifest as the nature of a mango tree—it should be viewed in exactly that manner.
If this were so, then such a clear manifestation would occur either through those very same sounds practiced previously,
or through subsequent sounds practiced alone; in that case, resorting to sounds of a different kind would be useless.

For if each [sound] were individually the manifestor, then there would be an unclear manifestation by the subsequent sounds and a clear manifestation by the preceding ones; consequently, pronunciation could even occur in reverse order.

Therefore, since one must rely on a combination of multiple heterogeneous sounds possessing a specific required sequence, one must necessarily accept that the *sphoṭa* is manifested by the final sound accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the preceding sounds.
The postulation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is equal [for both sides].

Or rather, this postulation of another latent impression belongs to you alone; in my view, however, the comprehension of the object is established by the very latent impressions that are the causes of memory, so that no further latent impression need be postulated.
[Objection: But will not those same [cognitions] belong to me as well? [Reply: No;
because they have no function other than memory.
In my position, however, it is the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) themselves that produce the comprehension of the object by producing memory.

For instance, by means of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced through the experience of each individual phoneme acting in concert, a single memory is generated that has all the phonemes as its object.
And within that memory, the phonemes appearing simultaneously produce the cognition of the meaning in combination, even without any further intervening mental impressions.
In your view, however, this is not possible;
for indeed, the sounds (nāda) do not manifest the sphoṭa by being themselves cognized,
nor is there simultaneous existence [of the sounds], because they occur sequentially.
Therefore, since concomitance occurs solely through the medium of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the postulation of additional impressions is unavoidable.
Now, it might be thought: "True, the manifestation of the sphoṭa does not occur through the causes of memory;

however, those impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by sound, residing in the auditory organ, which are the causes for the perception of the phonemes—by those alone will the manifestation of the sphoṭa occur, just as it does for the phonemes. What is the use of postulating further impressions?"
That is incorrect, because those [impressions] are momentary;
for the impression that is the cause for the perception of the first syllable does not persist at the time of hearing the final syllable.

If they were to persist, then even at the time of hearing the *visarjanīya*, the hearing of the letter *ga* would continue; therefore, they are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgin*), and consequently, they cannot collectively manifest the *sphoṭa*.
And it has been stated that if each [letter] were manifested individually, the subsequent ones would be purposeless.

Alternatively, the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*) consists solely in its conjunction with the sound (*dhvani*), and nothing else; and it has already been stated that this [conjunction] is clearly transitory. //3//

Alternatively, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ is nothing other than its conjunction with sound; and since sounds are transitory, it is quite evident that this [conjunction] is fragile. Therefore, other enduring refinements must be postulated.
Thus, it would follow that one must postulate a word distinct from the phonemes, which results in an abundance of unproven assumptions.
In my position, however, since the phonemes existing within a firm recollection are the expressive agents, nothing is lacking.

Now, if it were the case that letters are denotative when remembered simultaneously, then letters pronounced even in reverse order would be denotative; this is not so, because their sequence is also an essential factor.
But what is this sequence that serves as an essential factor?
For phonemes, being all-pervading and eternal by their very nature, do not possess sequential order;
nor does the sequence belong to the cognition, since that cognition, being of the nature of memory, is unitary.
In that case, there is no fault, for the sequence of sounds (dhvani) which is superimposed upon the phonemes (varṇas) and appears [in consciousness] is the constituent factor.

Therefore, it is established that the phonemes—which are being remembered as possessing that [sequence] due to its superimposition upon them by means of the sequential manifesting sounds—are the expressive agents; there is no other word.
Thus concludes the doctrine of the sphoṭa.

The commencement of the exposition on categories: Now, under the guise of commencing an exposition on the denoted object by asking "What is the meaning of this word 'cow'?", [the author] establishes the existence of the generic form (*ākṛti*) for the sake of proving the eternity of the relationship [between word and meaning]. For if the generic form did not exist, the non-human (eternal) relationship of the word with individual instances could not exist, because those individuals are impermanent.

Since there is no eternal entity even for that which serves as a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa), and thus no universal form (ākṛti) exists, it is therefore deliberated whether the universal form exists or not.
However, once its existence has been established, it will be stated in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that this very [universal form] is the denotation of the word.
The refutation of the universal (*jāti*) according to the Buddhist view:
In this regard, the followers of the Sugata, considering only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) to be the ultimate reality, do not accept the existence of a generic form (*ākṛti*).
For instance: "If the universal were distinct from the individual, it would be perceived as something separate."
If there were no difference [between the universal and the individual], there would be mere manifestation; if you say it is twofold, that is not so, because of contradiction.
For it is not possible for that very same [universal] to be both different from and non-different from [the individual], because difference and non-difference are contradictory.
Furthermore, if the universal were distinct [from the individuals], would it be all-pervading or restricted to the individuals alone?
It cannot be all-pervading.
Because it is not perceived in the interval.
If [the universal] resides in the individual, then since it was previously non-existent in that location when the individual has arisen, how could it be perceived therein?
For it does not arise there [at that moment].
Because it is impossible for that which is eternal to arise,
and because it is immaterial, it does not come from another individual instance.
Furthermore, it would follow that [the universal] could not be perceived in another individual instance;
nor can it be said that it remains in that very place while arriving with one part and staying with another, because it is eternal;
nor does it go elsewhere, because it is formless.
Furthermore, since the universal (jāti) was not previously present in another individual, it would be perceived as doubled upon its subsequent entry;
as they say: "It does not come from elsewhere, nor did it exist there before, nor does it consist of parts."
Alas, it first abandons its very support—how great is this succession of calamities! //10//
And as for its subsistence in individuals: if it were to subsist in one individual in its entirety, it would not exist in other individuals;
for a single entity cannot simultaneously subsist in its entirety in many places.
Since it is a single entity, it is incapable of subsisting in its entirety in multiple locations at once.
Nor does it exist by way of parts, because it is partless.

And how could a subsistence by way of parts be possible in various individual instances that are past, future, and present? Furthermore, if it were to subsist in an individual instance, it would experience the cognition of "this-ness" (idampratyaya) regarding that instance.

If [the universal] were to exist in individual instances—past, future, and present—it would have to exist in them part by part; and in each individual instance, it would experience the cognition of "this-ness" (idantā) as being present. However, no one has the cognition that "here is cowness"; rather, the cognition is "this is a cow."
Now, if it is argued that the universal (*jāti*) is the very self of the individual (*vyakti*) and not a separate entity serving as its substratum, this is not tenable.

For how could the universal—being unitary in form, eternal, and of a persistent nature—be the self of individuals that are manifold, impermanent, and of distinct natures? This would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a total confusion of the three worlds.
Furthermore, no means of valid cognition whatsoever is possible for the existence of a generic form (*ākṛti*); first of all, it is not perception,
because it is admitted that a universal (*jāti*) does not produce a cognition of itself.
And because eternal things lack the capacity for any purposeful activity;
for a universal (jāti) does not produce a cognition of its own object, since its eternity is admitted,
and because eternal things lack the capacity for any purposeful activity.
Furthermore, it is not possible for that which is not a cause [of cognition] to be an object, because being an object is defined by that very characteristic.
Therefore, the universal is merely the form of conceptual construction, or it is false.
But surely, [it may be argued] that this is because the variety of cognitions is logically established?

Even though conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are devoid of an object, they arise as if possessing the conceit of being the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) capable of performing various purposeful actions.

By engaging one who seeks practical activity (*vyavahāra*) therein, and by leading him to that [object] through a causal lineage originating from it—just as the cognition of a jewel regarding the luster of a jewel leads to the jewel itself—they do not contradict worldly practice (*lokayātrā*). Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the maintenance of worldly affairs.
Therefore, there is no birth.
By this, the substance consisting of a whole (*avayavidravya*) is refuted, for that too cannot withstand the conceptual analysis of its parts and so forth.

The appearance of grossness, however, is accounted for solely by the influence of multiple atoms of color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities aggregated together— just like the appearance of a mass of hair— and is therefore not sufficient to justify the postulation of a composite whole.
And in the absence of that [individual], since there would be no substratum, universals such as "cowness" and so forth are cast far away [as impossible].

How is it that, in the absence of a single common nature (*sāmānya*), individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) which are utterly distinct produce a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a non-distinct form?

And if they do produce it, why do some produce only a conceptual construction of a cow, while others produce only a conceptual construction of a horse, rather than all [of them] producing every [conceptual construction]?

Furthermore, for one who maintains the existence of a universal (*sāmānya*), how do individual entities (*vyakti*)—which possess distinct characteristics—partake in having a nature consisting of a distinct universal, or being its substratum, or being its manifestor?
If they do so partake, why is it that only certain individuals are connected with only certain universals, and not all [individuals] with all [universals]?
If you say it is due to their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then...
This answer is equally applicable to us as well.
The establishment of the universal (*jāti*) is according to our own view.

Now, if for the sake of establishing the connection of individuals with a non-distinct form of the universal, one were to admit a supreme non-distinct form [of that universal], then, for the sake of establishing the connection by means of that as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the dependence on further and further universals.
Therefore, this is merely conceptual construction;
in ultimate reality, there is no such thing as a universal.
To this it is replied: How can a universal, established by the power of direct perception, be subverted by fallacious reasoning?
Indeed, it is impossible to deny this, for that [consciousness] triumphs over everything.

In all things, perception— which arises unerringly across different places, times, and conditions, possessing both excluded and inclusive forms such as "this too is a cow, this too is a cow," or "this too is a tree, this too"—
establishes the object as having a dual nature; who else could possibly subvert this, which overcomes every semblance of reasoning?
For there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) more powerful than that, because all other means of valid cognition are rooted in it and thus lack the capacity to sublate it.
Furthermore, even inferences, since they depend upon universals (sāmānya), actually support the universal all the more; they are not able to sublate it.
For that which depends on something else cannot invalidate it;
for if it were to invalidate it, its own self would also not be established, since it too depends upon that [very thing].
For instance, one who rejects the universal by means of the dilemma of difference or non-difference must necessarily say this: whatever is a real entity is either different or non-different;
if the universal were also a real entity, it too would have to be either different or non-different.
Since neither of these two possibilities is possible, it follows that it is not a real entity.
And by speaking in this way, the universal "reality" (*vastutva*) must be admitted;
otherwise, how could it be possible to say that because reality is pervaded by both difference and non-difference, the reality of a universal is impossible due to the non-perception of its pervader?
[Objection: Surely the word *vastu* (entity) is based on an adjunct (*upādhi*) and does not have "genus" (*jāti*) as its cause; how then can the attainment of a genus be expressed by it?
[Reply: It is said: Whether it be a genus or an adjunct, in any case, a form of generality must necessarily be required.
For even those things that are based on adjuncts cannot acquire their own nature without a single underlying indicator.

Furthermore, for the Buddhist who maintains that the entire range of entities consists solely of mutually exclusive (vyāvṛtta) natures, not even the slightest recurring (anuvṛtta) form is possible anywhere; thus, conventional usage based on adjuncts (aupādhika) would be untenable.
Therefore, the universal (sāmānya), which is established by all means of valid cognition, cannot be denied.
What, then, is the rebuttal of these objections?

It has already been stated that even if they were not rebutted, they would not be able to deny the universal (*sāmānya*), because those [objections] themselves depend upon it; nevertheless, the rebuttal is now set forth.
An investigation into the difference and non-difference between the genus and the individual.
Regarding the dilemma of difference and non-difference, some say: the universal is indeed different from the individuals;
nor does it follow that it would be perceived separately, because it is related to the individuals.
But what is this relation? It is inherence (*samavāya*).
But what is this?
Some say it is the relation that is the cause of the notion of "here" (*ihapratyaya*) among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*). That is not correct.
Because the cognition "this is here" is not established;
for everyone always has the cognition "this is a cow," but never the cognition "here is cowness. And what is this inseparable inherence (ayutasiddhi)?
There is an absence of separate establishment (yutasiddhi). What, then, is separate establishment?
It is either the state of having separate motion or the state of resting upon separate substrata.
The absence of that [separateness] is inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*).

If this were so, the relation between part and whole would not be inherence (*samavāya*), because the parts would move even without the movement of the whole, since both the whole and the parts would reside in their own respective parts.
Likewise, since a universal has an individual as its locus, and an individual resides in its own parts, there exists a relation of distinct loci and located; thus, inherence (samavāya) is untenable.

Therefore, it must be stated as follows: that relation by which the contained produces in the container a cognition conforming to itself—that is, makes it known through its own form—is [the defining characteristic of the relation].
That relation is inherence (*samavāya*).

If the individual is perceived by way of its universal nature, then by the force of that very perception, the non-difference between the universal and the individual necessarily follows; how, then, can their difference be admitted?
It is replied: in both cases—"This is a spotted cow" and "This is a black cow"—the form of "cow" is seen to persist, whereas the forms of "spotted" and "black" are excluded.

Even if there were non-difference between those two—the spotted cow and the form of "cow"—then upon the persistence of one, the other would also persist, or upon the exclusion of the latter, the form of "cow" would also be excluded.

Furthermore, even when that very individual is perceived as having the nature of a cow in the cognition "this is a cow," these two cognitions do not appear to be synonyms like "cow" and "bovine"; therefore, there is no non-difference.

How, then, is the identity of form (*tādrūpya*) of the individual (*vyakti*) perceived? For this very thing is the identity of form of the individual: namely, its inherence (*samavāya*) as a relation.
This is its power (*mahiman*), by which it colors the substratum with its own cognition; therefore, there is no fault.
Alternatively, let there be non-difference as well, due to the cognition of identity;
yet by the previously stated reasoning, there is also difference.
Therefore, by the force of valid cognition, it is logical that they are indeed both different and non-different. //3//
[Objection: But how can difference and non-difference, being contradictory, exist in one and the same thing? [Response: There is no contradiction, because they are observed together.
For if difference and non-difference were perceived through mutual exclusion—like "this is silver" and "this is not silver"—then they would indeed be contradictory;
but there is no such perception of them through mutual exclusion. Rather, the two cognitions "this is a cow" appear simultaneously as a single [entity].
He establishes that the entity possesses a dual nature: for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) brings about non-difference, while non-synonymy brings about difference;
therefore, there is no contradiction due to the force of cognition.

And because of the difference in perspective (*apekṣābheda*). For instance, when the universal (*jāti*) is determined through its own form as "cow," the individual (*vyakti*) is perceived as non-different from it, as in: "This is a cow; this is a *śābaleya*. But when the universal is determined through the nature of another individual, then that very same individual is apprehended as having a distinct form, as in: "That *gauḥ* which is a *bāhuleya* is not this *śābaleya*."
In this way, for a substance as a substratum (*dharmin*),
there is difference from color and so forth by way of its other attributes such as taste, while there is non-difference [from them] by way of its nature as a substance.

Likewise, it should be inferred that for a whole (*avayavin*), there is non-difference from its parts by way of its own nature, whereas there is difference from its parts by way of the form of other parts.

In this regard, just as the contradictory natures of long and short and so forth are accepted— even when they reside in a single locus— as non-contradictory due to a difference in relativity on the strength of perception, so too should it be understood for difference and non-difference, since there is no distinction in their being perceived in the substance.
An objection regarding the non-co-referentiality of difference and non-difference according to the Prābhākara view:

Someone else, however, says that a cognition appearing as both difference and non-difference is simply not possible; for a cognition of a distinct form is indeed the manifestation of difference. Thus, at the time when difference is manifested, the universal form and the individual form must have been cognized.
Therefore, at the time of the cognition of non-difference, one of those two must be cognized;
in that case, there would be a double appearance of a single thing, but it does not follow that non-difference is cognized by means of the other.
Therefore, there is no cognition of both difference and non-difference in a single locus.
This argument is without substance.
For the cognition of two things is not itself the cognition of their difference, since [the cognition of difference] is absent even when those two are present.
Indeed, even when an individual is perceived for the first time, there is a cognition of both the universal and the individual, yet at that time no difference between them is apprehended.

However, it is your own established doctrine that the distinction between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): for when one perceives another individual, the universal is recognized through its presence (*anvaya*), while the previous individual is excluded (*vyatireka*).
Likewise, having previously perceived Devadatta, one sees at a later time and from a distance Yajñadatta, who resembles him. Upon perceiving the previously observed [Devadatta]—

Even when one remembers Devadatta and perceives two persons who are in fact distinct from him, one nevertheless does not ascertain their difference; for one remains in doubt, wondering, "Is this the same Devadatta, or is it another?
Therefore, it is said that the perception of two entities is itself the perception of difference.
Likewise, [one asks] whether it is that very Devadatta or someone else;
therefore, it has been stated that the cognition of difference is simply the cognition of two distinct entities.

Likewise, when one sees that very same Devadatta at a distance at another time, even while doubting whether "is this the same person or another," and even though perceiving him as a single entity according to the actual state of things, one is not able to ascertain his non-difference;
therefore, the perception of two distinct entities is not itself the perception of difference.
Nor is the cognition of a single object itself the cognition of non-difference;
rather, the appearance of difference is the cognition "this is other," while the appearance of non-difference is the cognition "this is not other.
And there exists [the cognition] of one perceiving a *śābaleya* and a *bāhuleya*: "this..."
The appearance of non-difference is in the cognition "this is white" and "it is a cow," while the appearance of difference is in the cognition "the brindled one is different from the black one.
Therefore, its nature as both different and non-different is established.

But surely, the universal (jāti) is pervasive, eternal, and characterized by neither arising nor perishing, whereas the individual (vyakti) possesses a nature contrary to these; how, then, can there be identity between the two?

Indeed, it is impossible for a single entity to be both inclusive and exclusive, eternal and non-eternal, subject to arising and destruction and yet devoid of those properties, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of a total confusion of the three worlds;
likewise, the universal (*jāti*) would possess properties such as non-eternality, and the individual (*vyakti*) would possess properties such as eternality.
This is not a fault.
For that entity, possessing various forms, will not be contradictory insofar as it bears permanence and so forth through one form, and impermanence and so forth through another.
Even the universal (jāti) is impermanent in the form of the individual (vyakti), and the individual is permanent in its nature as the universal; thus, there is no undesirable consequence here.
The objection regarding the omnipresence of the universal (*jāti*) and its refutation.
As for the alternative proposed— that the universal is either omnipresent or resides in the individual—
that too is refuted by the very statement that it is identical with the individual;
for how could this, being the very self of the individual, exist elsewhere?
Now, if this is so, how can a universal (*jāti*), which did not exist in the location of an individual (*vyakti*) prior to the production of that individual, come to exist there afterwards?

An individual, being produced from its own causes, arises as already connected with the specific nature of the universal, because the universal is eternal. Furthermore, it does not come from elsewhere, because it is formless (*amūrta*).

It is said: Even that which, having come from another location, becomes conjoined with this [present] location, was previously non-existent in this location; how then does it experience conjunction with this location? It is by virtue of causal factors (*kāraṇavaśāt*).
In the same way, a universal (*jāti*) also experiences connection with an individual (*vyakti*) solely by virtue of causal factors.

However, there is this distinction: that which is being conjoined, having been situated previously, first conjoins with the immediately adjacent location, and thereafter with the location beyond that; thus, it proceeds to conjunction with other locations in a sequential manner.
As for identity (*tādātmya*) and inherence (*samavāya*), however, their production from their own causes occurs without depending on an immediately adjacent location.
Indeed, the very nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) cannot be accepted as being identical to that of identity or inherence,
because there is no evidence for such a claim.
Because things possess a nature that is characterized by difference,
there is therefore no fault.
Alternatively, even if the universal (*sāmānya*) is omnipresent, there is no consequence of its being perceived everywhere, because it is manifested only by particular individuals (*vyakti*).
Furthermore, although the universal is omnipresent, it is either identical with the individual itself or inheres within it.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the universal occurs through the contact of *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in that which is conjoined).
Since this contact is possible only in the location of the individual (*vyakti*) and not elsewhere, there is no apprehension [of the universal] everywhere.

Even though there is non-difference between the genus and the individual, because difference also exists—as in the case of [the attributes of] eternality and non-eternality—it is not illogical that it [the universal] should be both omnipresent and non-omnipresent.
As for the alternative proposed— that [the universal] exists either in its entirety or by way of its parts—
that too is incorrect;
for "entirety" presupposes difference, and there is no difference in the universal either in terms of its own nature or in terms of its parts, because it is unitary and partless.
Precisely because it is partless, a mode of existence based on parts is simply impossible.

Therefore, one can only say here, on the basis of valid cognition, that "the genus exists in individuals," since there is no means of knowledge for, and indeed no possibility of, a division into wholes and parts.

Likewise, even for a whole (*avayavin*), existence in its parts cannot be "in its entirety" (*kārtsnya*), because multiplicity is absent and the conventional usage of "entirety" is dependent upon that [multiplicity].
Furthermore, existence "part by part" (*avayavaśas*) is also untenable due to the absence of further constituent parts.
Now, is the mode of occurrence of a universal in individuals, and of a whole in its parts, of one and the same nature?
No, it is said:
the universal resides in each [individual] separately, whereas the whole resides by pervading [its parts]; such is the distinction.

A universal (*jāti*), existing in one individual without depending on other individuals, produces a cognition corresponding to itself and is said to exist "in each" (*pratyekam*); however, its existence is not by way of pervading the whole (*kārtsnyena*).
An aggregate (*avayavin*), on the other hand, existing in a part while depending on other parts, produces a cognition of its own form and is designated as "existing pervasively" (*vyāsajya vartate*).
For a cognition of a cloth does not arise in a single thread, just as a cognition of a cow does not arise in a single individual cow.
An Investigation of Conjunction.
Now, how does conjunction (saṃyoga) subsist in the conjuncts? Is it like a universal (jāti), or like a part (avayava)?
We say it is distinct from both.
For it subsists in one conjunct in dependence upon another conjunct, not without such dependence; thus, it is not equal to a universal.
And in one and the same place, it produces a corresponding cognition: "this is conjoined with that" and "this is conjoined with that.
Therefore, even because of its being a composite whole (*avayavin*), it is not entirely identical [to the parts]; thus, there is a distinction between the two.
Now, regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*): is it one and the same for two conjoined things, or are there two distinct conjunctions corresponding to each conjoined thing?

The followers of Kāśyapa consider conjunction to be a single entity inherent in both; we, however, hold that—just as in the cases "this is similar to that" or "this is similar to that"—the similarity perceived in one thing in relation to its counterpart is distinct with respect to each substrate (*dharmī*).

Likewise, because conjunction is the object of such a cognition, we prefer [the view of] difference itself. Let us return to the subject at hand: therefore, even from the dilemma regarding the mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*), there is no denial of the universal (*jāti*).
As for the argument that because the universal is eternal, it lacks the capacity to produce a cognition of its own object and thus cannot be an object of apprehension—
That is incorrect;
we shall demonstrate in the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) that even eternal things possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).
Furthermore, being an object of cognition (*grāhyatva*) is not the defining characteristic of a cause.
For it is described in the *Śūnyavāda* that its characteristic consists in being the recipient of the fruit produced by knowledge;
therefore, this too is not a fault.

As for the claim that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of a genus (*jāti*) such as "cow" is devoid of epistemic authority because such conceptualization can arise through the experience of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves, that too is worthless.

For it is not the case that the genus is not perceived, such that this criticism would be valid; rather, the cognition that arises presents the genus which constitutes its own object. Therefore, there is no occasion for such idle chatter.

And how do individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are absolutely distinct from one another, produce a single-form cognition? For it is established that entities possessing this or that form are produced by causes possessing this or that form.

If you ask, "How then, according to your own view, can distinct particulars (*viśeṣa*) be the cause of a connection with a single-form universal (*sāmānya*)," [the answer is that they] partake in either identity (*tādātmya*) or inherence (*samavāya*).
Now, one might object: how can causes that are dissimilar produce particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) endowed with a single type of capacity?
They would not produce them if they were indeed dissimilar; however, they too are of one and the same kind.

[Objection: But in this way, if there is a dependence on a series of higher and lower universals (*jāti*) for the sake of establishing that connection, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[Response: This is not a fault;
for example, a single species of palmyra seed, through a succession of transformations, becomes connected to the palmyra species.
It produces an individual,
and that [individual] likewise produces another seed of the same genus as the seed which constitutes its own cause;
similarly, from semen of one genus, an individual of the bovine genus is produced, and in that [process],...
The production of semen of that same class does not imply an absolute identity [between the cause and effect].
Therefore, there exists a single entity—denotable by words such as "form," "class," or "universal"—which is common to and inherent in individuals such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others.
Thus ends the discussion on the theory of form (*ākṛti*). This is the refutation of similarity and other such factors as being the universal (*sāmānya*).
Furthermore, similarity itself is not the universal, because the cognition of that [similarity] does not occur.
The cognition is "this is that very same thing," not "this is similar to that";
moreover, for one who denies all universals (*sāmānya*), even similarity is impossible, because it consists of the commonality of many constituent parts.
Furthermore, even a universal in the form of exclusion from that cannot be cognized without accepting a universal in the form of a positive entity.
For one who cognizes the exclusion of the non-cow must necessarily first cognize the cow itself;
for it is not possible to cognize the individual instances such as horses by their own specific forms while setting aside the form of differentiation from those [non-cows].
Because one cannot ascend to those infinite [particulars], and because it is impossible to cognize a cow in the form of their exclusion while they have not been ascended; furthermore,
how can a universal understood as having a positive form— such as "cow, cow"— be accepted as being of the nature of an exclusion?
Therefore, this view is extremely feeble;
therefore, the universal (jāti) exists.
Thus ends the doctrine of Apoha.
An Examination of the Parts.
By this, the whole (*avayavin*) has been explained.

Regarding the dilemma as to whether that [whole] is distinct from or non-distinct from its parts, the Vaiśeṣikas assert its distinction, its relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and the production of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) therein from the qualities of the parts.

They say that those qualities which are qualified by their own inherent attributes and which serve to distinguish their own substratum from others of the same class are "specific qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
We, however, maintain that they are both different and non-different [from their substrata].
For neither a cloth nor Devadatta is perceived as something extracted apart from its constituent threads or from his head, hands, and other limbs.

The parts themselves, such as the threads and the hands, are perceived in the form of the cloth and Devadatta; and since there exists even a slight appearance of difference—such as "Devadatta has this hand" or "this head"—it is established that they possess a dual nature.
Therefore, the whole (*avayavin*) is merely a different state of the parts themselves, not a separate substance.

For it is those very [threads] that, by virtue of a particular conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*), attain the state of being a single substance; and while bearing largeness (*mahattva*) and the universal of cloth (*paṭa-jāti*) through that nature, they are apprehended by the cognition of "cloth.
Therefore, their unity is established in the form of the cloth, whereas their plurality is established in the form of the constituent parts.
Furthermore, as for the claim that form and the other qualities initiate a quality in the effect, we do not accept this because two distinct qualities are not perceived.
For if two qualities were perceived—one in the threads and another in the cloth—then they could be established as having the relationship of cause and effect.

Even in cases where a cloth is produced from threads of various colors, such as white, black, red, and yellow, it is those very same colors residing in the cloth that are perceived, and not some other distinct color.
The Refutation of the Single Nature of the Variegated:
Now, one perceives "a variegated cloth," but not "white" or "yellow";
therefore, another distinct color called "variegated" has arisen here.
It is not so;
it is improper to accept that a variegated [color] contradicts worldly experience.
Furthermore, even for various forms, their inherence in a single cloth through the medium of its distinct parts is not untenable.
By this, the conjunction produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) should be understood as refuted.

Just as the very conjunction with Devadatta becomes the conjunction with the earring in him, so too the very conjunction of the threads with the shuttle becomes the conjunction of the cloth with the shuttle once the threads have attained the state of a cloth; it is not a different conjunction, because there is no perception of such. Enough of this excessive detail.
Therefore, the whole (avayavin) certainly exists;
it has been demonstrated that its subsistence (vṛtti) upon its own parts is collective (vyāsajya).
Therefore, for this [individual], there exists both the substance consisting of its parts and the all-pervading universal.
Thus ends the discussion on the whole (avayavin).
The denotative function belongs to the phonemes, while the denoted object is the generic form (ākṛti).
Having thus spoken, the very narrative concerning their relationship is now related as the subject at hand.
And the relationship between the signified and the signifier has been previously described.
That permanence which was previously challenged is now being resolved.
For it was stated previously: "Since a word does not convey its meaning upon first hearing, its capacity to convey meaning is not inherent, unlike that of the sense organs.

This is the meaning: when a person says, "Its meaning is this," it then conveys the meaning; therefore, its capacity to convey meaning is surely produced by a person. Thus, the relationship [between word and meaning] is indeed human-made (*pauruṣeya*).
To this it is replied: this is not the establishment of a relationship by stating "this is its meaning," for this is merely a statement of a well-known relationship.
How is this understood? From the fact that many people prevent [the usage] when someone speaks of a different meaning.

For if anyone says to someone that the meaning of the word "cow" is a horse or a *gavaya*, others prevent him, saying, "This is not its meaning; its meaning is that which possesses the dewlap and so forth.

Furthermore, under the view that a connection (*saṃbandha*) is created [between word and meaning], just as in the case of Devadatta and others, the very person by whom the connection is made would be the meaning; thus, such a prevention would be illogical.
Therefore, even if contemporary persons were to say, "This is the meaning of this word," they should not be suspected of being the authors of that relationship [between word and meaning].

At most, it might be so: at the time of creation, the Lord Prajāpati, having created all things mobile and immobile, as well as dharma and adharma, established the relationship between words and their meanings for the sake of worldly communication and for the purpose of communicating dharma and adharma.

And having composed the Vedas by means of words whose relations [to their meanings] were already established, he imparted both the relationship between word and meaning and the Vedas themselves to his sons, Marīci and the others; they in turn imparted them to others, and those to yet others— thus, through successive transmission from each preceding one, the understanding of word and meaning and linguistic usage arose for each succeeding generation.
That too is incorrect;

for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a state [of being]. Non-comprehension upon first hearing [the word] is itself the proof. For if [the relationship between word and meaning] were conventional (*sāmayika*), then non-comprehension by those who have not grasped the convention and comprehension by those who have grasped the convention would be logical, just as in the case of words like "Devadatta.
However, if the capacity to convey meaning were inherent (*svābhāvika*), [such a distinction would be impossible].
If it is argued that comprehension should occur even upon the first hearing, we say no;

for it is logical that comprehension of the meaning does not occur at the first hearing, because the capacity to convey meaning, though inherent, becomes a cause for the understanding of the object only when it has been apprehended, not when it remains unapprehended.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a time called the "beginning of creation."
It is appropriate to understand, based on empirical observation, that the world has always been exactly like this;
however, it is not [appropriate] to claim that there was a time when all this did not exist,
because there is a lack of valid evidence.
If it is argued that the *mantras*, *arthavādas*, *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and so forth, are authoritative, we say no.

This is because, like the works of Śākya and others, these texts depend upon human authorship and are themselves of human origin; thus, they cannot possess authority regarding supersensible matters (*atīndriyārtha*).
And if they lack authority, then the authority of the *Dharmaśāstras* and other treatises based upon them is utterly cast aside.
Furthermore, if everything were non-existent, even creation would be impossible;
for jars and other objects are produced by means of material causes such as clay and threads. If everything were non-existent, by what material cause could all this be produced?
The prima facie argument according to the Advaita doctrine:

It may be thought that at the beginning of the world, the Self alone existed; by its own will, it transforms itself into ether and the other elements, just as a seed transforms into the form of a tree.
If it is asked, "How can Brahman, whose sole essence is consciousness, transform into an insentient form?

we reply: We do not speak of transformation in the ultimate sense; rather, that which is unchanging appears as if transformed, being one yet appearing as many, like a face in mirrors and other surfaces. Through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), the Self itself undergoes a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*) such that the non-dual Self, though its nature is consciousness, appears as if it were insentient.
One perceives it as if it were accompanied by a second;
this creation of the manifold world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), has ignorance as its material cause, like the manifold world of a dream.
And thus: "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
"There is only this Self, all this; there is not anything here that is manifold"—such are the many non-dualistic (advaita) teachings.
Likewise, in the passage "Indra moves in manifold forms through his māyās," the fact that the perception of difference is clearly based on *māyā* is demonstrated.
Similarly, in such passages as "The worlds desert him who perceives the worlds as other than the Self," there is a censure of the view of a non-unitary self, stating that he [is subject to death].

And the passage, "He who sees multiplicity here meets with death," is a censure of the perception of multiplicity; it reveals this meaning: that all this is indeed the non-dual Brahman as the ultimate reality, and that the vision of difference has ignorance as its material cause.
The refutation of the doctrine of non-duality has been stated.
Now, is this phenomenal world (prapañca) simply non-existent? If you say "yes," it is not so.
