Because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And thus, direct perception—which apprehends the existence of the manifold world (*prapañca*)—is established in the *Pratyakṣasūtra*. Furthermore, sublation by direct perception is not possible within scripture (*āgama*), because direct perception, due to its rapid occurrence, is more powerful than all other means of knowledge.
Nor should it be said that perception, having already functioned according to the principle of priority and posteriority, is subsequently sublated by scripture;
for there is a contradiction between the operation of scripture and that of perception.
Indeed, even at the very moment scripture functions, perception—which displays the manifoldness of the Veda—actually obstructs the operation of scripture itself.
Just as a jar, at the very moment it begins to arise, is unable to come into existence if struck by a staff, so too is the scripture.

Furthermore, for one who realizes the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the scripture must necessarily be understood as being of an unreal nature, since it is included within that proliferation.
How [could this be]?
Furthermore, the non-existence of a scripture would have to be cognized by means of that very same scripture;
for if it were cognized as having the nature of non-existence, it could not be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for any object whatsoever.
Or, if it were a valid means of knowledge, it could not be non-existent.
Someone else, however, says: we do not say that the manifold (prapañca) is non-existent, because it is established through means of valid cognition such as direct perception;
nor do we say it exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), because it is sublated by the knowledge of the self (ātmajñāna).
Therefore, this phenomenal world is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent.
This is without substance:
non-existence is simply being other than existence;
therefore, if this manifold (prapañca) does not exist as a reality, it is clearly nothing but non-existent.
Alternatively, in the absence of non-existence, there would be the consequence of [the object] being non-existent;
for the negation of one of the two—existence and non-existence—is invariably concomitant with the affirmation of the other.
Nor is another mode possible when both modes are absent. Furthermore, that which is never perceived is non-existent.
Just as a rabbit's horn [is non-existent],
that which is perceived and yet at some point sublated is real, such as the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); however,
it is held that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because it is both perceived and sublated, is indefinable in terms of being either existent or non-existent.
That is untenable, because it contradicts worldly experience;
for it is a well-established worldly consensus that whatever is perceived yet sublated— such as a mirage, a rope-snake, and so forth— is indeed non-existent.
For in the world there is no distinction whatsoever between things such as a rabbit’s horn and things such as a mirage;
if this phenomenal world (prapañca) is likewise declared to be non-existent, then it cannot be said to be "inexpressible" (anirvacanīya).

Alternatively, if one disregards worldly consensus and asserts that it is "inexpressible" merely by way of a technical convention (paribhāṣā), like the grammatical augment *vṛddhi* and so forth, [then the objection remains].

Nevertheless, this is incorrect—because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not subject to sublation; for it has already been stated that sublation by scripture is not possible during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, in the case of one who is liberated, a sublating cognition is certainly not to be suspected, because all the instruments of perception have dissolved.

Furthermore, since knowledge is impossible in the absence of its instruments, the non-existence of the phenomenal world (prapañca) cannot be apprehended when it is not being remembered. Moreover, in that state, remembrance is not possible because all latent impressions (saṃskāras) have been eradicated; therefore, sublation is not possible.

As for the claim that this phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), to whom does it belong? It cannot belong to Brahman, because its nature is pure knowledge (*vidyā*); for there is no possibility of darkness (*timira*) existing in the sun.
Nor can it belong to the individual souls (*jīvas*),
because they do not exist apart from Brahman, and because, due to the very absence of delusion, another entity that could serve as its cause is likewise untenable.
For those who admit both delusory cognition and its cause to exist apart from Brahman, there is a loss of non-duality (*advaita*).
And by what means is that knowledge of Brahman produced?
For there is no other cause.
If it is argued that it is innate (*svābhāvikī*), how could that which is of the nature of knowledge be of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Furthermore, if this [nescience] were inherent in its own nature, by what could it be destroyed?

If it is argued that scriptural knowledge such as meditation (*dhyāna*), or the knowledge of one's true nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) produced thereby, destroys the nescience (*avidyā*) of Brahman—this is not so;
for neither scripture, nor meditation and the like, nor the knowledge produced thereby, exists apart from Brahman, which is eternal consciousness, such that it could destroy nescience.
Therefore, this Mahāyāna doctrine is superior to our Māyāvāda;

for in it, the diversity of blue, yellow, and so forth, the relationship between cause and effect, and the distinction between the bound and the liberated are all established through the differentiation of mental continua (*saṃtāna*).

However, for those who have resorted to a self that is eternal, of a single flavor, and devoid of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), there would be the total cessation of all worldly and Vedic conventions.

As for what they also say— that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*), is destroyed by knowledge (*jñāna*), like a mirage or the world of a dream— that too is incorrect. If the phenomenal world, having arisen like a jar through ignorance which stands in the place of a potter’s activity, were destroyed by knowledge which stands in the place of a mallet, even so, the unreality (*asattva*) of the phenomenal world would not be established.
There would be only a permanence consisting in the connection with arising and destruction, but not absolute non-existence.
And by what knowledge is there destruction?
Not by the knowledge of the Self,
because there is no contradiction between them.

If it is argued that [the destruction of the world occurs] through the knowledge of the self as being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), we say no; for in that case, the portion consisting of the knowledge of the self is not contradictory [to the world]. By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it follows that the knowledge of the state of being free from conceptual proliferation is the destroyer; and the absence of conceptual proliferation is what constitutes being free from conceptual proliferation.

Furthermore, a cognition of the non-existence of that [world] cannot arise while the world of manifold proliferation (*prapañca*) is still present. For the world of proliferation must be destroyed by the arising of knowledge; yet prior to that knowledge, the world exists as something real. While that real form persists, how could there be the arising of a cognition whose object is its non-existence? Only when that cognition has arisen can the destruction of the world of proliferation occur.

And since the production of a cognition whose object is the non-existence of that [object] occurs only when that [object] has perished, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
By this, the notion that the water of a mirage is destroyed by knowledge is refuted.
For that water is not something real that is subsequently destroyed; rather, even previously there was no water at all.

Indeed, it is merely parched ground heated by rays of light that is perceived through delusion as having the nature of water, and is later understood in its true state by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*). Enough of this childish prattle!
Thus ends the refutation of the Advaita doctrine.
The prima facie position is based on the doctrine of non-duality that is like "half-old-woman-ism" (ardhajaratīya).

However, some followers of the Upaniṣads maintain that, in the ultimate sense, the Self itself transforms by its own will into the form of the phenomenal world; thus, [the Chāndogya Upaniṣad states]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" whereby the Self, which previously existed as the single essence of pure Being, [manifests] in the form of the phenomenal world divided into the manifold distinctions of ether and so forth.
The transformation has been shown to be like that of a seed;
therefore, the declarations of the Upaniṣads and the Purāṇas regarding this matter are seen by the hundreds, such as: "From this very Self, space was produced.
However, statements such as "The Person alone is all this; there is no diversity here whatsoever" intend to convey the non-existence of a difference between the substrates (dharmin).
For example, just as a single tree standing at a distance with its branches spreading out from a height of a span appears to those far away as many different trees,

so too, for those who perceive the manifold expansion of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*) in various forms and do not understand that this is the multiform transformation of the single Self, which is the root cause, such discourses are intended solely to explain the reality.
Everything is merely the expansion of the one alone; there is nothing here that is diverse.

Furthermore, those doctrines which speak of non-existence (*asattva*), which pertain to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and those which are doctrines of ignorance, delusion, and illusion—all these are merely figurative because conceptual proliferation is impermanent.

Just as the proliferation of a mirage, a rope-snake, a dream, and so forth, appears for a short time and subsequently vanishes, so too the transformation of Brahman in the form of the diversity of conceptual proliferation appears and vanishes; thus, due to this commonality of having the nature of appearing and disappearing, it is figuratively designated as "non-existent."
And since that [world] is like something non-existent, the cognition having that as its object is also established as being figuratively termed "erroneous.
Furthermore, it is appropriate to speak figuratively of its being "based on *māyā*" in such passages as "Indra, by means of *māyās*, goes forth in many forms," and so on.
And in the statement "The Self alone is real," it is said because that [Self] alone is eternal.
Just as cows and horses alone are considered "livestock" while others are "not livestock," so too should this be viewed.

But he who grasps such statements as they are literally heard would likewise have to grasp the statement that "animals are not animals" and the statement that "the sacrificial post is the sun," exactly as they are heard.

Now, if there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in those cases, that same [contradiction] applies here as well. Or, if it is argued that because those [statements] are mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), their literal meaning is not to be accepted, [then the same must apply here].
That too is the same:
the unreality of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is for the purpose of generating detachment,
and the ultimate reality of the Self (*ātman*) is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
This is clearly demonstrated by the illustration of the modification of a lump of clay.

Consequently, just as through the knowledge of the causal lump of clay, every modification made of clay—such as a jar or other vessels—is fully understood, for those modifications are merely a matter of words and names, being only clay; even so, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is likewise [unreal], while reality belongs only to Being (*sat*).

In this way, even the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is known through the knowledge of Being (*sat*). For modification (*vikāra*) is a mere beginning in speech, a mere name; it is said that "Being alone is the truth. When this is stated, it is understood as follows: various modifications such as bowls and the like—which possess the nature of manifestation and disappearance—constitute the phenomenal world, whereas clay is that which persists everywhere. It is the cause of them all. Since there is only a difference in state between cause and effect, and no difference in their essential nature, [the world] is known through the knowledge of the cause.
All that [effect], though unknown through its specific states (*avasthā*), becomes known by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Likewise, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is unstable, possessing the properties of manifestation and disappearance; however, its cause—the Self (*ātman*)—is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), all-pervasive, and not subject to decay.

When that [Self] is known, everything composed of it becomes known in its summarized form (*samāsena*), even if it was previously unknown in its detailed form (*vyāsa*); this is what is intended here.
Therefore, this manifold diversity of difference is merely a transformation of the one Self; it is indeed non-existent.
For if it were non-existent, how could it be known by the cognition of the existent, like the horn of a hare?
Indeed, when a lump of clay is known, the horn of a hare does not thereby become known; the same would apply to the manifold diversity.

Otherwise, there would indeed be the abandonment of the subject under discussion; for even the single Self is called a "jīva" when differentiated by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and through this distinction of jīvas, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation is logically established.
This is incorrect,
because a transformation into an insentient form is impossible for a self whose nature is consciousness;
and since the self is one, [the thought] "I have pain in all bodies" [would follow].
Just as one might say, "There is a face on my foot" or "There is pain in my head," there would likewise be the perception of all pleasure and pain [simultaneously].

Because of the distinctions among the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the single [Self] is called the individual soul (*jīva*); and due to the diversity of these individual souls, the distinction between bondage and liberation is logically established.
This is incorrect,
because a transformation into an insentient form is impossible for a self whose nature is consciousness;
and if the self were one, there would be a recognition [of identity] across all bodies— such as "I am Devadatta" and "I am indeed Yajñadatta."

Likewise, there would be the perception of all pleasure and pain such as "there is pleasure in Devadatta’s body for me" or "there is pain in Yajñadatta’s body for me," just as one might experience "pleasure in my foot" or "a sensation in my head."
If it is argued that the distinction is established by the differences among the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [we reply:
no, because they are insentient.
For the internal organ does not experience pleasure and pain, because it is insentient.
But the self is the experiencer, and since it is one and the same everywhere, who could prevent the synthesis [of experiences]?
Therefore, this view as well is not at all elegant.
Thus ends the refutation of the doctrine of the transformation of the self.
The prima facie argument is according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine.
The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the world consists of a plurality of selves and is a transformation of primordial matter (prakṛti).
Furthermore, Sāṃkhya is of two kinds: the atheistic (nirīśvara) and the theistic (seśvara).

First, the proponents of the doctrine of no-God (Nirīśvaravādins) say: "Prakṛti—non-conscious, consisting of the three guṇas, and denoted by the term Pradhāna—undergoes transformation into the form of the manifold world, from Mahat down to the specific elements, for the sake of the experience of conscious beings.

The proponents of the doctrine of God (Seśvaravādins) also say this much, but with this distinction: "Prakṛti creates the world depending upon the Lord, who is denoted by the term Puruṣa and is untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent dispositions."

For just as a seed, depending upon a cultivated field, begins to produce a great tree through the sequence of sprouts and so forth by virtue of its contact with that field, so too does the all-pervasive *prakṛti*, undergoing transformation through the sequence of the Great One (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) by virtue of its contact with that [puruṣa], begin the manifold world (*prapañca*) ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*).
Even in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, this is for the most part the very same view:
this creation has primordial nature (prakṛti) as its material cause (upādāna), while Īśvara is merely the efficient cause (nimitta).
The *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field), however, are the enjoyers,
while *prakṛti* alone is the agent of all effects and thus the object of enjoyment.
Furthermore, since that [*prakṛti*] is one everywhere, yet there is a distinction among the enjoyers, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation is logically established.

And thus it is said: "The one unborn [Self] lies beside the one unborn [Prakṛti], which is red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form; the one unborn [Self] enjoys her, while another unborn [Self] leaves her after she has been enjoyed. It is quite clear that Prakṛti is the object of enjoyment. How then can the followers of the Upaniṣads [be said to teach non-duality]? We reply: by way of non-distinction (*availakṣaṇya*). For in common usage, the word "difference" (*bheda*) is well known to signify distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*).
For instance, speakers say of things that are very similar,

"There is no difference whatsoever between this and that"; likewise, even for souls residing in bodies distinguished by the divisions of humans, animals, and beasts, once the connection with the body is set aside, [they are seen as identical].

When examined in their own true nature, there is not even the slightest difference between them, like two atoms of lotus pollen; it is with this intention that there are doctrines of oneness and doctrines denying plurality.
It is precisely with this intention that Bhagavān Vāsudeva spoke these words: "Whether in a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, or in an elephant..."
"The wise see with an equal eye even a dog and an outcaste.

Likewise, the meaning is that although the Self is itself devoid of distinctions, it is perceived through delusion as having various distinct forms due to its contact with diverse bodies such as those of humans, animals, and so forth— just as Indra is manifested in many forms through his powers of illusion (*māyā*).
And those who have been liberated remain in a state of absolute equality with the Lord due to their oneness with Him, because there is no difference between them.
Thus, another Śruti says:
"When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman..."
"Then the wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, being stainless, attains supreme equality"—this shows that liberation consists precisely in the attainment of similarity to the Lord.
Likewise, it was said by the Blessed Vāsudeva: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature."
"Even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer."

As for the Lord’s statement, "But that eternal portion of My own, which has become a living soul in the world of living beings," that refers to the relationship of master and servant; for just as ministers are designated as portions of the king, so too the individual soul (jīva) is said to be a portion of the Lord.
Otherwise, because the state of being a living soul would perish, its eternity could not be established.

Regarding such Purāṇic statements as, "When the knowledge that produces differentiation has undergone absolute destruction, who will create the non-existent difference between the Self and Brahman?"— the meaning of these is this: the distinction between the Self and Brahman, their otherness, which is absolutely non-existent and caused by ignorance, [ceases] when ignorance is destroyed.
"It dissolves by itself.
Indeed, the distinction between the lower and the higher Puruṣas has been clearly demonstrated in the Gītā and other texts: "But the Supreme Puruṣa is another, declared as the Supreme Self;
He is the Witness, the Permitter, the Doer, the Enjoyer, and the Great Lord."
And it is also said: "The Supreme Person (puruṣa) is called the Supreme Self (paramātman) within this body.
Enough of going too far [into these details].
Therefore, since this creation of the phenomenal world has primordial nature (prakṛti) as its material cause (upādāna), there is no objection on the grounds that it lacks a material cause.

Refutation of the Sāṃkhya Doctrine. To this it is replied: How indeed can Prakṛti, which is of a single uniform nature, give rise to the manifold world differentiated by the distinctions of humans, animals, and beasts? For a cause that is not itself diverse is incapable of producing an effect that is diverse.
If it is argued that the diversity [of the world] arises from the diversity of the auxiliaries— dharma and adharma— residing in the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), we say no;
for dharma and adharma are functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
and since the internal organ is included within the category of effects, all effects beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) undergo reabsorption into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Since both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) have dissolved into primordial nature (*prakṛti*), they are non-existent in that state; therefore, there can be no diversity [in the world] by their power.
Furthermore, what is the cause for this [nature] to initiate transformations such as the Great Principle (*mahat*)?
If it is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then there would be the consequence of constant initiation [of creation], and consequently, dissolution (*pralaya*) would be impossible.
If it is argued that [the world] undergoes transformation by the will of Īśvara, we say no;

for Īśvara is free from all afflictions (kleśa) and has cast aside all desires, so a will is impossible for him. Furthermore, since will is a property of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), it cannot exist in him at that time.
Furthermore, in the primordial dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya), only primordial matter (prakṛti) and the pure selves (ātman) remain;
and all selves are without distinction, because they consist solely of the nature of consciousness (caitanya).
Nor is any differentiation among the selves possible, even that which is produced by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).

It has been stated that this is because those two lack the nature of being attributes of the self (*ātman*), as they are functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and that [organ] is absent at that time.

Thus, if it is argued that when the selves remain in an undifferentiated state devoid of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), Nature (*prakṛti*) binds the self by initiating the formation of a body at the time of creation;

Those who existed in the previous creation and those who committed the murder of a Brahmin— all of them would be subject to the same single state, because the merit and demerit performed in the past have perished.

Now, is it not the case that so-called "destruction" is not absolute non-existence, but rather the mere disappearance of effects within their cause; and likewise, "origination" is merely the manifestation of existing effects from their cause? Otherwise, there would be no such things as cloth from threads or a jar from clay.

As they have said: "Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because everything does not arise from everything, because the efficient cause produces only what it is capable of producing, and because of the nature of the cause, the effect exists [in the cause].
Likewise, there is the word of the Blessed Vāsudeva: "The coming into being of the non-existent does not occur; the non-existence of the existent does not occur."
Therefore, since at the time of dissolution dharma and the other factors exist in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), it is logical that the diversity of creation occurs by virtue of them.
This is not so; for the form of a jar does not exist in the state of a lump of clay or in the state of potsherds, because this would contradict the non-perception of what is perceptible.
As for the statement, "The existence of the non-existent is not found," that refers to the Self;
for in the preceding [verse], it was said: "Never indeed was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men."

And by saying, "None of us shall not exist hereafter," he has already begun to establish the eternity of the self; for he states that there is no arising of a non-existent self, nor is there destruction of one that exists— thus, all selves possess the nature of being neither born nor destroyed, and are eternal.
Furthermore, it is not intended that the entire class of produced things is eternal;
for this has been stated [to be so] because they are not all-pervading and because such a claim would contradict non-perception.

If, moreover, one asserts that the pot is established in the nature of the clay by relying on the non-difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), the purpose of the effect is not thereby accomplished;
for water cannot be carried by a pot while it remains in the state of mere clay.

Likewise, merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), though existing in their own nature and abiding as the essence of *prakṛti*, are not capable of producing their own effects; thus, the diversity [of the world] cannot arise through their power.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the transformation of *prakṛti* into the sequence beginning with the Great One (*mahat*); for human words cannot function as a means of valid cognition regarding objects that fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition, and because the Vedas are also of human origin, they lack authority just like the words of any other person.

If, however, having accepted an infinite succession of creation and dissolution, one maintains the authority [of the Vedas] by relying on such statements as "At the beginning of every creation, He fashioned the names and actions of all beings, as well as their distinct dispositions, from the words of the Veda alone"— thereby asserting that the eternity of the Vedas and their words, which are connected to eternal objects, is established through the production of things that are the basis for linguistic usage and the power of names, according to the logic of the seasonal signs (*ṛtuliṅga-nyāya*).
Nevertheless, if only a single Prajāpati were the originator of the tradition, there would certainly be a suspicion that [the Veda] is a human composition (*kṛtaka*).

However, in accordance with such statements as "eighty-eight thousand [sages] are the originators of the tradition," one may rely on the fact that many great seers— who remember the Veda studied in another creation— act as originators of the tradition according to the analogy of waking from sleep.
Even if one were to dispel the suspicion that [the world] is created and thereby establish its eternity,

it would still be impossible to accept the creation of the world by one who lacks material causes (upādāna); for the status of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the like as material causes has already been refuted.
As for the doctrines of creation and dissolution found in the Upaniṣads and the Purāṇas, they must be interpreted as *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory statements).
Even if this were so, it would cause us no harm whatsoever,
because there is no contradiction regarding the eternity of the relationship [between word and meaning] or the authority of the Veda.
Thus concludes the refutation of the Sāṃkhya position.
The prima facie argument according to the Vaiśeṣika school:

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, accepting that the relations between words and their meanings as well as the Vedas are indeed of human origin, and desiring to establish through inference both cosmic creation and dissolution as well as God (Īśvara), formulate the following syllogism: "For the entire class of existing things is threefold."
Pots and the like have as their agent a conscious being who is commonly accepted;
space and the like do not have such an agent;
and the earth, mountains, blades of grass, sprouts, and so forth, have as their agent one whose existence is the subject of dispute.
Regarding that, it is said with reference to the final [member of the syllogism]: "The earth and so forth have an intelligent agent as their creator, because they are effects, like a jar.
And the earth and so forth possess the nature of being effects because they possess constituent parts, like a jar."
Furthermore, what is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of earth and the other elements?
The collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) belonging to the earthy, watery, fiery, and airy [categories] is, respectively, the inherent cause of earth, water, fire, and air;
for according to us, there is no dissolution of atoms at the time of cosmic reabsorption (*pralaya*), as there is for the Sāṃkhyas and others.
All composite substances, beginning with dyads, dissolve through the will of the Lord with their constituent parts separated;
the atoms, however, remain unjoined to one another, as do ether and the other elements, while the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) persist endowed with their respective merits and demerits.
At the time of creation, however, actions arise in the atoms upon encountering the will of the Lord and the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) of the individual souls as the efficient cause.

And by virtue of that [adṛṣṭa], the four types of atoms, conjoined with one another, initiate the four elements— earth and so forth— respectively, through the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). Furthermore,

due to the diversity of the *adṛṣ�ṭa* of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) acting as the efficient cause, and by virtue of specific conjunctions brought about by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*), the atoms initiate the various types of bodies distinguished as womb-born, egg-born, sprout-born, and sweat-born.
Refutation of the Vaiśeṣika View:
Now, this too is logical—namely, that the production of motion in atoms is not possible through mere will alone without effort;
for even today, the production of motion in the body is observed to occur by virtue of effort brought about by will.
If it is argued that even the Lord exerts effort, we say no;
for effort is impossible for one who is bodiless.
Indeed, although selves are omnipresent, they initiate effort only within the region of the body and not outside of it.
Therefore, effort is dependent upon a body.
Furthermore, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), since all effects have dissolved, even the body of the Lord has dissolved; how then could he who is bodiless exert effort?
Nor can desire arise in one who is bodiless, as is the case with liberated souls (*muktātman*).
Nor is knowledge possible, because of the absence of the sense faculties and so forth.
If it is argued that his knowledge is eternal, his will is eternal, and his effort is eternal, we say no;
for all knowledge, will, and effort are pervaded by non-eternality.

Indeed, one can formulate the following argument: "The earth and so forth do not have an incorporeal intelligent agent as their creator, nor do they have an agent whose effort, will, and knowledge are eternal, because they are effects, like a jar."
[Objection: But surely even a jar has God as its creator; thus, the example is devoid of the property to be proved (*sādhyahīna*).
[Response: Even so, since the potter also possesses agency, the jar does not have God alone as its creator.
Therefore, the argument should be formulated thus: "The earth and so forth do not have a bodiless self (*ātmā*) alone as their creator, just like a jar."
The reason (*hetu*) "because it is a real entity" and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) "like space," etc., are in every respect free from fault.
Likewise, one should directly formulate a counter-proof as follows: "The earth and so forth do not have an intelligent creator, because they lack a corporeal creator, like space.
Now, if one were to accept that God’s body is eternal and maintain that God possesses a body even at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), [the following would apply].
Consequently, the property of having parts (*sāvayavatva*) in the body of the Lord would not be an invariable concomitant (*anaikāntika*) to prove that the earth and so forth are effects;
furthermore, it is untenable to claim that sprouts of durvā grass and the like have a creator possessing a body, because this contradicts non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, every distinct effect must arise from a distinct effort;
for the effort involved in moving the feet is indeed different from that involved in raising the arms.
This being the case, even if God’s effort were eternal, it could not be the cause of the emergence of diverse effects because of its unity; thus, such an effort would be entirely useless.

If, however, [the *prakṛti*] were infinite because it conforms to infinite effects by persisting even at the time of creation, and if the uniter—the cause of creation—also persisted at the time of dissolution, then, due to the mutual obstruction of both, there would be neither creation nor dissolution.
As for the argument that the diversity of the *kṣetrajña*'s unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is thereby established: [that too is untenable].
That too is incorrect; for the distinction between effects is not established merely by the distinction of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) without a distinction in the observed causes.
Indeed, even with a hundred unseen factors, a palmyra tree is not produced without a palmyra seed.
If it is argued that everything is accomplished through the majesty of God even without a seed, we say no;
for there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) regarding that very point.
For once the eternity of the Vedas has been established, the immeasurable majesty of God [is inferred] by the force of their authority.
Whether the creation and dissolution [of the world] can be established by relying on the logic of seasonal signs or not—

if, disregarding the Vedas, one were to apply inference based on mere observation to a matter that is utterly beyond the scope of worldly experience, as if inferring the existence of a mountain— then the only appropriate response is indifference; therefore, I shall desist.
Therefore, even at the time of creation and so forth, there is no cause for the [eternal] relationship.
The relationship between word and meaning is eternal.

Furthermore, it is impossible to establish the relationship for all words; for when not a single word was yet connected with any meaning, how could a relationship be established? Indeed, one who establishes a relationship must necessarily do so by means of some sentence.
It must be formulated as "a cow is that which possesses a dewlap," and so forth.
One cannot utter the word "dewlap" and other such terms for the purpose of conveying meaning when their referent is not already established, nor can one do so with hand gestures and the like.
Because the status of being a communicator is unestablished.
But even so, how is it not impossible for one whose relationship [to the words] is unestablished? For although at that time the speaker, because his relationship is established,

may utter a sentence in order to express that relationship, nevertheless, how could infant listeners— who have not yet established the meanings of all the word-components— comprehend the relationship through that sentence?
Therefore, the claim that [the Buddha] speaks like an instrument is also untenable.
This is not a fault; for the speaker does not lack capacity in the same way as an agent, because the necessary means are available.
To claim that practitioners do not practice because of a lack of means is contrary to what is observed;
for we see children who have not yet mastered the relationship between all words and their meanings learning that connection from elders.
Furthermore, there is a method for children: it is not necessarily through a sentence that explicitly states the relationship that children acquire the understanding of that relationship from elders;

rather, when elders whose relationship [with words] is well-known engage in worldly activity for the sake of their own purpose, children who listen to them acquire the understanding of the relationship.
For when someone is told by another, "Bring a cow," and he brings an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth, the child standing nearby understands.

Since this person proceeds toward this specific meaning immediately after hearing this sentence, one understands in a general manner that "this meaning has been communicated by this sentence. Subsequently, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) across numerous usages, the communicative capacity is specified:

among the parts of the sentence, namely the words, and among the parts of the words, namely the bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), [each] is assigned to its respective portion of the sentence-meaning, such as the meaning of the root or the meaning of the stem.

Therefore, since the relationship [between word and meaning] is not of human origin, there is no dependence on a person by virtue of that; thus it is established that the authority of the Vedas is independent.
Thus ends the refutation of the objection regarding the relationship [between the means and the end].

And as for the claim that because the result is not perceived immediately, sacrifices such as the *citrā* do not have cattle as their fruit—this would indeed be so if only the five means of knowledge beginning with perception were valid. For in that case, the status of something as a means to an end could only be established through the immediate perception of the result, and not otherwise.

However, since verbal testimony (*śabda*) is also a means of valid knowledge because it generates cognition—just like perception and the others—the fact that sacrifices such as the *citrā* are means to obtaining cattle is understood through it; thus, even in the absence of immediate perception, their status as the means to that end is established.
The refutation of objections concerning objects such as paintings and the like:
Now, it was argued that [the scripture] lacks authority because it contradicts other means of valid cognition; this is not so, because such contradiction does not exist.

For the word does not state that the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the various fruits follows immediately [after the action], which would cause a contradiction; rather, it expresses only the fact of being a means of accomplishment, and since that is possible even at a later time through the mediation of the *apūrva*— just as drinking oil [yields results later]— there is no inconsistency.

As for what was said previously—that at the time of determining the meaning of the scripture before its performance, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) was not included—even if that is so, one later understands it thus: "When the word expressed merely the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*), I mistakenly understood it as being a direct means; since that is now seen to be otherwise, surely this [action] bears fruit at a later time through some intermediate door."

Furthermore, it was indeed possible to understand the *apūrva* even prior [to this discussion], because since the constituent (*aṅga*) and principal (*pradhāna*) rituals are momentary, their simultaneity is impossible without an *apūrva*;

and since the production of animals and the like depends on visible causes, their production cannot occur in a mere instant—thus, an *apūrva* must necessarily exist. Nor is the mere production of the animal the result; rather, because enjoyment (*upabhoga*) takes a long time, there must be something that persists for as long as that enjoyment lasts.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for an action to persist for such a length of time, one must admit the existence of the *apūrva* (the unseen potentiality); through this medium, it is logical that the ritual act yields its fruit at a later time. Thus, the authority of the scripture is not sublated by the non-perception of the result immediately following the action.
Thus ends the refutation of the objection regarding the variegated nature [of the world]. Now begins the critique of the doctrine of the self (*ātmavāda*).

As for the statement presented that contradicts direct perception—namely, "this very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes straight to the heavenly world"—it is by means of this expression that the visible body, associated with the sacrificial implements, is being taught.

To this it is replied: because this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and is intended for another purpose, there is no fault of contradicting other means of valid cognition regarding its own literal meaning.
Furthermore, no contradiction exists at all;
for by this [passage], the going to heaven of the body is not stated, but rather that of the self (*ātman*) to whom this body belongs.

For he too, by means of the metaphorical identification (*upacāra*) of the body and the embodied self as non-different, is designated as being present in the body through his status as possessing sacrificial implements and through his perceptibility;
or else, the soul’s journey to heaven is metaphorically attributed to the body—thus there is no contradiction.
The word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is also a designator of that very [Self] because of its being the owner of the sacrifice and its being the agent.
Nor can its non-agency be asserted—as by the followers of Kapila—because that would contradict the Śruti;
for everywhere, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "agent" and "experiencer" is observed.

Just as in this very context it is said, "The sacrificer goes to the heavenly world," so too, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, truly prospers; he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Dvirātra, [prospers]"—thus the agency of the agent is stated with respect to the volition directed toward heaven.
Moreover, even for a self that has gone to heaven, agency in respect to sacrifice, knowledge, effort, volition, and so forth, exists directly;
for we do not accept that action is merely physical motion, as the Vaiśeṣikas do, whereby the self would lack agency.
Since the mere meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) constitutes action (kriyā),

this [self] can possess the status of agent (kartṛtva) even with respect to physical movements (spanda) by virtue of being their instigator; for it is through effort that it impels the body toward movement.

However, direct [agency] is not possible because vibration is impossible in that which is all-pervading; with this intention, the doctrines of non-agency (akartṛtva) are found in the Purāṇas and the Upaniṣads.
The proof for the self as distinct from the body:
Furthermore, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a self distinct from the body? It is the signs of breathing and so forth, as well as pleasure and the like.
By the term "breathing and so forth" is meant the effort that serves as the cause for the specific upward and downward movements of the abdominal air, which are denoted by the word "breathing."
It is said in reply: pleasure and the other [qualities] cannot possibly be attributes of the body, because they do not persist as long as the body exists.

For those specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) such as color and so forth, which reside in a produced substance, perish either due to another contradictory quality or due to the destruction of the substance itself.
However, since vital functions such as breathing cease even while that [body] exists during the state of death, they are not qualities of the body.
Likewise, knowledge also is not a property of the body precisely because it does not persist as long as the body.
Furthermore, those things which are objects of perception that are not qualities of the body are perceived by others just as they are by oneself, such as color and so forth.
Pleasure and the like, although they are perceptible, are not graspable by the perception of another; therefore, they are not qualities of the body.
Thus, this pair of arguments, while precluding the status of being bodily qualities for pleasure and the like, indicates that they possess the quality of something else.
That "other" is the self (ātman).
Furthermore, all specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇas), even while existing in their causes, only attain the status of being qualities of an effect-substance when they reside in that substance;
and since consciousness does not exist in the earth-atoms which constitute the cause of the body, how could consciousness be a quality of the body?
Therefore, the conscious being must be something other [than the body].
The Proof of the Self as Non-different from the Body:

Furthermore, someone says—first of all, the knower necessarily appears within cognitions; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that there is no distinction between what is known by oneself and what is known by another.
And yet, there is no such appearance of the body as characterized by the specific arrangement of its parts, such as hands and feet.

Therefore, the claim that the self is something other than the body is illogical; for even when there is an appearance of a configuration, an appearance of the body is possible. Indeed, the configuration itself is not the body.

For configuration is indeed a property of the body, and it is possible for a substratum to appear even when its properties do not appear; otherwise, there would be no appearance of the self either, since its properties—such as omnipresence and so forth—do not appear in the cognitions of objects.
Furthermore, the appearance of the knower is not an absolute necessity in the cognitions of objects.
For at that time, only the object appears, not the knower.
Nor is there no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another;
for this distinction is not produced by the appearance of a cognizer, but rather consists simply in the fact that something appears to one person and not to another—there is no other distinction.
Therefore, the separation from the body is not established by the appearance of a knower.

However, for the very reasons stated previously— namely, because knowledge, pleasure, and so forth cannot possibly be qualities of the body— their substratum must be something other than that, and that is the self (ātman).
The doctrine of the self as consciousness according to the Buddhist view.
The Buddhists, however, say: "The postulation of qualities [occurs] once it has been established that cognition, pleasure, and so forth are qualities;
but for us, that is not established, because their existence is accounted for by that much alone.

For cognition in its mere form is not untenable without a substratum; why then is cognition not accepted as being entirely independent? Pleasure and the rest are also simply independent objects of cognition, since no other substratum is perceived."

And it is cognition itself that is determined as the knower—through the distorted vision of those whose insight is perverted by such thoughts as "I know the blue"—and nothing else, because there is a lack of valid evidence for anything else.
But surely, since cognition is also momentary, how can there be recollection on the following day of what was perceived on the previous day, as well as desire and recognition?
For these are not possible regarding something not perceived by oneself—just as recollection and so forth are not possible for Yajñadatta regarding an object perceived by Devadatta.

True; they are not possible when there is a difference in the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*). However, within a single identical continuum, the occurrence of recollection and so forth by one [person] of what was perceived by another is established, because it is observed to be so.
For the identity of the perceiver and the rememberer has never been observed anywhere,
because a single, stable person is never perceived [as such];
therefore, cognition itself is the knower, and there is no other knower.
To this it is replied: That agent who is recognized as being the same in both the earlier and later times [is the self].
For that which is stable, there would be a distinction from consciousness, which is momentary;
for if one assumes the unity of the knower based on the recognition of objects, this answer might indeed hold—that it is possible because of the unity of the continuum (*saṃtāna*).

But when the knower himself is recognized as one across prior and subsequent times—thinking, "I who saw previously am the very same I who see now"—then, since the unity of the knower is understood through that very recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), [the objection does not apply].
And because consciousness is momentary, a knower distinct from it is thereby established.
Could the knower be the object of the "I"-cognition?
If that were so, then the body itself would be the object of the "I"-cognition, because of its grammatical coreferentiality with cognitions such as leanness, as in "I am thin" or "I am going";
for it is impossible for a ubiquitous self to possess leanness and the like.
It is said: There is no dispute that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) has the knower as its object;
for whoever reflects [upon something] reflects upon his own self as "I," and [reflects upon] another as "this.
Therefore, it is beyond doubt that this [notion] has the knower as its domain, and the status of being a knower in the body has been refuted.

Therefore, due to the delusion of oneness regarding two things that are utterly conjoined, there arises a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just like the cognition of hot water or the cognition of a glowing iron ball.
The demonstration of the distinction between the body and the self:

likewise, a cognition of difference is also observed, as in "this body of mine is thin," where the referent of the word "I" (the self) is distinct from the body due to the use of the genitive case; furthermore, the body is an object for another [the self] and is the locus of the notion of "mine."
Therefore, from this manifestation of discernment and by the previously stated reasoning, because the body is not a knower,
and because the realization of non-difference can occur even as an error through the influence of the defect of association,
and because it is impossible for one newly born to experience joy, fear, or grief without the continuity of memories practiced in a previous life; [the Self is distinct].

Furthermore, some who possess the memory of their past births (*jātismara*) are observed even today to recall events that occurred in secret during another body; thus, the distinction between the body and the self is established by direct experience.

Even if, in this manner, the distinction between the body and the self were not established with absolute clarity, nevertheless, non-distinction is likewise not clear, since there is also the manifestation of the discernment "this is my body. Therefore, regarding that reality which is thus obscure, a definitive conclusion is reached either through scriptural presumption (*arthāpatti*) based on what has been heard, or through direct scripture.

For scriptural passages such as "one who desires heaven" imply the existence of an agent capable of experiencing the fruits of the afterlife that transcends the body; since these [passages] would otherwise be untenable without such an agent, they necessitate its postulation. And the Upanishads directly support what has been thus implied by them, as in: "Verily, this Self is indestructible," and so forth.
Thus, it is established that the knower is distinct from the body, of the nature of mental perception, and accessible through the notion of "I."
But how can there be knowability for the knower?
For it is not possible for a single entity to possess both agency and objecthood, since an action directed toward itself is a contradiction;
therefore, what is called the "cognition of the 'I'" does not exist as something distinct from the cognition of objects such as jars.
However, it has been stated that in the very cognition of a jar and so forth, the self appears just like the object;
thus, the self is accessible through the mental "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). But what indeed is this so-called contradiction regarding action within itself?
The meaning is that the action in which someone is the agent does not produce its own fruit for that very same person.
But what, then, is the fruit of the act of cognition?
Regarding "illumination," why should this not occur in the sense of the agent? If you say "yes," then how does it illuminate?
For it cannot be said that what does not exist shines;
therefore, even if one accepts that the self shines within cognitions of objects, the contradiction of an action operating upon itself remains exactly the same.
If it is argued that the fruit of cognition is merely its fitness for linguistic usage and nothing else, let it be so.
There is indeed a result;
and you have admitted that this arises through cognition with respect to the self just as it does with respect to objects.
Therefore, the contradiction is equal.

If it is argued that, having pointed out a contradiction with ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the designation "object" (*karman*) and the case-ending for the object do not apply to the self even though it possesses the fruit produced by an action— on the grounds of the statement that "being an object consists in possessing the fruit of an action inherent in another"— that is incorrect. For the grammatical correctness of words must be understood from actual usage (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, in both common worldly usage and in the Veda, there exists the conventional treatment of the self as the object (*karman*) precisely when it is the agent (*kartṛ*) of its own action.

For instance, in the Bhāṣya itself, there is the use of a gerundive suffix (*kṛtyapratyaya*) denoting the object in the phrase "it is possible that it is self-cognizable" (*svasaṃvedyaḥ saṃbhavati*). In the Veda as well, there are numerous such usages: "one should meditate upon the self" (*ātmānam upāsīta*), "one knows the self" (*ātmānaṃ veda*), and "the self is to be known" (*ātmā jñātavyaḥ*).

Furthermore, the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the goer with respect to the act of going does not exist because of the absence of such usage; for in matters of linguistic correctness, we are dependent upon actual usage and cannot determine it ourselves.

Just as, although they share the same meaning of "moving," the verb *gacchati* is transitive while *calati* is intransitive because usage is seen to be so, in the same way, the knower will be the object and the goer will be intransitive.
Therefore, the self is cognizable through the mental *ahaṃpratyaya* (the notion of "I").
Thus says the Śruti: "He is the self dwelling in the mind of men.
Consequently, although the self appears at the very moment of the cognition of an object, it does not appear as the agent of that objective cognition.

It does not appear as the agent of the cognition of objects, but rather it appears as the object of the mental notion of "I"; it does not appear as the object of that [objective] cognition, because [the former] pervades [the latter].
[Objection: But is not the conceit of "I" with respect to the self, just like [the conceit of "I"] with respect to the body, merely an error? [Response: No, because there is no sublation [of it].
If it is argued that there is sublation for yogins, we say no, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, even those who have reached the highest pinnacle of yoga [do not perceive such sublation].
Even those lords of yoga conceive the notion of "I" within themselves.
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world.
I know all those things, O scorcher of foes, but you do not know them.
Because I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable.
In such passages, the word "I" (aham) certainly refers to the Supreme Person;
for the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), being a transformation of the Mahat-tattva, is not the source of all things,
nor is it superior to both the perishable and the imperishable.
Nor does it deposit a germ in the *pradhāna*, which is denoted by the word "Brahman," because the agitation of *prakṛti* is caused by contact with the *puruṣa*.

Likewise, in the Upaniṣads: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, 'I am Brahman'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10); and the Vedic mantra also says: "I was Manu and I was the Sun" (Ṛgveda 4.26.1).
Therefore, those who do not accept that the Self is cognizable through the notion of "I" should disregard [that view] precisely because it contradicts the Śruti.

As for that statement regarding being "free from the notions of 'I' and 'mine'," even when considered in its proper context, it does not intend to negate the very nature of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
For such is that statement: "He belongs to no one, nor does anyone belong to him; he is simply free from the notions of 'I' and 'mine'.
The meaning of this is as follows: because he belongs to no one, he is therefore free from the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*).
Because this [self] belongs to no one, it is therefore free from the notion of "I.

If there were a negation of the very nature of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra), it would not connect with what precedes it; for how could the statement "because this belongs to no one, therefore the sense of 'I' regarding this is an error" be coherent? What would be connected with what?

Therefore, this is not a negation of the essential nature of the "I" (ahaṃtā); rather, it is the notion of "I" in the Self as being connected to birth—such as "I am his father," "I am his son," and so forth—which is an error. This is consistent with the fact that this Self is not related to anyone in the form of son and so on, because the relationship of producer and produced pertains only to the body.

For the body is born from a body, but the self is not born from another self; therefore, the notion of "I" with respect to the self—which is actually connected to something else—is an error for those who do not perceive the distinction between the self and the body, such as [the notions of] "lean" and so forth.
This very point is stated by way of negating its connection to other things and by withdrawing affection toward objects such as sons, in order to generate dispassion (*vairāgya*).

This negation does not apply to the very nature of the "I-maker" (ahaṅkāra), because it would be useless, incoherent, contradictory to other means of valid cognition, and contrary to the statement "I am Brahman.
Therefore, the knower who is apprehended through the notion of "I" is distinct from the body and distinct from the sense organs.
The distinction between the sense faculty and the self.
How is there a distinction between the sense faculties?
For even in the absence of the sense faculties, there is recognition of a single cognizer: "I who saw a form, I am now touching it," and "I who perceived [an object], I am now remembering it."

The mind (*manas*), however, is postulated as the instrument for the cognitions of pleasure and so forth—on the grounds that for the cognizer, whose existence is established by perception, there must be a dependence on an external instrument in the case of the cognitions of color and so forth; thus, one should not suspect that it possesses the status of a cognizer.

As for those who claim that the self is established solely as an agent and not as an object, for them, memory and recognition would be impossible regarding the self, because even in those cases, the manifestation of the self as being connected with a previous time must be admitted.

Furthermore, since agency belonging to a previous time is not possible within a present recollection, how could [the self] be established as the agent? Therefore, it is most reasonable that the self is established solely as the object of the notion of "I. //***//
Now, why is self-luminosity not accepted for the self and for pleasure and so forth?
For no self-luminous entity whatsoever is observed, since every object is necessarily characterized by being illuminated by something else.
Furthermore, if the self were self-luminous, it would manifest even during deep sleep.
And yet it does not manifest, as it has been said: "One who is not conscious at all is called 'in deep sleep'."
However, even in deep sleep, the Self indeed shines forth, endowed with its own natural supreme bliss;
otherwise, how could there be the recollection upon waking, "I slept happily"?
No other object—whether the body, the senses, or any other thing—shines forth; this is the distinction between deep sleep and dreamless sleep.
This is not so, because it contradicts direct experience;
for neither the self nor pleasure manifests to those who are asleep,
and it cannot be maintained that what does not manifest becomes manifest merely through conventional usage.

Moreover—having awakened from sleep, lovers indeed become disillusioned, thinking: "This night has passed in vain without my beloved; though she was embraced, I did not even realize it, and thus I have become disillusioned with her."
And having experienced supreme bliss, this world-weariness arising from the recollection of that [bliss] is not possible through the loss of even the slightest amount of ordinary pleasure.
If that happiness were forgotten, this worldly convention— that "happiness is to be experienced"— would not be tenable; however,
this [convention] holds provided there is no experience of suffering.
Therefore, it is certain that the conventional usage of the term "happiness" [with respect to deep sleep] is based on a figurative application of its qualities.

For those who have awakened do not recall even the slightest suffering experienced during deep sleep; by the very non-arising of such recollection, they understand, "In that state of deep sleep, there was no suffering for me at all," and thus they employ the conventional usage of "happiness" toward that very state through a figurative attribution of its qualities.
And thus people speak in this way: "For all this time, not even knowing myself, I was sleeping. Therefore, because the self is not manifest during deep sleep, its self-luminosity [is established];
hence, it remains settled that this [self] is indeed accessible through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).
The self is all-pervasive. Furthermore, it must be considered whether this self is atomic, the size of the body, or omnipresent.
In that regard, if it were of atomic dimension, the simultaneous experience of sensation in both the head and the feet would be impossible.
If it is argued that even though there is no simultaneity, simultaneity is perceived due to extreme rapidity,
this might indeed be so if atomicity were established by some means; however, since that is not established, it is more logical to conclude non-atomicity in accordance with what is observed.
In that case, if it were of the same size as the body, it would possess parts;
for a partless substance is of only two kinds— either atomic or all-pervading— and thus,
being commensurate with the body, it would necessarily have parts.

In this regard, the postulation of many constituent parts, as well as the assumption of the extreme contraction and expansion of exactly that same number of parts—neither fewer nor more—in the bodies of an ant and an elephant, does not particularly satisfy the heart.
Therefore, all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) alone is logical.
And thus says the Śruti: "Endless and boundless."

And there is this statement in the Bhagavadgītā: "This [Self] is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient. Furthermore, those declarations in the Upaniṣads concerning its atomic size, as well as in the Purāṇas such as "the Person the size of a thumb," are intended to mean that it is within the range of perception by means of subtle [faculties].
Now, if there were omnipresence, let there be only one Self in all bodies; what is the use of accepting multiple Selves?

It is not so; for if there were oneness, then just as when there is a difference in persons, Yajñadatta recognizes with his own sense of sight an object seen by Devadatta because the agent is one—thinking, "That which I saw, this I now touch"—so too Yajñadatta would recognize an object seen by the Self residing in Devadatta’s body.
Even upon the dissolution of the body, there is no [cessation of memory] for the self, because the self that recognizes remains one even when the body is dissolved.
If it is argued that, despite the oneness of the agent, the distinction [of memory] is determined by the difference in the minds, we say: no.
It has been stated that because the mind is an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is impossible for a distinction among instruments— such as the eye and so forth— to establish a distinction [in the self].
If it is argued that although the instruments such as the eye are non-determinative, the mind (*manas*) is the determinative instrument, we say no;
for there is no difference in their status as instruments.
This conceptualization might hold if there were firm evidence for the oneness of the self;
however, such evidence does not exist.
As for those doctrines of the oneness of the self found in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, or Purāṇas, they state: "The stainless one attains supreme equality."

Because of contradictions with such scriptural statements on the distinction of the self as "They have attained similarity with me" and "But there is another, the Supreme Person," as well as with perception and other means of knowledge, they are not able to definitively establish the oneness of the self.

For when there is a mutual contradiction among statements, and since conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are impossible because they refer to established entities, a definitive conclusion must be reached through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that other means of valid cognition is capable of establishing only difference; thus, by the reasoning previously stated, it should be understood that doctrines asserting a single self (*aikātmya*) are intended to convey non-distinction.

And this is clearly evident from the employment of the analogy of the wind: "The distinction designated as the six musical notes arises through the difference in the holes of the bamboo flute and so forth."
"Or rather, it is like that great self, the wind which pervades without distinction.

For the substance of wind is not one and the same everywhere, because the difference between individual instances is clearly evident; however, for the wind whose nature is undifferentiated, the distinctions such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth are produced by the shape of the holes in the bamboo flute.
Thus, the very point is that even for the self (ātman), the distinction from cattle, humans, and so forth, is caused by its connection with a body and is not inherent.
The use of the singular number in "of the wind" (vāyoḥ) and "of it" (tasya) is intended to refer to the universal [nature].

Therefore, the selves are indeed distinct in each body, yet they are eternal and all-pervading; and in this way, the established distinction between those who are bound and those who are liberated becomes even more logical.
Thus ends the discourse on the self.
The commencement of the discourse on liberation:
What, then, is this so-called liberation?

It is the state of abiding in pure consciousness alone, having abandoned the diversity of blue, yellow, and so forth, through the total eradication of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the stream of cognition (*jñāna-saṃtāna*) which otherwise flows in the form of diverse blue, yellow, and other appearances under the influence of various latent impressions.
Some [hold that there is the cessation of the stream of consciousness], while others [hold that there is the cessation of the stream of consciousness] like the extinction of a lamp’s flame.
Both of these views are rooted in the non-existence of external objects; therefore, they are refuted by the very demonstration of the existence [of external objects].
Others, however, declare that liberation (*apavarga*) is the dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).

For phenomenal proliferation is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); like the proliferation of a dream, it dissolves of its own accord once ignorance has dissolved through the knowledge of Brahman, just as [a dream] dissolves upon awakening.
Thus says the Śruti: "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"
Thus it is said.

This [objection] is also refuted by the demonstration that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consists in the very fact that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, "all this is indeed the Self" means that the Self is the enjoyer of everything.
Just as one who desires, "May I be the kingdom," means "May I be the enjoyer of the kingdom";
and just as one who desires, "May I become all this," means "May I be the enjoyer of all."
Likewise, the statement "the Self is everything" means that the Self is the enjoyer of all.
As for the scriptural declaration that the state of duality is an illusion—namely, "for where there is, as it were, duality"—that is figurative;
for just as the manifold world of dreams, a magician's trick, a mirage, and so forth, appears within the range of vision for a certain period of time.

Just as that which has dissolved later transcends the state of being an object of enjoyment, so too this phenomenal world— consisting of the body, the senses, and their objects— is enjoyed by this Self for a certain period of time, but subsequently, due to its destruction, it becomes no longer an object of enjoyment; it is spoken of metaphorically as being "like that" in order to turn men away from attachment to the enjoyment of sense-objects and to generate a longing for liberation.

Furthermore, even that statement regarding the non-duality of the Self in liberation—namely, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone"—is not intended to negate the intrinsic nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); rather, it is intended to negate the relationship between the existent phenomenal world and the Self.
This is because of the use of the word "his" (*asya*).
For it is not stated here, "When everything has become the Self," but rather, "But when for him (asya) everything has become the Self."
What then?
[It refers to the state] where "all this is indeed the Self for him.
Therefore, the meaning of this is: "where," that is, in which state—namely, in the state of liberation (mukti).

Since this self has no other related entity whatsoever—whether as an object of vision, as a means of seeing, or as a locus of seeing—but rather the self alone is everything for it and nothing else, then by what could one see what?

This is just as when someone in the world who possesses neither kinsmen nor wealth says: "I have no one; I myself am everything. In that case, the intended meaning is simply that there is no other related entity whatsoever.

Thus, in the statement "In liberation, the self alone is everything for the self," what is intended is merely the absence of any other related entity, not the non-existence of the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Therefore, liberation is not the dissolution of the phenomenal world, but rather the dissolution of one's connection to the phenomenal world. For the phenomenal world binds the person in three ways: the body as the locus of experience, the sense organs as the instruments of experience, and the objects such as sound and so forth as that which is experienced.
And "experience" (*bhoga*) refers to the direct perception of the objects of pleasure and pain; the absolute dissolution of these three kinds of bondage is liberation (*mokṣa*).

What is this "finality"? It is the destruction of the body, sense-faculties, and objects that have previously arisen, and the absolute non-arising of those not yet arisen. How is there this absolute non-arising?

Because of the complete exhaustion of both merit and demerit, which are the two causes of birth, this very connection with conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is bondage; liberation from that is release (*mokṣa*).
This is the doctrine of bliss as liberation.
[Objection: But in that case, because all dharmas have been extinguished, there would be no happiness whatsoever for the liberated one;
consequently, liberation would not be the supreme human goal (apuruṣārtha).

[Reply: This is not a fault. For the bliss of the liberated self is not produced by dharmas; were it so, being something that has an origin, it would be subject to destruction, which would contradict the scriptural teaching of non-return (apunarāvṛtti).

The innate bliss of the Self, being overwhelmed by transmigratory existence, becomes an object of enjoyment upon the manifestation of that which is liberated from *saṃsāra*; and as for the innateness of this bliss, thousands of scriptural passages such as "Brahman is bliss" (*ānandaṃ brahma*) serve as the authority.
But is there not also a scriptural text stating that even in the absence of pleasure, "pleasure and pain do not touch one who is indeed bodiless"?
True—but such a passage refers specifically to sensual pleasure; otherwise, it would contradict the scriptural texts concerning bliss (*ānanda*).

Now, why is it not explained that the very statement regarding bliss (*ānanda*) has the intention of referring to the absence of suffering (*duḥkha*), by virtue of the statements regarding the absence of happiness? It is more appropriate to interpret those few statements regarding the absence of happiness otherwise, rather than the numerous statements regarding bliss.
Furthermore, if the word "bliss" were intended to mean the absence of suffering, there would be a complete abandonment of its own primary meaning.

However, since the word *sukha* (pleasure) is a general term, even when it is explained in a specific sense, there is no significant loss of its own primary meaning; therefore, that [specific interpretation] alone is appropriate.
But surely, even if bliss exists, it is of no consequence if it is not experienced;
moreover, an experience of bliss is impossible for one who is liberated and devoid of all instruments of perception.
If it is argued that this bliss is self-luminous, we say no.
Because it is unmanifest during the state of saṃsāra.
[Objection: But even there, the Puruṣa, whose nature is bliss, is indeed manifest, since love arises toward the self; [Response:
No answer need be given to such an audacious person who says "that is true."

If even those in saṃsāra were to experience supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), then there would be no distinction between one who is liberated and others; thus, liberation itself would result in being a non-goal for man (*apuruṣārtha*).
Therefore, this [bliss], though not consisting of suffering, is not manifested because it is overwhelmed by [pain].
What indeed is this so-called "overwhelming" of that which is manifest?
For "overpowering" (abhibhava) is indeed the obstruction of manifestation;
and it is not possible for that which is manifesting to be non-manifest.

However, if it does not manifest at all during the state of saṃsāra, then a cause must be stated for that manifestation which arises in the state of liberation, given that it was non-existent in that [prior] state.
Furthermore, consciousness alone is the cause of the fruit known as illumination, and that [consciousness] is dependent upon the sense organs;
since the sense organs do not exist for one who is liberated, how could there be an experience of bliss?

It is said: It is determined solely on the strength of the scriptural texts concerning bliss (*ānanda*) that for the liberated one, the external senses alone cease, while the mind persists in that state.
Likewise, there is knowledge, because of the scriptural text, "For there is no loss of the knower's consciousness," and because of the text, "A mass of consciousness."

Therefore, in the state of liberation, the self remains abiding while experiencing supreme bliss through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). As it has been said: "The self is never truly released from its own innate consciousness, that which is desired as bliss, and its eternal omnipresence and other attributes."
As for the Vārttika statement: "But one is liberated from that very karma through the exhaustion [of its cause], because of the absence of a cause;

for there is no cause for the permanence of liberation other than that which consists of non-existence," this is the view of those who maintain that liberation is bliss (*ānanda-mokṣa-vādin*), and it represents the opinion of others. //***//

Others, however, say: the statement that [the self] consists of non-existence is their own view, because it is supported by reasoning; whereas the statement regarding bliss is merely an introductory concession (*upanyāsa-mātra*) representing the view of others.
For the experience of bliss is not possible for one who is liberated due to the absence of the instruments [of perception].
If it be argued that the mind (*manas*) would exist [as such an instrument], we say no.
From the scriptural teaching on "mindlessness," it is said: "He is without mind, without breath, and without speech."
Regarding the demonstration of the absence of knowledge in the state of liberation:
as for the statement, "Indeed, there is no loss of the knower's capacity to know," that refers to the power of knowledge;
otherwise, it would imply the persistence of [actual] knowledge even during deep sleep.
And it has been stated that this consciousness would be obstructed;
moreover, its intentionality regarding power is quite clear.
