For thus it is heard in scripture: "Verily, when he does not see there, he is indeed seeing, though he does not see."

For there is no loss of the seer’s vision, because it is indestructible; yet there is not a second thing existing apart from it, distinct from it, which he might see. In the same way, other passages [should be understood]:
"Indeed, though smelling, he does not smell, for there is no loss of the smeller’s sense of smell."
There is no destruction of the hearing of the hearer,
nor is there any destruction of the touch of the toucher,

nor is there any destruction of the knowledge of the knower; in each respective case, the terms "seeing," "smelling," "hearing," and "touching" refer to those functions produced by the sense organs of the eye, nose, ear, and skin.
The [words] denote the objects of form, smell, sound, and touch, neither other objects nor the generality of consciousness;
nor do they denote these particular cognitions, nor other objects, nor the generality of consciousness;
and it is not possible for these particular cognitions to be lost in any way whatsoever during deep sleep or liberation.
For at that time, the sense organs do not exist, nor are odors and so forth perceived; and in the absence of both, those specific cognitions denoted by terms such as "hearing" cannot possibly occur.

If it is argued that just as the sun's nature as an illuminator is eternal even in the absence of objects to be illuminated, so too vision (*dṛṣṭi*) must be eternal even in the absence of the sense organs—
if this were so, it would be correct only if the word "vision" and the like denoted mere cognition (*jñāna-mātra*).
But it is not so,
because it lacks worldly consensus;
for the determination of word-meanings follows the world, not one's own whim.
For in the world, it is not said that the nose smells anything other than odor;
furthermore, even when one cognizes odor through means such as inference rather than by the nose itself, one is then said not to "smell" it.
Therefore, words such as *ghrāti* (he smells) denote specific cognitions of objects such as odor that are produced by the nose and other [senses].
Furthermore, their non-cessation does not occur in deep sleep or in liberation;
therefore, the metaphorical designation of "nose" and so forth refers only to the capacity for smelling and so forth, intended for the sake of encouragement.
This is just as in the statement, "For by that [fire] food is made," where the present tense is used metaphorically for the sake of encouragement because the capacity exists.
Therefore, even the statement that "there is no destruction of the knower or of knowledge" refers precisely to [the persistence of] capacity.
As for the argument that it is like the sun's illuminating power, what is intended by its "illuminating power"? If it is the dispelling of darkness, [then...]
That [light] is indeed constant for him, for it always dispels darkness in unobstructed locations;
but surely, if that were so, the self would hear at all times, since there is no hearing during deep sleep.
Now, if it is the production of cognition that dispels darkness in the solar regions, [then...]
But the self does not hear in this way at all times, because there is no hearing during deep sleep.
Now, if the sun's nature as a producer of cognition were its illuminating power, that would not be eternal;
therefore, it is only the capacity for that which is eternal in that case as well.
Therefore, this designation of "eternality" refers to the power of cognition.
For this is the meaning of the statement here: that which the Self does not see in deep sleep or in liberation—it does not see even though it is seeing, even though it is capable of seeing.
Indeed, there is never any loss of that power of vision which belongs to the Seer, the Self; for that [power] is indestructible.
Thus, in that state, there exists no second thing other than the Seer—neither an instrument of vision such as the activity of the eyes, nor an object of vision—by means of which seeing could occur.

Although the visible object, such as form and so forth, exists in its own nature during that state, nevertheless, "visibility"—that is, the fitness for being seen—does not exist in that state; because it is absent in that form, it is said that "the visible does not exist.
Therefore, one does not see in that state due to the deficiency of other means [of perception], and not due to a deficiency of power, for the power is never lost at any time.
The application of this principle should be understood for other statements as well.
Similarly, it is said that the non-destruction of the knower (*jñātṛ*) is precisely the non-destruction of the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*);
and here, the word "cognition" (*jñāti*) refers to inferential and other forms of knowledge, since the cognitions of the eyes and so forth have already been mentioned by their own specific names.
In this way, it should be understood that passages such as "consciousness is Brahman" and "a mass of consciousness" also have the sense of referring to *śakti*.

The Śruti itself explains this sense of *śakti*: "Having arisen from these elements as a mere mass of consciousness, one perishes after them. Thus, due to the destruction of the elements and the senses, the Self also reaches a state beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and becomes, as it were, destroyed.
"There is no perception for that deceased person who has been liberated from here.

When Yājñavalkya had spoken thus, Maitreyī raised an objection: "In this very matter, my lord has confused me; for there is a contradiction in stating both 'a mass of consciousness' and 'there is no perception.'"

The distinction is that in the sixth chapter, however, the contradiction between destruction and non-destruction will be raised. Being thus questioned, Yājñavalkya offers this resolution: "Indeed, O Maitreyī, I do not speak anything mutually contradictory. Or rather, this is sufficient for understanding: the meaning is that the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is capable of being understood in all its states; therefore, the designation 'mass of consciousness' (vijñānaghana) is intended to signify that capacity."
This has been explained.
The intention is that there is no contradiction, because even for one who possesses the capacity [to know], the absence of knowledge is possible.
And by this scriptural statement, all scriptural passages concerning omniscience are explained as having the capacity [for such knowledge] in mind.

If there were such capacity, then at that state, for what reason would there be no production of knowledge? [It would be] due to the absence of the sense organs, which are the instruments of knowledge, and the objects, which are the things to be known.
Thus it is said: "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another;
but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? and so forth.
This has already been explained previously.

Thus, when the possibility of knowing another object has been refuted due to the absence of a means of knowledge, one might suspect that the Self itself should be known in the state of liberation; anticipating this, he says:
"By what, my dear, should one know the knower? For even the Self cannot be known without a means of knowledge, since it is indeed by means of the mind that it is known.

In the state of transmigratory existence, [the self] is known; however, for one who is liberated, there is no connection with the mind. Therefore, by asking "by what means could the self be known?", the scripture clearly demonstrates the absence of self-knowledge in the liberated state, showing that only the power of cognition remains.
Consequently, liberation is devoid of connection and devoid of bliss.
The refutation of the self's nature as consisting of knowledge and bliss.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no consciousness or bliss other than the Self, but rather the Self itself is consciousness and bliss, according to the scriptural texts, "Brahman is consciousness" and "Brahman is bliss"?
And since the Self exists even in the states of deep sleep and the Fourth (turīya), how can there be an absence of consciousness and bliss? [Reply:
This is not so.

For that entity which, by its very nature, produces the manifestation of another object, and in whose presence some other object necessarily becomes manifest, is designated by the term "cognition" (vijñāna) in the world;
however, when the self exists, nothing else whatsoever necessarily becomes manifest, even though it is present.
Since no other object whatsoever is perceived in that state of deep sleep, the self is therefore not mere cognition.
But surely, even that which has the nature of producing illumination might not produce it due to the absence of auxiliary causes?
True, it does not produce it.

However, when those auxiliary causes are present, or when some other adventitious factor produced by them exists, that which is designated by the term "cognition" necessarily illuminates another object.

Likewise, the words "bliss" (āhlāda) and "the happiness of joy" (ānanda-sukha) denote the delight produced by hearing pleasant songs, embracing a beloved, the sweet taste of seeing the moon, smelling fragrant scents, and so forth;
yet the Self does not possess such a nature.

For while the nature of happiness is recognized as such in other instances of pleasure, we do not recognize it as such in the Self, which is why the designation "Bliss" (Ānanda) is used—neither a worldly nor a Vedic one.
If, at most, it were to be defined by analogy with "growth" and so forth, let it be as you wish;

however, as for the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in such expressions as "Brahman is consciousness" and "Brahman is bliss," they function by denoting only [specific] attributes (dharmamātra).
This is true.
They do not occur in abundance; however,

there are occasions when words expressing merely a quality are used for the possessor of that quality, such as "the taste is cold, sweet, unctuous, and heavy," where the word *rasa* (taste) is applied to the substance (*dravya*),
because otherwise it would be impossible for it to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "cold" and so forth.
Furthermore, in the passage "For he who knows this [taste] alone," and "That is one [measure] of the bliss of Brahman," Brahman is distinguished from bliss by means of the genitive case.

Furthermore, since at present I have no pleasure whatsoever, but rather suffering in its entirety, how could the self—which is being continuously perceived as such during the absence of pleasure and the experience of suffering—be of the nature of bliss?
Moreover, for us who accept that the self is of the nature of self-luminous bliss, there is no dispute on this point: that liberation is equivalent to deep sleep.

Only the mere persistence in following the course of *saṃsāra* differs; everything else is equal. Thus, scripture also—by stating, "These creatures go day after day to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), and day after day they return," using the term "world of Brahman" for deep sleep—shows the equality of these two states.
Furthermore, deep sleep is within the scope of our own experience, and it is evident that there is no experience of bliss therein;
therefore, liberation is devoid of bliss,
and its status as a human goal (puruṣārtha) is due solely to the cessation of suffering.

If it is argued that pleasure is not the human goal because it involves the loss of happiness—no, for in this way [it is shown that] pleasure in saṃsāra is indeed meager, and even that is [so regarded] by the wise.
Because it is accomplished through great effort, they consider it to be nothing but suffering.
Birth, death, old age, disease, and sufferings afflict human beings day after day.
Without any effort, [the body] itself falls apart into a thousand pieces due to constantly failing to perform what is prescribed and practicing what is forbidden;
such great suffering in the next world cannot be avoided even by great efforts.
That which is called pleasure, though it be indeed slight, is embraced by much suffering.
Like the pleasure derived from drinking liquor and other such things, it should be avoided by those who seek solitude.
Even though saṃsāra is of such a nature, those who are attached to it out of thirst for pleasure—
They have no qualification whatsoever for the scripture of liberation.
Those who have seen the higher and lower worlds and tremble at the cycle of existence—
they alone are indeed liberated, and not the ordinary person.
For those very great-souled ones, the human goal known as liberation (apavarga) exists.
And the authority for those wise ones lies precisely in the scripture concerning liberation;
therefore, even though liberation consists of non-existence, it is not a non-purpose of human life.
For the experience of pleasure and pain is what is designated by the term "saṃsāra."
But those who know liberation understand that liberation is the non-enjoyment of these two.
The Śruti also declares this very distinction between transmigratory existence and liberation.
Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there can be no freedom from pleasure and pain.
Indeed, neither pleasure nor pain touches one who dwells bodiless.
Those who declare the Self to be of the nature of bliss and self-luminous;
And even in that view, this much is the difference between liberation and cyclic existence.
For this Self, whose nature is bliss, shines forth even within saṃsāra.
Even in liberation, those two alone [exist]; there is nothing further for him whatsoever.
Then, at the time of saṃsāra, bliss does not manifest.
For it is not logical that a self-luminous entity should fail to manifest itself.
If that [Self] were not manifest, what else would be manifest?
If you say it is the nature of the Self, is it not indeed bliss itself?
If that [consciousness] shines forth, then bliss surely shines forth as well;
therefore, [there is no difference] between the pleasure and pain produced by objects such as sound.
It is said that liberation from cyclic existence is simply cessation;
consequently, because happiness is thereby abandoned, liberation would not possess the status of a human goal.
If this [pursuit] were for our own human purpose,
then it would be equal for you as well;
for the abandonment of pleasure and pain is achieved by further avoiding that which is non-existent and painful.
The fact that liberation is the supreme human goal is equal for both of us.
Therefore, being devoid of pleasure and pain, he remains liberated and established in his own nature.
Thus it is said.
An exposition on the nature of liberation.
"What is this 'being established in oneself'?

It means that having abandoned those qualities (dharmas) which are subject to appearance and disappearance— namely, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impressions— one abides in that which is one's own, innate nature, such as the capacity for knowledge, existence, and substantiality.

If, however, it is asserted that bliss, though non-existent during the state of saṃsāra, is produced in the state of liberation, then liberation would be impermanent due to its having an origin (*janimattva*). Furthermore, by whom could it be experienced?
For it has already been stated that self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is not possible for anything [other than consciousness itself].

Furthermore, it has been stated that experience by means of the mind is not possible because the liberated soul lacks a mind, as attested by the scriptural teaching on its "mindlessness" (*amanaskatva*).

For this very reason, the following view is also refuted: that although bliss is eternal, it is not experienced during the state of transmigratory existence because it is obscured; yet, once liberation occurs and that obscuration ceases, it is experienced by the mind.
Furthermore, the experience of the self as distinguished by happiness is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), not the mere experience of happiness;

nor is the experience of the self possible in liberation, because it has been explicitly prohibited by the Śruti itself in the words, "By what, my dear, should one know the knower? And by the Śruti, "Enough, indeed, of this for the sake of knowing," the word "knowing" (*vijñāna*) [is denied] for the liberated one.
It is impossible to maintain that consciousness [is not mentioned].
For it is not possible for this scriptural passage, nor the passage concerning the non-contact with the pleasant and unpleasant, to have any other purpose than the statement of reality.

However, it is logical that the passages which do not mention consciousness employ the metaphorical designation of consciousness precisely when there is capacity [for it], for the sake of generating interest.

In this way, even the scriptural passages concerning bliss (*ānanda*) proceed by means of a metaphorical attribution of "happiness" due to the commonality of being a human goal, for the purpose of creating interest.
And this is logical: when there is a contradiction between two statements, the determination [of the truth] is made through other means.
Here, the contradiction lies between the statement regarding bliss and the statement regarding the absence of pleasure (*priya*).
Nor can it be said that the statement regarding non-existence refers to a contingent [or adventitious] intention, while the other refers to an intrinsic intention;
for in both cases, because a general term is employed, the scope of the subject matter is absolutely identical.

Therefore, it is logical that the statement regarding bliss (*ānanda*) refers to the absence of suffering due to the force of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the other [statements] are to be taken literally.
Consequently, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the total cessation of all specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) of the self, such as pleasure, pain, and so forth.
And there is the cessation of pleasure and pain through the cessation of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);

and the cessation of merit and demerit occurs because of the contradiction posed by the experience of already arisen merits and demerits, by the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, and by the knowledge of the Self;
and because of the non-arising of those merits that are to be produced—which have their cause in the performance of optional (*kāmya*) rites—due to the non-performance of such rites.

Furthermore, since unrighteousnesses— which have their cause in the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited— are avoided through the performance of what is enjoined and the non-performance of what is prohibited,
when there is no further commencement of a body and the previous body has fallen away, one remains bodiless and becomes liberated.
The utility of the knowledge of the Self for both ritual action and liberation.
Now, is it not the case that the knowledge of the Self serves the purpose of the ritual?
True.

Furthermore, that [knowledge] serves the human goal (puruṣārtha) as well, due to the difference in its connection [to ritual action]. To begin with, the knowledge of the existence of the nature of the eternal self as distinct from the body— as expressed in the passage, "Indeed, this self is indestructible," and so forth—

is for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha) by virtue of its capacity, just like the knowledge of ritual action, because it is connected to the sacrifice through its utility for the performance of actions that have results in the next world.

Just as the study of sentences such as those concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is enjoined by the injunction of study for the purpose of producing knowledge— which serves the performance [of the rite] through its visible utility— so too, the very injunction of study prescribes that sentences such as "Indeed, this Self is indestructible" are for the purpose of producing knowledge of the Self that is useful for the performance of ritual action.

Therefore, if the distinction of the self from the body and so forth were not established with certainty by means of another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the fruit of the Upaniṣadic passages that set forth this firm distinction would be perfectly clear.
As it has been said: "Thus the author of the Commentary (Śabarasvāmin), wishing to refute nihilism, establishes the existence of the self here through reasoning."
"This awakening, which has this [truth] as its object, attains firmness through the study of the Vedānta.
Now, if it is established even by other means,
then just as when the knowledge of a sacrifice can be obtained otherwise, [only those whose nature as ritual acts is understood from Vedic sentences acquired through formal study]—
The qualification of men for ritual actions, as well as the qualification of those who have understood the reality of the Self through the Upaniṣadic statements acquired by study,
is postulated precisely by the force of the injunction to study.

As for the affirmative-sounding statements such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen," which appear at the beginning of the demonstration of the existence of the self, they serve the purpose of ensuring that—
because the subject matter about to be explained is exceedingly profound and of great utility— one might abandon indolence and grasp the meaning about to be taught with a special degree of faith.
Therefore, this knowledge, because it serves a visible purpose, is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).

Furthermore, those meditative practices (*upāsana*) that are enjoined as being associated with specific ritual procedures (*itikartavyatā*) have an invisible fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*), because they lack any visible utility within the sacrifice itself.
And this invisible fruit is of two kinds according to the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*): the form of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the form of ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*).
The fruit of prosperity is illustrated by such passages as, "He obtains all desires," and "He enjoys all desires."
The distinction is that the fruit of supreme beatitude (niḥśreyasa) consists of such statements as "he does not return again" and so forth.
The conclusion of the section [on the self] by means of the permanence of the self.

As for the suspicion that the Brāhmaṇa passage, "But this mass of consciousness, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death," teaches that consciousness belongs to the elements— that is itself refuted by the Brāhmaṇa in this very context with the words,
"O Venerable One, you have led me into the depths of delusion, for having previously declared [the self] to be ageless and immortal, you now declare it to be perishable."
Having stated the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), which is termed an objection, the resolution of the established conclusion (siddhānta) has been stated.

Having declared, "Verily, this Self is indestructible, its nature is not subject to annihilation," and having raised the doubt as to how there can then be talk of destruction, it was said that [the appearance of destruction] occurs due to contact with the *mātrās*.
By the word *mātrā*, the elements, the sense organs, and merit and demerit—which are denoted by the term "modifications" (*vikāra*)—are expressed.
This is what is meant: by the term "mass of consciousness" (vijñānaghana), there is the designation of the Self, whose intrinsic nature is the power of cognition.
For that [Self], having arisen from these elements and being liberated, perishes after them; upon the destruction of the elements, it becomes as if destroyed itself.
Indeed, while residing within the elements, it is said to perish through its own direct perception.
Therefore, in this manner, it is said that there is only the destruction of the constituents (mātrās) and not of the self (ātman); thus, there is no contradiction.
As it has been said: "The person (puruṣa) is indestructible by its own nature; as for that which is destructible," [it refers to the constituents].

Regarding the statement that "the elements and so forth, which possess their respective functions, are without perception (asaṃjñitā)," what does this "absence of perception in the elements and so forth" mean?
If it is first of all an explanation of the phrase "there is no perception after death," [then...]
That is incorrect;
for by the statement "there is no consciousness after death," it is not said that the elements and so forth lack consciousness.
Rather, by this, the absence of consciousness is stated specifically of the liberated self.

This is because the absence of consciousness is established by the passage beginning with "By the absence of that very means, who would see whom? and ending with "by what could one know the Knower of the Field?
True;
this is not its [the previous statement's] explanation.

This is the summary of the meaning of the section: Since, by the reasoning previously stated, consciousness cannot belong to the elements (*bhūta*), and it has been stated by the Brāhmaṇa as well that this is so, therefore the elements and the sense organs are insentient and lack consciousness;

rather, there is another, eternal conscious being who is capable of going to heaven, and thus there is no contradiction with perception regarding the statement, "he does not go to the heavenly world."
The Section on the Impermanence of Sound //6//
Some [hold] that it is action, because it is seen there. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.6)
Because it is impossible. // Jaimini 1.1.7 //
It is so because of the word. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.8)
And because [the cognition] occurs simultaneously in other beings. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.9)
And [the same applies] to the relationship between the original form and its modification.
And its increase [in frequency] occurs through the multiplicity of performers.
But in that case, the perception is equal.
The non-perception of an existing thing is due to the non-arrival of its objects [to the senses].
The final [element] belongs to the preparatory ritual act.
The simultaneity is like that of the sun.
The change of phoneme is not a modification [of the word].
It is for the purpose of increasing the sound.
But it must be permanent, because the act of seeing is for the sake of another.
Because [the Veda] exists simultaneously everywhere. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.19)
Because of the absence of number. (Jaimini 1.1.20)
Because of independence. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.21)
And because there is no manifestation of yoga.
And because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.23)
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Jaimini 1.1.23)
The claim that a word’s capacity to convey meaning is innate is now challenged: because a word is impermanent,
it is not possible for the innate capacity of a newly produced word to be grasped through the lineage of usage among elders.
Even if it were to convey meaning by its own nature despite not being apprehended—just like the eye and other sense organs—it would convey meaning even upon the first hearing.

Therefore, if sound were impermanent, its capacity to convey meaning would necessarily result in being produced by a person, just like the names "Devadatta" and so forth. But how, then, is sound impermanent?
Since it is perceived immediately after [the effort] while not being manifested by that effort, its being produced by it is determined, just like a jar or similar objects.
Otherwise, why would it be perceived only immediately after that and not previously?
Furthermore, because that which has been perceived vanishes instantly, its perishability is determined. Nor is the fact that it is not manifested [by the effort] unestablished.
Because manifestation is impossible;
for that [manifestation] would have to occur either through the removal of an obstacle or through a particular refinement (*saṃskāra*).
First of all, it is not the removal of an obstacle, because no obstacle is perceived.

If it is argued that stagnant winds remain covering the auditory organ and thus obstruct the perception of sound, and that sound is perceived when those winds are driven away by the internal breaths produced through effort—
then, in that case, all sounds, having reached the auditory organ and remained there, would be heard simultaneously once the obstructions have been removed.
Now, regarding the production of an embellishment (*saṃskāra*), there too it is threefold: they might produce an embellishment either of the sound, or of the auditory organ, or of both.

If it were of the sound, then because sound is unitary and all-pervading, and because an embellishment of something partless is impossible, a sound embellished by the winds located at the base of the throat would be perceived even in Pāṭaliputra;
this is what was stated [by the author] with the words, "In that case, it would be perceived by everyone," and so forth.
Even in the position that the auditory organ is refined [by sound], this very same fault applies.

If, according to the views of the followers of Kaṇāda, Kapila, or the Vedas, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) were either space (*ākāśa*), the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), or the direction (*diś*), then— because it is unitary, all-pervading, and partless—

the auditory organ would be one and the same for all persons. And since it would be refined by the articulations (*dhvani*) even of those situated in only one location, who could prevent the perception of sound by everyone?

This very point has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "In the view that space is the auditory organ" and ending with "this same direction applies to the auditory organ and so forth. And on this view, because the auditory organ is common to all sounds, even when refined for the purpose of perceiving a single sound, it would— by necessity— perceive all sounds, just as an eye opened for the purpose of seeing a jar would perceive cloth and other objects situated in the same location.
This very point has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with, "And the auditory faculty is refined all at once," and so forth.

And this same fault must be shown even regarding the previously proposed position that the auditory organ is refined (*śabda-saṃskāra-pakṣa*): for all sounds reside in the location of the ear; thus, when one [sound] is refined there, the refinement would necessarily occur for others as well.

Indeed, it is impossible to establish a distinction where some are refined and others are not among things occupying the same location and being perceivable by the same sense organ, as this is never observed in the case of jars and other such objects.
This has been stated [in the text] by the words: "This very point is to be examined," and so forth.
But in the case where both [the auditory organ and the sound] are considered to be conditioned (*saṃskāra*), all the faults [previously mentioned] for both sides should be shown collectively;
for only in that case is it logically consistent that only certain sounds are heard by certain people,
otherwise neither the restriction of the auditory organ nor that of the sound would exist.

Furthermore, the *Śābarabhāṣya* states: "Moreover, a word uttered by speakers situated in various locations is perceived simultaneously in those various locations; this is impossible for a single, eternal [entity].
In this context, "impossible for a single [entity]" is the proposition (*pratijñā*), and "of a single [entity]" is the reason (*hetu*).
For that which is eternal must be non-dependent; it is impossible for a single entity to be perceived in multiple locations simultaneously.
Now, it might be argued that necessity does not entail unity even when there is permanence;
for let the phonemes such as *ga* be many and yet permanent. To this, he says: "When there is no distinction, there is no multiplicity for that which is permanent" (*Śābarabhāṣya*).

What is meant is this: on the strength of the cognition of the qualified object called recognition, one understands the identity between the *ga* of yesterday and the *ga* of today, and thereby permanence is established.
Furthermore, there exists this non-distinctive cognition even when the letter *ga* is uttered simultaneously by various speakers; for in that case as well, no distinction in the cognition occurs.
And in the absence of such a distinction, it is impossible for an eternal entity to possess multiplicity.

For if there were multiplicity, then for you too—just as for us—the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) would lack authority, and if that recognition lacks authority, [the eternity of the word-sound cannot be established].
Permanence is untenable;
therefore, if permanence is to be admitted, unity must be accepted,
and for that which is one, perception in multiple locations is impossible.

In the *Vārttika* as well, having introduced the two points— that there is a distinction because of simultaneous perception, and that because of this distinction there is the state of being an effect— it is shown how the distinction arises from simultaneous perception by the passage beginning with "for if [the self] were not all-pervading, [they would not perceive] simultaneously," and it is likewise shown that "if [the self] were eternal, there would be a single cognition.
For the proponent of eternality does not accept that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is an error.
And so it will be said: "Moreover, if there were identity of form, then by virtue of the difference in location, it would be only the locations that are different, but not the sound.
For its eternity cannot be established through the absence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) if it lacks validity;
therefore, if it were eternal, it would have to be one, and that would contradict its being perceived in various locations."

Furthermore, because they are perceived simultaneously, there is a difference [between them]; and if there is a difference, recognition lacks authority; and if that recognition lacks authority, then due to the absence of permanence, [sound] must be an effect. This sequence is established independently.
And since impermanence is firmly established, recognition occurs through similarity, as in the case of a lamp. Therefore, sound is impermanent—this being the position reached.
The demonstration of the permanence of sound is stated as follows:
Because [sound] is observed immediately after effort, its being an effect is not certain;
for such observation is equally applicable to the position that it is manifested by that effort.
As for the question of how there can be manifestation [of sound], we reply: it is by means of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ (*śrotra*).

As for what was said—that if space (*ākāśa*) or the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) were the auditory organ, and its refinement were the cause of perception, then all persons would perceive [sound] everywhere—we reply to that: if these two were indeed the auditory organ, this [consequence] would occur.
This is a fault. Let the ear be the ear-cavity itself; since that cavity differs for each person, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
And even if space alone is the ear, it is not directly refined, but rather by means of its physical substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Consequently, although the auditory organ is one for all, nevertheless, because its physical substratum is distinct, the restriction of hearing will be established through the restriction of the respective refinements (*saṃskāra*).

Indeed, if the sense faculty were one, then even though its physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are distinct, since the faculty would be refined by the refinement of even a single base, the faculty of all persons would be refined;
consequently, there would necessarily be perception for everyone.
As it has been said: "If the sense faculty, having obtained refinement upon a single base..."
"For one who maintains that there is a single sense-faculty, there would be an awakener among all causes," [it is said].
This means for persons residing in all bodies.
To this, the reply is: "For one who maintains that there is a single sense-faculty, it would exist in the various regions of the bodies of persons."
The meaning is: "of persons existing within all bodies.
To this, the reply is: "The arising of consciousness in the bodily regions of persons is accepted [as occurring]."
"Therefore, because it is located in a different place from the primary [organ], that refinement (*saṃskṛti*) is deficient.
This is the meaning: for all persons, knowledge arises only within their own body as the locus of experience, and not elsewhere;

and this refinement of the substratum is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of sound. Furthermore, being located in the same place as the primary [organ] is a quality (*guṇa*) of the auxiliaries; therefore—

For a person residing in another body, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) located in that very body is what produces the cognition that must be accomplished within your body, not one located in another body;
for that [impression], being in a different location, would be deficient in quality due to its distance from the primary cognition.

[Objection: But surely, since the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*) is one and because its distance [from the ritual site] is the same, the difference in location is entirely irrelevant to its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the consecration (*saṃskāra*).

Just as, because the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is one, the consecrations performed for it—such as those at the time of the guest-offering (*ātithyā*)—are not prevented from being subsidiaries of the *upasad* and *agnīṣomīya* rites, so too should it be here. [Response: No;
because such a thing is not observed.
For cognition is not observed to arise for all [beings] upon a single substratum;

therefore, by the force of observation, it is determined that even a common sense-faculty produces cognition only when accompanied by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose location is identical to that of the cognition, and not otherwise. Consequently, there is no over-extension of the principle.

Nor is it necessarily the case that there is only one sense-faculty (*indriya*). Although space (*ākāśa*) is one and partless, its conjunctions with localized objects such as jars are themselves localized;

consequently, because the conjunctions with the ear-cavities (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) differ for each person, and since the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is space delimited by those [conjunctions], the established order [of auditory experience] is maintained through the distinction between the auditory faculties in their delimited forms, even though space is one in its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
In this same way, it should be understood regarding the ear, whether in relation to the portion of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) or the portion of the directions (*digbhāga*). // *//*

As for the objection that the auditory organ, once refined, would manifest all sounds simultaneously, it is replied as follows: Sounds (dhvanis), indeed, arise from contact with specific locations such as the palate and so forth; being of different types, they are produced with distinct capacities.

Consequently, only a particular sound produces a refinement (saṃskāra) conducive to a specific word-sound (śabda), not one common to all. Thus, even in the view that the refinement pertains to the sound, the restriction regarding perception is established.
It is indeed more logical to establish that only a particular sound (dhvani) manifests a particular word (śabda), and not every sound manifests every word.
Furthermore, we observe a restriction regarding manifesting agents even among things perceptible by the same sense organ; for instance, solar light manifests jars and the like, but not the stars.
The bark of the *nimba* tree merely manifests the fragrance of sandalwood and does not produce other fragrances;
therefore, there is no fault.

Nor does it follow that all people would perceive [the word] once the sound has been refined; because the articulations (dhvanis) are localized, the sound is refined only in that specific place and not everywhere.
Therefore, it is logically consistent that only one whose sense organ is in contact with the refined sound hears it, and no other.
The perception of sound in multiple locations.
And there would be a difference in location for a single entity simultaneously, as in the case of the sun.
Those who dwell in the Vindhya mountains and those who are established in Kāmarūpa.
For the sun, as it rises, is perceived by everyone in the eastern quarter of the self.
Likewise, when it sets in the western quarter, it stands above at midday.
And their front portions are split, as are those behind and above.
For these [atoms] which are being perceived, their distinctness of location is clearly evident.

Likewise, in whatever distant region the rising of the sun is seen by some, others situated in that same region see it at the same distance beyond that point; therefore, there is both difference and non-difference.
Nor should one suspect a plurality of suns, for no one perceives the sun as being distinct [in number].
Furthermore, what is the cause for perceiving the sun, which occupies only a single location, as being in various locations?
It is said: those who do not know its true location because it is situated at an extreme distance imagine a difference in location by superimposing their own proximity [upon it].
And this is quite clear.

For instance, when someone in the afternoon sees the sun at a certain distance in a particular place— thinking, "The sun is in this field, on this mountain"— and while still looking at the sun, he goes to that very place and sees it exactly as before beyond that point, it is understood from this that the sun, though standing in front of all places, appears as if it were close at hand.
Furthermore, even those mountains which occupy a small space relative to the sun appear identically to persons situated two *yojanas* away as well as to those situated three *yojanas* away;
therefore, although [the object] is a single entity, its perception in various locations is possible.
Likewise, a single face is seen simultaneously in various mirrors.
Is it not the case that a reflection, which is a distinct entity, is seen there? No;
because it does not exist and because it is not perceived, for another material object cannot exist within a material object.

Furthermore, when water contained in a shallow bowl is held above the ground at the height of a navel, and one places one's face at a distance of one *aratni* above it, people standing at the side do not perceive any reflection of the face at a depth of one *aratni* beneath the water, nor do they see anything in that location. Therefore, since the object called a "reflection" is refuted by the non-perception of what ought to be perceived, it cannot be accepted.
Consequently, it is logical that the visual ray, struck back by the light of the mirror and by the water, perceives [the object] after turning back.
Therefore, the perception [of sound] in various locations is inconclusive; it does not prove the multiplicity of sound.
[Objection: Surely, the perception of sound in various locations is justified by the superimposition of the proximity of the sun; but how can this be so for sound?

[Reply: Because it is omnipresent—for sound is indeed omnipresent, and being manifested in its own respective locations by articulations (*dhvani*) located in different places, it appears as if it were in those different locations.

For it is accepted on the strength of observation that articulations, even though they reach the location of the auditory organ, manifest the sound while making the sound appear as if it were at their own place of origin.
Now, the auditory organ functions by reaching its object;
yet the place where the sound is produced is not reached by the auditory organ. How, then, can that place be perceived by the auditory organ?
And if it is not perceived, how can there be a perception of the sound as qualified by that place?
It is said: this cognition of sound as qualified by direction does not arise from the auditory organ itself;
rather, although the auditory organ perceives the sound situated in its own location, it does not perceive it as qualified by direction, but only in its essential form.
However, the sounds (dhvanis) that have arrived from a particular direction cause the sound to be perceived as qualified by that direction.
For that direction, having reached the ear, can be grasped by the auditory organ;

even though direction is not independently graspable by the ear, nevertheless, when sound is being grasped, it is grasped by all the sense organs as a qualifier of that [sound], and likewise when their respective objects are being grasped, it is grasped as a qualifier of those objects.
Consequently, the apprehension of a specific [object], namely that "the sound is in this direction," is thus established.
